Monday 2ist July

0020. We cleared the harbour end headed for Dungeness, having spent three hours of a fair tile in a fruitless but necessary operation.

0135. We were vack where we had to break off, and once again on looking astern for traffic I spotted flares in the same position. However, this time they were three green flares and meant that the coastguards were standing by ready to assist anyone coming ashore at that position.

0400. Found us just off Dungeness Point as dawn was making the eastern horizon visible,

0415. Clear of Dungeness, moderate swell, good visibility, wind SW 2-3. Set 255 deg. on the grid compass for Beachy Head.

0500. Frances and the dog turned in after coffee and biscuits. Full daylight, visibility 10 miles, but signs of fog to the south of us,

Started using the Seafix D.F. radio, and was Jelighted to hear the light programme giving reports of the American moon landing.

Soon we were in lense fog and had to shut down to three knots for safety, anxious about collisions, despite having edged well inshore of the direct line between headlands.

0530, Came into a clear patch and sot a bearing of a Headland with cliffs. Hastings or Fairlight. The D.R. position was marked up every hour.

0900. Still patchy, occasional clearances showed cliffs and coastline about 4 miles N of us. Set sail, filled petrol tank and headed 330 deg. to close the coast. I was not k-en to cross the Royal Sovereign shoals. Had a delicious fried breakfast.

0930. Obtained a good fix at 4 miles S. of Bexhill.

1030. I turned in leaving Frances and the children to tack westwards in fair visibility and with sure knowledge of our position.

1145. Prances called me on deck again as we were approaching more fog. Fortunately it did not really clamp down as it had earlier on.

1220. We were almost stopped by strong tide, so the engine was started and motor sailed round Beachy Head, which we cleared at 1430, stopped the engine once clear of the tide. The stretch from Beachy Head to Newhaven was made on the port tack with the old boat striding over the long swell and going like a train.

1600. Entered the outer harbour and dropped sail. Quite literally! The stopper at the base of the main track had turned and as I freed the haliiard the sail ran down and out of the track, all over the decks. Replacing the sail and stowing allowed time for the "Falaise" to enter, then we got clearance and in we went.

1720. Alongside the fuel pontoon we paid 7s. Od. harbour dues and took on 12 gallons of Petrol and six gallons of water. I took the children and dog for a walk on dry land, the latter being delighted at finding grass, the last was at Stansgate! We walked round the marina and up to the coast guard cottages where I gave full details of our incident.

LADY ANNE'S SUMMER CRUISE

Thursday 7th August

'Freedom' left on her homeward voyage, taking with her memories of a very happy
time spent in lots of "old familiar places" under the finest continuous spell of Sunny weather I can remember. :

We spent a lazy day on the beach, but the spell was broken. The return part of the voyage was now imminent and I was itching to get going whilst the weather held fair. Bembridge is a very shallow harbour and the entrance channel all but dried out, Gonsequently we should have tO leave within two hours of high
water. 5

Friday 8th August

“The forecast was NE-E 4, good; fair. The morning breeze seemed firmer than of late, and if it followed:
the same pattern of freshening during the day we were in for a rough ride.

O800. All was stowed, the dinghy lashed on deck, kedge retrieved from the beach, a good meal inside us and we were homeward bound.

We left under’ engine, but on getting outside, where it was blowing about 5 by the number of white horses, I decided to stay under engine and plug away to the Owers Lightvessel and then close reach to Newhaven. It was very rough and wet, just keeping one's balance was a major effort. The steep seas were short enough to badly hamper Lady Anne and progress was pretty slow.

1000. Alongside” the Nab Tower, at this rate ETA Owers was 1300, and it seemed
that we would not be able to lay Newhaven from there. e children, despite their medicine, were showing signs of distress and I was not keen to plug away to windward for ‘he whole leg singlehanded.
1030. Decided to turn back, set headsail, stopped engine and ran back to Spithead. By this time Bembridge-entrance was too shoal.

We decided to have a day out and sail to Cowes, On the way we passed the Malcolm Millar beating out of Spithead, the SS 'United States’ passed us about 300 yards off, and then we passed ‘Queen Blizabeth 2' at about a quarter of a mile. These big ships made very little wash and no noise and. present a grand spectacle on a sunny day. The children also found the large number of hovercraft ferrics absorbing, although to my ear the noise level was appaling. May we long keep them out of the Blackwater! In the evening we had a grandstand view of the traditional Cowes fireworks much to Fiona's delight.

Saturday

Funny wet stuff fell out of a grey sky on and off all day, the coachroof leaked, (+00 much sun), we had the dinghy on deck and the children could not go ashore. It was blowing hard most of the day, but did moderate in the evening. The forecast for was SE3- 6, thundery showers, poor, fog patches, Not so good.

Sunday 10th August
_ One week left. We missed the early forecast, but the weather seemed to have settled fair again. The midday forecast gave us variable 3 fair, with moderate visibility. .

1345. We were under way again bound for Newhaven.° “The breeze was fitful and we .

did not make sail until we were well past Ryde. +

1500. I turned in below and managed to doze off for nearly two hours.
1700. ‘Frances was at the helm, taking us fairly close.
to the Nab when suddenly it let out a VERY LARGE HOOT. There was a slight haze, and a liner about 3 miles off was changing course.

Frances took this hoot as a personal criticism by this concrete behemoth, -and felt there was injustice in the world of seafarers. Why had it done it? What did it mean? The skipper was roused and mumbled somtething technical about fog in the western approaches, but really it was not foggy. Once started these things catch on, and soon we could hear the moan of the Owers Lightvessel off ahead of us.

- 1930. ‘We had to motor the last mile to the Owers as the wind had died completely,
leaving the sea like a great heaving mirror. The wind did not pick up again that night, and shortly after sunset I handed the sails.

Monday.

Wednesday.

By departing Newhaven at the correct time one can carry the flood up to nea Hastings, where the tidal streams change direction, then the ebb will also carry? you to the east. Hence by planning to be at Hastings or Rye about an hour after

CONCLUSIONS

We Had achieved the object of our cruise, by getting to and from the Solent, and in successfully meeting up with Freedom,

The engine was used far more than we expected, although to be fair we had headwinds for all but our first mornings sail. It was quite uncanny how the Easterly wind swung round to the N.East when we could at last use an easterly for our last leg homeward.

The catering had panned ut very well, 2 crates (36 pints) of Long Life milk had been consumed, 7lbs. of tinned butter and 1 gallon of orange squash. Occasional fresh meat, fruit, eggs and veg. supplemented our stores, the only regular demand being for fresh bread.

After a.few days we had all settled down to-live in the confines of a boat, and I was surprised how readily we fell into the new routine.

We lost the boathook overboard, and one warp disappeared. Extra fenders and one more long warp would have been handy.. Also I feel that the seven gallon fuel tank is not sufficient, as we often had to refuel from cans. —

Now we are laying up, but already we are planning to take Lady Many to Holland for next summer's cruise. She did us proud this year, and we thank her.

FOR ENTHUSIASTIC DINGHY S..ILORS

Are you still locking for the pacemaker amongst dinghies?. Well now youtve found it, the HORNET! This is the modern fast racing dinghy that achieves its enviable performance from sheer efficiency, not by brute force.

The option:
of sliding seat or trapeze permitted to the Hornet Class only, enables ever lightweights or girls to compete on even terms with good chances of success.

The Hornet is 2 boat for the individualist too, unlike many other classes, ‘the Hornet has freedom for the development of original ideas, within a basic one design concept of hull shape and sail plan. This means that one can ‘ Gesign a deck layout to suit your own ideas for efficiency and comfort, :nd
also try new arrangements for sail control etc.... without the fear of
breaking class rules. _

One of the most recent developments is the introduction of spinnaker (yy chutes which provide a nearer foolproof system of spinnaker handling. The Chute houses the spinnaker when not in use and allows hoisting and lowering without the crew having to go on 2 foredeck excursion, the latter has been known to end in involuntary bathing!

So be an individualist and enjoy your Sailing by joining the Hornet
Class.

THIS MONTH'S SATLING
AT STANSGATE

April 18th and 19th sees the continuation of the a Points, and
the Spring Points races as outlined last month.

On Saturday, April 25th is the first Pursuit Race. In this event everyone starts from the shore at staggered intervals, the slower classes first. The staggered start times are calculated so that, theoretically, everyone should cross the finishing line together at a certain time. The .
Race Officer ends the race as near to, this time as possible, at the mark er} which the leading boat is about to round. The final positions are then the, finishing order of the boats participating. This race can be quite exciting as you know your position as you. approach. the finishing line, and: can manoeuvre to defend or improve it.

On the following morning, the 26th, is the first of the Ladies Points races. This year, for the first time, there will be a series of 5 races for the Ladies Cup. (Ladies must helm but not necessarily crew). If all the races are sailed points from three will count.

The trophy is an elegant little silver cup presented to the Club by Queenie Hallum, our Vice-Presi dent's. wife. -In the afternoon the first of the six Cadet Points races will be sailed. This series is for any type of dinghy, and any crew, the helmsman only must be a cadet member of the Club (over 10 and under 18 years on the lst em dee

The Cup for this devies was presented to the Club by Eric Payne, another of our Vice-Presidents. acne eh acer a

We are visited by a team from the Ariel Sailing Club on May 2nd. This is the sailing section of the B.B.Cts. Sports and Social Club. The home event will be sailed in Enterprises. This is our longest standing team fixture in
which we compete for the Twin Flags sneony - a little silver mast flying
both Club burgees.

For those not familiar a team racing, each Club usually enters three boats, and the team scores by their boats final positions. There is often a . lot of tactical movement to slow down the opponents, and allow one's own team mates to sail through. Each Club is given a match point for each race won, that is, two races at home and two away, only in the event of a tie do “Overall boat points, for each Club, get taken into account.

The Spring Points series continues on May Srd. On May 9th is another Ssingle-handed dinghy Handicap Race, while the Cruisers meet on the River ‘Roache. The following day, May 10th, sees the second Cadet ods race in the morning and the Ladies Points in the afternoon. * .

Now that most of the dinghy registraticns have been received, it has been possible to allocate the majority of berths. In most cases these are the same as last year, however, as there are quite a number of new inembers, several new dinghies complete and some which have changed owners, : there are a few Changes. In consequence, anyone whose berth is not shown on the ‘current chart displayed outside the DEBDEOESS) is requested as temporary, measure, to use Rows X & Y.

There are a few points which, if observed, can make things more comfortable

for all who use the area.

1. Keep the grass short and tidy around your berth.

z- Leave the gangways clear for people to move in or out by not using them for rigging, repair work or drying of sails.

3. Unrigged masts are better stowed behind your dinghy and not left

An Enterprising Editor, who shall remain nameless, said, “Write something different; something rude even’. RESCUE LAUNCHES

. At a time when we are anxious to recruit and train people to man the:
rescue launches, prospective helpers may find it useful to read the Re
"Suggestions and Advice to Skippers and Crews of Rescue Taunches', in the: |
Publication YR3/69, as follows:- :

The first responsibility of the rescue launches-is the safety of the helmsmen and crews, and they should not return to harbour until all competitors have fini shed; ‘but if the crew of a capsized boat is yee di stressed, points to be born in mind are as follows:-

(a) The boats will not sink and there is no hurry. Avoidance of damage to
hull and mast is an important consideration.

(b) The crew should lower sails, right the boat and collect floating gear
before boarding the rescue launch.

(c) Once the boat is righted, the stem” :should be lifted as high as
Beet ue to empty Mates

(do) Gace can shen get into the boat, finish bailing, and, 2
rule, sail home under reefed sail or foresail only. |

(e) Once one boat has been emptied, her crew can manage while another
is assisted.

“ey! Buekets and spare bailers should be carried in the rescue launches,
(g) In rough or cold weter it may not be possible for the crew of the
boat to lower sails. In this case, the crew should be taken on board the rescue launch,.. The crew of the rescue launch should then get hold of the mast head of the boat, unshackle the head of the - mainsail, then work down the mast and unshackle the head of the jib; then work down the forestay while righting the boat, so ending up: with the: boat upright and held by the bow. _ CRUISER MEETING

On Thursday, April 16th, members were given a really magnificent evening at the M.A.S.C., uhen John Todds, despite his recent activities in the U.S.A., still managed to find time to organise a very full programme of matters relating to cruising, for a large and appreciative audience.

Firstly, Dr. Woods told us about his cruise to Friesland in his Snapdragon cruiser, showing us some delightful colour slides taken in the Dutch canals, and of his family life on board. Then our old friend, Rod Baxter, who has been with us from the early days of the barge MAMGU, told us, with the help of diagrams and the blackboard, about a cruiser he was building, which he hoped would incorporate many of the good” features he had gleaned during his not inconsiderable experience of sailing. “We had some difficulty in stopping him, and I am sure he would have continued until midnight, but we were anxious to have an interval for refreshments, during© which John had thoughtfully laid on some tasty sandwiches £3

/ Although it was now well after 10 pm, Valter Standing then told us about his cruise to Cherbourg, and the Channel’ Islands, in his magnificent steel cruiser JONELLE. In spite of the hazards of his navigation between the rocks into the harbours (which would have made some of us with less substantial hulls shudder) he still had the temerity to enter for a race during his stay at Guernsey!

ie different from an English Sunday; the main post office was open for business, although obviously at s reduced tempo. An oxificial at a special switchboard obtained the call to England and then politely indicated the telephone booth I was to use.

Back to the Club for a pre-lunch drink, But first the immigration officer accompanied by a heavily armed policeman. Passports? Yes. Ships papers? Ah, there was a difficulty. The R.Y.A. The next days, encouraged by a force 5-6 N. to N.W. wind, we sampled the delights of Ostend and chatted and drank with all our friends and acquain- tances from the Maldon River. It seemed that half the boats on the Blackwater were visiting the Continent at the same time ss us. There was only one :

COMMODORE COMMENTS ON REGATTA

Phew! its over, and what a show! What a success! What a credit to our Club!

Strains and stresses there were many, but "the few survived against all adversity including broken water mains, severed electric cables and other difficulties which might embarrass if mentioned,

To those of you who gave your time, services and/or assistance, however large or small the part you played, I would like to- say .on behalf of those who either took part, looked on or just had something é¢lee to
do - Thank you! and again Thank you! ters SER ;

Those of yOu who did not stay to learn of the official results will be pleased to know that the Club was thanked by the Visitors for the wonderful weekend of sailing which they sharéd with us. I am sure that the results proved the value of the competition which they gave us.
Indeed the Stansgate weather persisted and supplied the whole sailing mixture of flat, good and robust conditions which always seem to appear at Regatta time.

“One hundred and cighty Entries and someone said two hundred next
yeart!!

I won't repeat what someone else said, but, its something that needs to be said and possibly.at the Annual General Meeting of the Club when the Membership should be asked to consider the assistance needed by the Officers and Committee if we are ever to stage another Regatta on the'° lines of that so recently accomplished. :

Fair comment? With another large event a few weeks ahead of us new helpers must be found and the amount of new help needed must not be under estimated if we are to have another success.

Thanks for listening -

Now H.E.L.P.

Stan Campbell and I have each had a look at most of the moorings from B row inshore and we are agreed that the general state is very poor. ‘Chain is often badly worn, swivels are worn and seized up, and where the gear is in good order the shackles are often unwired and too small for the job.

There is a further hazard for the moorings on B row outwards, namely severe pitting of the chain. Last year_one boat went adrift due to the chain having parted. The reason was that although the chain was only a year 014d, it had been scraped across the bottom by wind and tide. The ebrasive action of the shingle exposes fresh metal and the result is very severe local pittine and corrosion.

Bearing this in mind I inspected the lower end of my own A row mooring at the end of May this year. I had been confident that with new chain at Easter 1969 my tackle would be in excellent condition, particularly as I had used chain 50% thicker than the club moorings sheet recommends.

me

I was most disturbed find that it was nowhere near as good as I expected, and that it will have to be discarded at the end of this summer, The damaged area is the lower end of the scope, and the centre portion of the bridle. My swivel is*not seized nor is the pin worn, but:there are signs of pitting onthe body where ithas touched the bottom.» I have been warned, you have been warned: .

Another place where trouble can occur is on-the connection between a large buoy and the chain. Some buoys have the lower ring swivelling, and the swivel is held by 2 welded nut which is not always-as strong as it should be. The answer here is to follow our cruiser captain's example and secure your buat

by chain, to the top of the scope chain, Do not rely on a single rope from deck t» the top of the buoy, a short length of new galvanised chain: will not stain the decks and will outlast any form of rope.

Tuesday 1st July

From log:

Three miles in thirty minutes with a light, force 1-2 wind, some tide!

Later the land breeze dies away and after a half hour or so of calm and fitful catspaws the breeze settled down in the West about force 2. A wide berth was given to Zeebrugge and we reached Ostend at midday. The next two days, Wednesday and Thursday were spent in similar fashion tide-hopping from port to port during the mornings. Dunkirk, then Calais, - each day was a little more hazy with a little less wind. Contrary to expectation we found Dunkirk yacht haven a pleasant little place although the town is rather mean and dirty. At least around the dock area.

At Calais we picked up a mooring in the Event Porte, until high water, when the lock gates and road bridge open to allow passage to the very quiet and clean Bassin de l'Ouest, where on the northern side the new and very pleasant club-house of the Yacht Club is situated. The club harbour-master speaks excellent English and the charges are not too unreasonable.

A warning however - the water is suspect. We emptied, cleaned and refilled our containers from the club stand pipe only to find after two days a growth of green slime around the neck of the bottles. We emptied them in Ramsgate harbour! Others, we found when discussing it, have had the same experience.

Two days were spent lazing on the beach, sampling the excellent mussels and watching dinghy racing near the shore.

SAIL SETTING

At about lunch time on a very warm Sunday, a group gathered at one end of the hard, around Mr. Donald Forbes of Musto and Hyde, Sailmakers.

His talk opened with a statement of priorities: Sails are the equivalent of an engine, the mast and rigging merely support the sails, and the hull is to keep your feet dry!

Ustng an Enterprise as a demonstration model, Mr. Forbes showed us various jib settings for various weathers, tight leach, loose foot for light winds (cone effect), and loose leach and tight foot for heavy winds. The latter setting is required so that the leach goes away at the top and does'nt backwind the main. On the Enterprise used, the sliding track needed to be fixed diagonally across the side decks a few inches aft of the shrouds, set about 3-4 inches further back on the outside, end than the inner end.

The mainsail settings were also clearly described, including the order
of
setting. .

1. Pull mainsail up to black band.
2e Pull out foot of sail by means of the clew outhaul until the sail is
a nice full’ shape - further in than you think.
Se Pull dow kicking strap when afloat and close hauled.
4, Adjust Cunningham hole setting until the creases going up and back from the mast disappear.
5. Setting of track width at the stern depends on wind - in light wind it
may be central. This keeps the leach tight as the sail is pulled down, A wider setting allows the main to be held down,- but the leach can go- away at the top to reduce heeling in heavy a

The general rules were:~ Strong wind flat sea, everything tight. — Strong tee wind lumpy sea, baggy sails and don't try sailing too close to the wind. Keep . ‘sailing fast. In a light wind keep everything baggy and full. seek

Another general. rule was that at any time during 2 race you are pulling - in the. mainsheet and stretching the leach, you-should also pull down the Cunningham to stretch the luff as well. In this way there are no peculiar stresses in the sail. Each time you let out the mainsheet, the Cunningham
should also be lct out. 7 |

Spreaders

Spreaders are designed to keep the mast straight laterally whilst allowing a limited amount of bend fore and aft. Spreaders allow a thinner section of mast to be carried than would otherwise have been possible. It appears that the shroud should'nt be dead straight from hounds to chain plates but they should be pushed about 2" forward by the spreader in anything up .to hard winds, when any restriction should be removed to allow a straight can

Bailing is almost impossible, even providing there isa bailer or it has not been lost through insecure fitting ete. Adequate and securely fitted bouyancy and bailers are essential for the safety of both yourself and others. Observe the M.S.C. and Class Associations' Rules and Recommendations. Fit extra bouyancy in the bows where it greatly assists both alongside and astern towing.

"I would like to support Ian piedn-his plea for more adequate moorings and in particular for regular inspection. Last year my own boat went adrift
2 chain only 9 months old.

inspite of having a riding scope of I was appalled at the condition when I inspected it orter lifting it at the end of last year. A great number of us tend to use black chain which is only too frequently lift chain. This seems to explain the peculiarity that the surface of the links breaks up into irregular lumps. I have never known this happ en with galvanised
chain and can only assume that this is because the material from which lift chain is made is a harder steel, more prone to corrosion. Similarly, shackles used for lifting gear seem to corrode more than galvanised shackles used for
rigging.

Finally, may L.offer my congratulations to the Commodore and those responsible for what was a most successful regatta. I was unfortunately unable to be there as I was cruising by the coast, but from the result sheets and what I have heard, it was quite an affair. I know from experience the amount of sheer hard wore that goes into these events!
Terry Hallam.

Team racing events against the up river clubs have been a complete failure _ this year. Both races against the Maldon Y.C. have been cancelled,.and ag far as I'ecan determine the situation will not improve for the 1971 season.

~--=The Mulberry Trophy attracted 49 boats to Thorpe Bay Y.C. over the weekend 19-20th September.

Conditions were very light, the last race on Sunday being cancelled because of the lack of wind. The only Marconi boat present was 7552, and she finished 3lst, llth, and 7th, to gain 10th position overall. The winning boat sailed by P. Connolly came from Chase S.C.

Limited swing spreaders were noted on some of the boats in attendance. Leigh-on-Sea S.C. are running 2a winter series consisting of 9 races commencing on the 31st October, and finishing with the BressMonkey race on the

geries. Tony and I will enter 7532 and subject to a rapid and successful. paint job Dave Draper will enter Gunga Din (possibly renamed Eskimo Nell).

1970 HORNET NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIPS

Thorpe Bay Yacht Club were chosen as the Host Club to run the 15th Hornet National Championships, “confirming the-Club as one of the premier Clubs on the East Coast, and confirming the Hornet as a thoroughbred class with a phenominal rate of development” (" Yachts and Yachting Sept. 70 issue}.

' The total entry was seventy boats, this was up on last years: entry, we were TORE by no less than five Marconi boats.

Thorpe Bay is a fine place to sail from, and the Club Peeliveies were excellent, but unfortunately the Championship was dogged by the most varied of weather Conse Peas
SUNDAY:-- The practice race was cancelled due to gale force winds, although
two boats ventured out to give the press photographers something to Due in the papers.

MONDAY: Race was postponed and taken forward toTuesday due to gale force
winds. aces es

TUESDAY: Morning lst race, very little wind, first beat leg, the leaders
2 mins, ahead at the windward mark only to experience an 180 shirt WW and have the rest of the fleet catch up by running under spinnices up
the beat leg of the course, whilst they beat down the reach leg. |
Following this the leaders sail into a big hole and the fleet gleefully sails right round them.. !

These conditions were to become typical for the whole week, put spirits were not dampened. The Social organisation was well up to Hornet standards, and Southend gave us a fine Civic Reception, with free eats, drinks, and mod music, in their new super Civic Suite, Other items in the Social programme were as follows:- free Bar-B-Que, free Barrel of beer! to the chap who could bring it
back from the Mulberry harbour wreck at low tide, 10 Pin Bowling Champs. ctc...-.

Midst the plush opulence and polished plastic of the M.A.S.C. Committe room, the Fleet met to discuss its past and future activities. Articulstc mumblings went on until about half past Doom Watch hour, and the following is 2 condensed report on our deliberations.

Sailing Past.

Generally regarded as rather glorious.

Sailing Future.

It was agreed that the Spring and Summer Points Series were sucessful, should continue unchanged. Despite the rather poor showing in the Saturday Points Series members felt that it should continue, and some promised support for '71'., Midweek racing was also considered a must for next season.

Cruising. Two dates to appear in the programme, one up river venue and cic down river (See Gunga Drapers' write up "G.P.70" in this issue). Thoso cruises will be organised only so far as the date&start time are concerned.
Where to gO will be decided on the spot, on the day.
im

Inter-Club Racing ow
Maldon/Mearconi Team Race. We will try to arrange a team event with the Maldon Y.C., arrangements as before, iece 2 races at home and 2 away.

Osea/Marconi Team Race. It was decided to pursue last years policy 2nd arrange an event against Osea S.C.

Stone/Marconi Event. We will not be team racing against Stone S.C. this year. Instead we will have a type of “invitation points” series. On certain dates we will invite Stone to participate in our points races, and they will offer a reciprocal invitation to us. Each club will extract from the result points for its own series of races; each race being two races in One. There will be no formal prize offered to the winner of the invitation points, the idea is to provide a change of opposition and a chance to meet other C.P. sailors. Unlike team racing this will not be limited to 3 boats on each side - everyone can have a go.

Various types felt that we might encourage more participants in our races if we made the courses more interesting. “Interesting” in this case being something like a figure of eight course round the two islands. Anything like this would of course have to be arranged on the day, and I have requested that certain dates in the Yearbook are marked with an asterisk. On these occasions we will arrange our own courses in consultation with the race officer of the day.

Courses were further discussed with an .eye to handicap points series (Heolmsman of the Year). Basically the argument was this. If a spinnaker carrying boat is to sail down to her handicap number, then she must be raced on a course which permits the correct amount of spinnaker work. Three out of four classes sailed within the club carry spinnakers.

Taking an Olympic type course cs the "right course" the ratio of boating, reaching and running approximates to 1:1:1/3. It is very rare that this stcto of affairs exists with our present selection of courses.

It is not difficult to arrange courses with the 1:1:1/5 ratio. I have devised some for all the main wind directions and submitted them to the committee for consideration.

That, apart from a few swift halves, ended the meeting.

Racing

Racing has improved tremendously in quality, if not in entries. In 1969 racing tended to bs processional, with Norman Palmer usually clear ahead, and occasional place swapping at a respectful distance behind him, although he was beaten outside the Points Series.

1970 in contrast, saw frequent place changing in every event. In some races each entrant was at the front for a time. It is no longer possible to make mistakes and get away with it. For example, in the last 2 races in the Summer Points, one boat made one error in the morning race and one error in the
afternoon race - resulting in 3rd in the series instead of lst.

As a direct result of the keener competition, spinnaker techniques have greatly improved. Now more regard is paid to wind direction and less to Wind strength. Some have used the beast in every race this year when the wind has been abaft the beam. si ;

HOW .TO GET THE BEST OUT OF YOUR SATIS

Last June, Donald Forbes from the famous firm of sailmakers, Musto and Hyde of Rayleigh, paid a visit to our club at Stansgate and we spent a most interesting and instructive day, with plenty of practical demonstration, learning how to get the best out of our sails.

In the July issue of Navigans, Eleanor Witter wrote a most lucid and detailed account of the various points discussed and members are urged to male a further study of this article before embarking on next season's racing and to read it in conjunction with this less adequate description.

During Donald Forbes' visit to Stansgate he dropped the hint that he would be willing to talk to us about sails during our winter lecture programme, so our social secretary, Avril Stevens duly arranged this and the meeting was held at the main M.A.S.C. hall on February 19th.

We spertt a most interesting evening with a real dinghy completely rigged on the stage to enable Mr. Forbes to demonstrate as his talk proceeded. Some cruiser owners raised various points concerning sails from their point of view, as Opposed to the main dinghy coverage.

At one stage in the lecture when Mr. Forbes asked if anyone used spreaders, some amusement was caused when Eric Payne rushed forward carrying an enormous spreader attached to a very ample stainless steel shroud from his Atalanta cruiser, which up to that point, had been discreetly hidden behind the stage and had been brought to the meeting for another purpose altogether.

It was a most enjoyable evening, again with the attendance around the 100 mark, and questions continued to be answered until a late hour and we are most grateful to Donald Forbes for giving up his time so freely on our account. Our thanks are due to Avril Stevens for organising the meeting so
efficiently - to Julian Bigden for lending his Enterprise for the demonstration -
+o Nick Tovey for lending his sails and to the other members who went to the trouble of bringing their sails and dinghies to the club in reserve.

‘Our chairman for the evening was Vice-President Eric Payne and the vote of thanks to the speaker was proposed by our Rear-Commodore, John Witter.

TO THE WESTERN ISLES VIA THE CALEDONIAN CANAL, 1970

DR. DONALD Mc KENDRICK

For our summer holiday we usually tow to the Mediterranean but after repeated persuasion from friends we’ decided to join them this year in the Western Isles. With the Forth and Clyde canal closed it is quite a long haul from the Hast coast so I arranged to use one weekend prior to our holiday proper to knock off the first hundred miles.

The tJayess' is a Snapdragon 27 and although bearing the official number 2 she was in fact the first one built and appeared at the Boat Show in January. She had already proved herself during a gale in our shakedown cruise in March and later during a rough passage to Holland at Whitsun. She has an Albin 12 H-P. auxiliary with the usual navigation equipment which includes a Mercia electronic log. This has the great advantage of being able to mount the speedo head in the cockpit and the log by the chart table. There are six berths and three or four can cruise in comfort for prolonged periods.

On Friday July the 3rd three of us arrived at a cold ad blustery Stansgate for the first leg to Wells. I had two of my normal crew with me for this hop - my son-in-law Peter and an old friend Michael. Both would have liked to crew the whole way to Inverness but time would not allow. Peter and my daughter were to spend a week with us later in the Western Isles.

We quickly got the life-raft on deck in its position at the foot of the mast and were under way by 1400 hours, deflating the 10 ft Avon as-we went as we had already lost a valuable part of a spring ebb. The wind was NWS and we reached Clacton before the tide turned and the wind fell light. We had an uneventful = motor-sail past the Cork L.V. and Orford Ness, being off Lowestoft by dawn. I w decided to close the shore inside Corton sands to cheat the tide and then went below for my first sleep only to be woken in an hour by a change of motion. A quick look at the Seafarer showed we were in 10 feet instead of 4 fathoms, having come a cable or so too far off-shore. The tide turned again off Cromer. In the morning the wind had backed to the west and had given us a good sail, in fact our progress had been so good that I decided we could easily make Wells on the evening tide instead of waiting for Sunday morning as originally planned. Our course during the afternoon turned more and mare to port until the wind was on the nose and we finally motor-sailed the last five miles to the entrance. What a help Blakeney Church is in an otherwise featureless landscape. Frequent bearings gave us repeatedly good position lines which combined with echo soundings confirmed our dead reckoning. This was particularly important <s off Sheringham the speedo, which had developed a tendency to be rather optimistic over 6 knots slowed unaccountably and then dropped to zero as I was watching it. The diagnosis of the sensor unit rod falling off was easily confirmed by withdrawing the unit. A spare rod only takes a moment to fit but inserting it at sea can mean 2 or 3 pints of water in a locker so I decided to wait till we act to Wells as we would be drying out during the night. Vv

We picked up the Wells buoy at 1710 - ten minutes later than estimated.
Like so many offshore harbour entrance buoys this seemed unnecessarily small and difficult to see and we were certainly within a mile of it before we were sure it was what we were looking for. Although the wind of 34 against the tide was only producing a gentle chop outside the breakers at the entrance certainly gave promise of what it could do here in a blow. The channel is not well buoyed for strangers. We followed the prescribed route closely, running in under main alone, but fluctuated from 15 to 3 feet and grounded twice, the first time well within the channel. The second time the bow was hard aground
so wo dropped the hook - but it would'nt go - half the shank was above water!
When I discovered that the stern was in 20 feet a quick burst astern put us back in the 4 knot flood to reach the quay without further trouble. There we were greeted officially and kindly by the HM. Mr. Taylor, berthed alongside and made comfortable for the night. We had an excellent chicken ghoulash, dining on a peaceful summer evening on our cockpit table before turning ii. We slept well.

/continued.

On Sunday morning The H.M. led us to a mooring as arranged taking us ashore in his launch from where we returned to London by car. I was very satisfied. 138 miles in the first 27 hours seemed to be a good omen for our holiday and we had a good northing achieved.

Friday, 10th July.

I arrived back in Wells at 1800 hours with my new crew, George, the .s&inest psychiatrist in the business, and a delight to have aboard any yacht, and John, a young engineer who had been introduced to me by 4 mutual friend. John has a boat of his own in the Solent but is always keen to increase his experience. He proved to be a most pleasant and extremely competent seamar, and I. ceculd not have hada better or happicr crew. There was the added bonus that both of them have cast-iron stomachs and as I have never (yet) been sick in a small boat we felt fairly confident on that score.

The
tJayess' was hard aground on the sands as the H.M. had forgotten to bring her alongside as: promised. A friendly yachtsman tock us over the water in his dinghy and we took advantage of sur unexpected ground to scrub the bottom. We motored to the quey at 2300 hours. There is about 2 ft. alongside at icw water so we sat comfortably on our twin keels for an hour while we slept.

We cast off at 0920 on Saturday llth and were soon at the outer Wells —
buoy. It was a glorious warm sunny day and with a 3-4 W we made 55 - 6 knots
f% under genoa and main. The Humber L.V. was abeam at 2100 hours - 52 miles on
the log in just under 12 hours of sailing. The wind increased a bit during my watch so the working jib replaced the genoa. When John took over it was Si 6 and a gale warning on the 0640 forecast came as no surprise; so we o>, altered course for Bridlington. With four rolls now we were still béing over-pressed as the wind got stronger but lazily we spilt the excess instead of tucking in more reefs 28 we were near to shelter. We tied up alongside 2 fisherman, 22 hours out of Wells with 101 miles on the clock. The H.M. greeted us during our bacon and eggs and moved us to a drying berth alongside the quey where we were comfortable enough. The Yacht Club made us very welcome end we
, wallowed
in their simply enormous baths. Gales persisted and kept the rescue services busy. One yacht could not make round Flamborough but was eventually towed in safely and there was a tragic drowning in the bay. I do not normally set sail during gale warnings but by Monday evening we were getting restive and as the forecast was marginally better’I decided to press on. We left just before midnight and were soon round Flamborough Head. With working rig and an off- shore force 5 we had another glorious sail on clear warm night with a few fishermen and the odd coaster for company. During Tuesday afternoon the wind veered and increased to NW6. By 1700 hours the sky looked really awful, storm % clouds interspersed with brilliant yellows and sudden squalls. We prepared for trouble, George seeing to the storm jib and putting extra lashings on the other jibs and everything else on deck, while John rigged the trysail and I looked around to see if I could find anything else for them to do. (Not entirely idle, I was trying to keep the ship fairly steady!) ' The 1800 forecast was
f%
imminent so we downed the jib and motor sailed like hell for Sunderland which we reached at 2050 before the trouble started. This is a very easy entrance which would obviously offer shelter to a yacht in just about any conditions but the masses of empty quays made it seem a sad and rather derelict harbour. We spent a peaceful night alongside a ship quay although we would have been better to have joined the yacht moorings (which we did the next morning,
Wednesday) but we could find nobody about in the whole harbour to tell us where
tO 20-6

TI should mention here that I do not in fact have a trysail but I do have deep reef points in my mainsail. By rolling loosely down to this point and leshing the cringles with the boom topped we get = very serviceable storm sail. The reof points are just below the numbers. If a trysail is not carried I think some arrangement of this sort is essential in a cruising yacht as even with a well tapered boom there-is a limit to the number of rolls which can be put in without the boom dropping too low. When beating with this rig I think it is probably worth while keeping the topping lift just tight enough to take
a little strain out of the leach. 7 |

With regard to watches, with a three man crew I prefer three hours on and six off. This of course shifts the watches and allows for four hours sleep at a stretch (enough at my age). I always do the navigating on my own boat so
seldom get more than 2 - 3 hours consecutively anyway. We were “on a 66% (Yacht
Passage Form) and had a long chat with the coastguard in his station who advised us to stay in Sunderland. However time was beginning to geta little short and “northerly winds were not going to be any help so we left on Wednésday at 1450 under trysail and engine with a fair tide, waving to the storm cone as we passed the C.S. station. This was not foolhardy as we could safely have run back to Sunderland had this proved necessary. In three hours the wind veered and cased to NE5-6 so the storm jib went up and we sailed into Blyth for dinner and to await the next fair tide. We were greeted by the club boatman in his launch who put us on a mooring, booked a table for us at the best local restaurant and even arranged for a club member to run us there in his car. Such kindnesses really are appreciated.

Our night in Sunderland was to be our last night in harbour before Inverness although head winds from now on were to mean much motoring and hence calls for petrol.

THE SHADOW AND THE FUTURE

Perhaps I ought to commence by apologising for keeping you in the dark -
perhaps.

At the A.G.M. last November I concluded my report by making the statement - "It is your Club and your decision". Perhaps in any Club such a statement should be treated with a certain amount of reserve but within the context applied I felt, have felt during the following months, and still feel that the decisions made in the “report” I am about to give were and are indeed your
decisions.

It was at that same meeting you all accepted without contradiction the need for the Marconi Sailing Club to exist and flourish at Stansgate and to that end agreed to pay the new rent upon a course of “succeed to buy or bust".

Turning back to my opening remark therefore you can now understand why I have-not previously come forward with news of the state of negotiation, such news has either been “subject to further negotiation" or I have been in a hurry because of fear of “Busting”.

As so many of these negotiations have by their netaoe been delicate I would like to pay tribute to the faith and patience of my fellow officers i allowing me the freedom to negotiate “in the dark" and for supporting me to the present stage where we await permanent planning approval before the contract Ky is signed and our Sailing Site is purchased.

My appreciation also goes to the Chief Executive of the M.A.S.C. and the Chairman of tho M.A.S.C. Committee also, especially to the Company Property Officer = Mr. A. Hi dset

Basic Conditions of Purchase

(1) The Site comprising some 7 acres is to be
purchased freehold by the Marconi Athletic and
Social Club for use by the Sailing Club as'a
Sailing Site and for associated recreational
purposes.

(2) Licence is to be granted to us by the
M.A.S.C.e in the first place for a period of 5 years based upon a rental system of £1,000 pea. ww increasing by 10% per annum. At the end of this period rental for following years will be w
hegotiated.

(3) All other expenses of the Sailing Section
will in future be met from Section funds.

There are obviously many questions.to be asked at this stage by many people but we must be patient and let things fall into their natural places as "that shadow” is not lifted until the contract is signed. Only then can we get down to the future which will bring greater responsibilities upon all members which you have signified to be acceptable as long as the Marconi
Sailing Club may stay - at Stansgate.

Amongst the things which may have puzzled you is the application for permanent planning permission. This‘had to go forward as obviously we wanted to buy property to use as a Sailing Site showing a new building in a different position to those at present, we obviously expect and have very good reasons
to think that we shall get approval - BUT this does not mean that the building
drawn up is the exact building intended neither does it mean that we shall
start building in the foreseeable future, but - who knows?

HANDICAP FLEET NEWS

The Handicap Fleet season started well with an ene curaging turnout for the first meeting held in the M.A.S.C. bar lounge on Tuesday April 20th despite competition from the M.A.S.C. Annual General Meeting.

Discussion revolved around finding some of the answers to the questions put to the fleet
in the April Navigans, with some of the conclusions summarised below:-

Most fleet members considered themselves to be in the beginner or ‘not terribly skillful" class. This meant that, if racing were to be encouraged ‘and enjoyed, lengths of courses and the prevailing conditions if adverse might deter many helmsmen from racing. It was concluded that more laps of fairl;:
short courses (similar to those for Mirrors) would be advantagcous and would enable boats to retire if their crews became fatigued. Racing might well be abandoned if conditions were not suitable even if more experienced fleets were
racing.

/continued.

P

Most handicappers
were family sailors whose sailing involved the fairer sex and youngsters who should not be scared off by “hairy” paeines ‘There should
be a weaning in process based. on| gentle initiation.

Very few of the fleet had any experience of racing and fewer were well versed in the racing rules. Many thought that this lack of knowledge meant that they would make poor job of racing or that others might not want to race with them. All felt that, for them, racing should not become so competitive that there would be a risk of damaging boats. It was concluded that, as long as the nommul safety rules were observed (i.c. the Starboard rule) and competing boats otherwise kept clear of each other, there should be no reason why racing should not be enjoyed by even the novices. In other words early racing: should be alan to all competitors pottering in one direction, with these keeping pace with the increasing skill of the participants.

All agreed that not the least important part of fleet activity was the social side and camaraderie among the fleet (and indeed club) members should be
encouraged.

It was decided to hold = further meeting at 8.30 pm in the M.A.S.C. Bar Lounge on Tuesday 18th May to discuss mutual problems and to try and sort out some of the technicalitics. It is hoped that the meeting will be well
patronised. ;

weekend come along - your efforts will be appreciated.

ALL who attended the meeting agreed to do their bit, some had already arranged to help with rescue. I shall be passing on relevant names to the
committee.

The annual general meeting of The Royal Yachting Association was eventually held on May 6th; after having been postponed from the original w date of March 17th; because of the postal strike. By a refermdum previously a) held, it was decided
to start the meeting at 1730 instead of at 1430 as
heretofore, in order to enable members to attend after leaving their work, but this did not appear to have been effective as the Caxton Hall was only sparsely filled with little over 100 members or half the number atta@mding
last year; . out of a membership of 33,000 from some 1,500 clubs; the average
age of those. attending appeared very high.

The routine business and elections passed off quickly enough, but when it came to the increase in subscriptions, argument began. Some members said that the removal of S.E.T.should help the finances while someme mentioned the rent of the present premises at Buckingham Gate was well over £8,000. The present rate of £2.2s. had been maintained all this century and it was finally agreed to increase it to £3. It will be remembered that the subscriptions from clubs had already been increased two years ago, md it was agreed that the subscriptions of life members should be upgraded.

The committee wanted to make R.Y.A. membership compulsory for all who entered races or tO impose a levy On race entry forms or introduwe a fee on all racing boats but this was vigorously opposed from the floor and the difficulty in collection of these fees was appreciated, so finally,after much discussion, it was agreed to refer this matter back to the committee.

/continued.

The National Coaching scheme was discussed and it was agreed that this should be conducted on a regional level with greater involvement by the local clubs, so that all who wished to lear or improve their ability should
benefit.

The R.Y.A. was pressing for the inclusion of sailing in the Commonwealth games and choice of classes to be used is to be considered.

It was pointed out that about half the association's finances are devoted to racing.

It is interesting, and not without significence, that while Jack Knights gave a full report of the meeting in Yachts and Yachting, Yachting World published just a paragraph about it, while Yachting Monthly did not even mention it!

The amount of paper work that one is required to produce for & visit to a Communist country, is incredible. Although we began our enquiries at Whitsun; three weeks before our departure we were still uncertain of an entry, even thouga we had a file eight inches thick with the "necessary! forms.

The trip was relatively uneventful across Belgium and West Germany, and it was'nt until we reached Helmstedt on the West/East German border that we began to have doubts. At the Allied chec:point igs a model of the East German border security precautions; three barbed wire fences, one minefield, completdy devoid of vegetation end further fences punctuated with machine gun searchlight posts On entering the Eastern sector we had to purchase our ‘transit visas and vehic insurance, ss well as declaring all our currency. Naturally all the forms have to be filled in duplicate, the whole operation to clear the border, for the four of us, taking about two hours. visas stated quite plainly that you are not allowed to deviate from your route, I could'nt help wondering what would hap .sen _if we broke down or over run our visa time.

Our first mistake was, obviously, to act lost. To correct our route we had to cut beck around Berlin via Tetsdam and here we had our first surprise. Potsdam is still in a state of semi-desiccation. There are still huge bombsites with rubble lying
in’ the streets, almost as if the war finished yesterday.
Obviously at one time the urchitecture was superb - but all these buildings were
now covered in shell marks. It occurred to us that this was not the place ts be round/ Md boats with Union Jocks on their sails; as it was, the locals made it fairly plain that they either disliked us, or were frightened to be seen talking to capitalist British. One or two pointing guards made it plain that they too did'nt take kindly to us driving past their barricks, so when we were eveitually back on our stated route, we all breathed a sigh of relief. (To emphasise the tight security, one of the Dutch competitors bed:me completely , lost. Minutes later a helicopter flew over head and five minutes 2fter that Ww the military had stopped him).

Polend was extremely pleasant after Bast Gemaeny, the people are friendly and the roads are good, with the exception of the towns and villages which invariably are still. cobbled. The cobbles started our problems, slowly the trailer wheels grew nearer to Father William is it curled up like bean can. Two wheel studs broke off like carrots and the most support broke clean away; with six masts, (4 British team spares), this presented quite a problem.

Eventually we arrived, Solin: at last! Fortunately we had no accommodation problems as the Poles had awarded two British boats and two Dutch boats free
lodging - “Father William” being one of them. Solina on = sunny Sunday locked
good. The sailing area was 2 dammed up river, producing a lake about 4 by 1+:
miles, with few small islands scuttered here and there. Solin: was obviously being turned into a tourist centre, and 2 lot had gone into it for the World Championships benefit. The concrete hurd for the boats was on the verge of being finislcd, and likewise the hotel, which had been built originally for the workers on the dam, and was now being given a face lift. Feople milled everywhere, holidaymakers, sightsccrs, T.V., bandsmen etc. Dozens of helping hands unloaded "Curved Air” from "Father Willicm’, ond then hundreds of faces solemly watched over the barrier wall as boats were rigged and tuned.

Better late than never - Here beginneth the first installment of Margaret
Campbell's log of their Summer Holiday - 1970.
* * *

This was to be~our first trip foreign complete with family on board our 24ft Gallant Class Cruiser “Pepito", therefore our plan was to make the shortest
possible crossing, i.e. Ramsgate - Calais. The crew consisted of Stan Campbell
(Skipper), Margaret Campbell (the Writer) and Juniors - Ian aged 10 and Jimmy 8.

The week prior to our holiday, “Pepito’ had been sailed around to Leigh on the first stage of the journey from the Blackwater. We were sailing in Company with friends from Leigh, and for us it was a convenient point of departure being only about five miles from home.

On the evening of July 24th, after numerous trips with necessities in the dinghy we appeared to have everything we needed for our 14 day holiday “iY turned in for an carly night.

Our aim for the next day was Ramsgate and after.
an overnight stop there,
on to Calais on Sunday - however, this was not to be. During the night the wind
steadily increased and by morning a full gale had developed.

Saturday, July 25th.

On waking and hearing the wind howling and the rain lsshing down, the youngest crew member peened our of his sleeping bag and said “Perhans something exciting has happened like our dinghy has blown away or sunk!" Ten minutes later when we decided to take a look outside, we discovered that our dinghy had indeed filled with water in the night and sunk, and of our cars there was no
Sign. Uneasy thought - is our youneer son a Jonah? Lesson learnt, make sure
oars arc securely lashed in future.

Since it was high tide end the water looked most uninviting we could'nt get ashore yet anywny, with or without oars, so the only alternative was to get the cards out. Thoughts of making for Ramsgate had already gone, if it was like this in sheltered Snr S, the open sea was certainly not for us today. Ar midday there was only a short stretch of water to cross, sc with the aid of do stout stout piece of wood discovered on board, we ferried out way to the shore to stretch our legs and hunt our ogrs (vnsuccesfully) though one turned up later, apparently picked out of the water by our friends from "Yaratah" in the early hours of the morning.

The rest of the day was spent uneventfully, new oars were purchased and we turned in hopefully for an carly night and a better start the next day.

conferred on that boat by its genoa introduced five years ago - a feeling which
is reflected in our Sailing Secretary's article in last month's Navigans, and

shared by our G.P. fleet, who simply do not believe that jiheiy boat is as;fast as the Entermrise.

I understand that the change came as a complete surprise to them and that there was for some weeks an indetcrminate though strong feeling that a fast one had been pulled. It seems now however, as though they have philos.phicslly accepted their. fate, so perhaps there is nothing more to be said. Except perhaps to ask whether it. is not possible that the decision would have been taken in a happier atmosphere is there had been some prior informal chat with all of. ‘the interests most affected.

7h . After at least one Aprii Points race, which ended with fleets becalmed and drifting helplessly towards the North Sea, we can, I hope, expect ' increased emphasis. by R.0.'s & 0.0.D.'s upon Rules and Sailing Instructions.

The approach of our annual Regatt= is, I am sure, viewed with mixed . feelings in the Clubs. One can discern at least three views.

For sane members it is with gloom that they foresee an overcrowded club with all facilities grossly overloaded, and people as thick on the ground as on the Costa Brava in august. These members will probably stay 2t home and dig their gardens.

For many others the Regatta incans a weekend of fellowship end sport, an opportunity to test themselves and their boats against friends from other Y clubs. These people will throw themselves with glee into the whole business, racing and social, and their enthusiasm will perhaps be some recomponse for the organisers.

These are the people I have most in mind, for they must surely feel nothing but apprehension at the inevitable approach of their annual shindig. I refer not only to our Flag Officers and Committee who carry the responsibility for the whole exercise, but to the tent arrangers, the prize buyers, the latrinc men, the bartenders (two sides of the same coin!), the rescue launch crews - to say nothing of the many people involved in organising the racing itself.

I am sure these good people consider that it is worth all the hard work they have to put in, but they can be forgiven if they hope for more active and reliable help with the more menial tasks than they usually get from the brighter stars in our RBGLRE firmament, and for more interest and support from the stay-at—homes.

Thursday 30th March *

Launched at Dixon Kerly and motored to Stansgate in a rather fresh wine, anchored off the hard to collect Walter who had travelled down by car. Jobs to donGand of course sleep before the last member of our weekend crew was to arrive by boat at 02.00 in the morning.

| Friday, Slst March

Kyle of Bute sailed straight past and into the night with the skipvex shouting instructions as to where they would anchor, Off Stone we thought he
said - and in fact we never did meet our extra crew. It was bitterly cold and
with a good fresh S.i/. wind at 07.30 am sails were hoisted and a course set for Harwich and perhaps Holland. As the day drew on we succeeded in convincing each other that a cross channel trip so early in the season would probably our:
us of the sailing habit for good. It is difficult to recall how cold it was that weekend and just to keep warm the primus cooker was kept going full blast all weekend when we were moored or anchored. kRefore long we were heading up the Orwell and glad to pick up a mooring at Pin Mill still with only a handfull of yachts in occupation.

Saturday, lst April 7)

After a couple of trips ashore for food and fittings we’ were only too happy to sit in the fug caused by the cooker being full on for warmth, till. a feeling, probably of guilt, made us hoist sail for Walton Backwaters. The day was brilliant sunshine but still cold and most of this short trip was occupied with determining the compass deviation which is as much as 30°! 4 bouncy sail into the Backwaters and an evening ashore pertalking in the legendary night life of Walton (one half of bitter in the Yacht Club). We were glad to clamber into our sleeping bags and let the warmth seep buck into our bones.

Sunday 2nd April

A very early start to clear Pye End buoy well before low witer. - Wit.
a draught of 4'9" and a charted depth of 3' in places we succeeded with only oc. incident where we touched. Once clear of the shoals we sailed till we wore’ — between Medusa and Walton Tower and there hove to for breakfast whilst the tid. sorted itself out.

With the wind freshening, we turned our bows into what was to bacon a healthy force 7 (against the tide). Jonelle ignoring these facts of nature, put her best foot forward and off we went with stanchions rigging and at times the cabin combings half submerged. For the greater part of this journey the Aries self steering gear did most of the work wishout hesitation or causing yacht to miss her stride.

Eventually, we had to send up our smallest jib and a sense of * proportion gradually returned, the cabin sole was where we always wanted it and we could now wipe the footprints from the desk head.

The motion in the Blackwater was not much better than out in the ba with a few gusty squalls lurking about ready to welcome us home. With a sich of relief we picked up a mooring at Stansgate and disappeared below for-tea ani
SOUP.

So ended our shakedown and warm up cruise which was to be the first stage in our plans to sail Jonelle to the Mediterranean. A few littiIe jobs wore still to be done but Jonelle inspires much confidence with her ability to take on the rough seas which we all face with some trepidation. eric we

COMMODORE'S NOTES

In spite of the fact that we did not hold our Open Day when originally planned, it was certainly most successful in terms of enjoyment, weather and new. larconi members.

We changed the date to avoid clashing with the H.4.S.C. Barbecue, and then discovered we'd clash with the Essex Show, and several away meetings. I. must admit I was apprehensive half way through the afternoon when Geof Farnie told me he'd only had one application, but thereafter. business was much more brisk, and we were delighted to end up with at least twelve new members.

Hany thanks to all our helpers, sailors and organisers. The sailing deronstrations were well received, and the boat trips exceedingly popular.

Incidentally, Jack Bigden's appeal qver the P.A.- for new members was heard by the crew of 2 passing cruiser, who came ashore and asked for an application form: For the benefit of our Associate liembers, the main idea of the Open Day

~2~

is to"show off" the club to Marconi people, in order to attract more ordinary members. This, incidentally may also allow us to take more associates, whilst still maintaining our membership ratios.

The detailed plans for the clubhouse have now been completed, and subrnitted to four builders for quotations and to various authorities. There are likely to be some modifications regarding siting, but at present these don't seem serious. By far the most important consideration is the cost and we won't know this for a week or two yet.

The weather has been most kind to us this year, and this has been reflected in the sailing activity. In particular, the cruiser fleet has been much more active. The lst Barnacle points heda record entry of seven boats, and the cruise to Brightlingsea (dare I say Pin 1ii11?) was a great success.

On Saturday a force 4 wind gusting 5 prevailed for those sailing, with temperatures in the 70's for those left behind. Although I'm told it. was too cold for a bikini in the committee boat, those involved in the organisation proved themselves very efficient, and, with their olympic courses, ran an excellent meeting. The first race began at 11.15 an, rather difficult for those with long distances to travel, but none the less there were 36 —— The result was a first for Malcoln Goodwin in Revolution, second was a local boat, the dread of the result sheet writers, Doreni Fasol Latido, third was ilo Snoothic Holnes in Yabatoo. In the norning's race, Revolution did not have such a good stxrt and was well down on the first lap, with Bruce leading a lot of the way. However, he fought back to win, with Yabatoo second. Discovering that the season was nearly over withowt any major event —- apart from races etc., Frank Savill and I decided to have a'grand potter’. (Perhaps I should explain that two years ago we had reacheda similar decision, being proud
new owners of Mirrors, and made elaborate plans - and provisions, for a trip to
Brightlingsea, dropping in at Mersea. This started off in a force six gale and we were glad to seek the shelter of liersea, where we picnicked and explored the creeks, then made our way more slowly feck, having to walk the last hundred yards.) This tine it was Brightlingsea or bust.

Saturday morning came and by ten o'clock we were on the hard and the usual
gale blowing. Casually remarking to the gathering throng (two small boys and one man) that we.were just going for a trip down to Brightlingsea, we set out at low tide, Frank in.a nice fitting wet suit and I in the few odd things I call ny sailing gear, but proudly clutchinga new life jacket I had bought for the sake of convention. With a force six behind us and a turned tide against us it was one long run, Frank holding the boom and I manning the tiller and clutching ny life jacket. The sun shone and it began to feel like surfing in the South Seas and in 2y hours we were off Brightlingsea.

We decided to put in to the bank opposite, have a cup of coffee and make
ourselves respectable for. the grand entry - Frank never having been to 'B' before.
On the beach we chatted with-the-sole occupant, a beachcomber type who said he had worked on Osea for a few years. and had left, selling his boat to lirs. Pye of Steeple. He said he now earned his living as part time artist and boat repairer. We remarked on the few people about and he said all the robots were packed awa on Bank Holiday Monday. The salt on us fairly glowed. Crossing over to the
harbour after a friendly warning about getting back up river - we were glad there
were few about as there was little room to get even a Mirror in. With the friendly loan of a trailer from the club, we left our boat well .up the beach and walked to the boating pool ‘to have our sandwiches etc.

The sun shone, it was nice and sheltered, in fact a Snangrila and I suggested we rang up and said we were storm bound, but Frank, who is the con- scientious type, reminded ne of the beachcomber's warning and reluctantly we made our way back to the club beach, to find our boat floating nicely in a foot of water all ready for us -

lesen the harbour at about 3.45, we soon met the wind and seas and a lunp cane in ny throat as. the little old tub complacently ploughed her way through it. She was aptly named 'Frantic'. From then on it was one long hard beat after another, with one on the helm and the other bailing and we realised we were going to have to pay for our hilaricus morning. By the tine we reached Bradwell I was beginning to envy Frank his wet suit as we slowly and painfully edged up the river, the wind and tide pressing us stubbonly back. After effecting another of our acrobatic changes of duties, we decided on smaller tacks, which helped for a while but fearing the mud flats -we- went back to the longer beats across river. Slowly the Stone cane nearer as darkness began to fall and by the tine we were opposite it was dark and wo were glad of the friendly lights.

I suggested neckly to Frank that perhaps wc ought to put in there, but the gallant fcllow was not to be beaten and so out we wont across the river again.
Coning back,‘having decreased the distance to the clubhouse by sone 100', we began — notice the burst of activity at Stansgate. Lights were being lit and several are:could be seen streaming dcown and there was a general hub—-bub. I suggested to rise that it could only bw a large scale rescue operation and began to feel warn again with importance. Slyly I pointed out that we shouldn't waste the tine of police ctc. or put‘our wives to further nisery when we could drop in at the Stone and telephone. at this blow below the bclt he capitulated and thankful for the friendly glean of the Stone Sailing Club's lights, we sank our bow into the soft sweet mud and stepped ashore. — . -

SAiTLING BARGE HOLIDAY.

In August I joined the sailing barge Marjorie at Maldon for a 4 .. day cruise.. Marjorie. is -a common sight on the Blackwater.as‘she ; ; Sails. to and.from the Hythe Quay, Maldon, with charter ‘parties aboard. “and is easily recognizable by the white cross in her “topsail,

she is a: coasting barge built for R & W Paul of: Ipswich in 1902, rth. a length of 86.ft.:. and a -beam of. 20ft.The.:hold has ‘been fitted out to provide cabin accommodation for.1l2 charterers, a spacious
saloon and.a' well-appointed: gallery... The crew. (skipper and mate)
_ live.in. the. traditional skipper's: cabin but eat. with. the charter Ww ie “party (who. supply and: cook the food).

The barge has a ketch rig, the ‘mizzen being sheeted to the rudder blade to assist. steering and countcract the force of the foresail and
“""Staysail.

“Our party consisted of 5 chaps, including myself, the rest. of the party having backed down,
There is a moral there for any one interested
. in. organising a charter party. However, the smaller ‘party is an " Advantage as it gives plenty of opportunity “to be involved in the semaanines and Lie of the barge.

“We were Sones ‘away from Hythe Quay at 5.20 am. on Howey chow the 20th. by a small tug. The tide had just started to ebb, but the Wind was almost. non-existent. All the sails were set off Heybridge, we chartocrers being given various ropes and told to pull, and the tug cast off. We drifted rather than sailed down Colliers Reach and some extemely strong language was used to attempt to 'whistle-up a — wind', It became apparent as the days progressed that little could WW be achieved in or around the barge without the use of certain quaint old barging phrases and sayings, although no harsh words were ever directed at the barge herself, she being almost sacred amo. ng vessels, Such was the rate of progress that we had time to start cooking breakfast off Northey Island and to be washing it down with a cup of tea whilst passing otansgate. At last the tide turned at Bradwell and it started to rain, and wc anchored to catch up on some sleep. The wind freshened in the afternoon and at 4pm. we hoisted sail and- raised anchor. The barge set off towards Mersea at a grand space, A few of us climbed into the barge's dinghy and-spent some time ‘circling the barge taking photos as she. sailed. She looked splendid under sail, close-hauled, and I took some fine colour slides. That ni get “found us anchored off Brightlingsea in company. with: Dawn, Walter Cook's other charter barge.

. Next morning we left Brightlingsea at 9.30am. and headed down the Colne for the Spitway. There was a fresh easterly breeze blowing and ‘Marjorie. ploughed her way out of the Blackwater -estuary. Heavy rain and rough water made navigation difficult and it was a comfort that at least the crew appeared
.to -know-the way. The seas in the Spitway were quite rough.and confused andthe old barge creaked and. groaned .eclow decks. I4 was the: first time I.have ever made tea when the cups wouldn! t.. stay where I-put them. Our’ cruiser colleages.-aré,no- doubt, used.to this.We hadito.go.about twice in the: ininiiins ‘to clear the

“/ continued.

“11-.

the Buxey sands, this was8 quite:as memorable. experience in the cond- .Swin' into the ‘Thames, crossed over to the Medway channel:and anchored [op Gillingham 63 hours after -leaving a Ceortainly @ «3 journey: for a dinghy sailor. to remember.

Wednesday we spent anchored at Gillingham where we weent ashore
for a few hours in the morning, and:went up to Hoo Marina in the dinghy jin the.afternoon. As the tide was to turn about 6pm. it was” decided to move down river to Stansgate Creek (near Shcerness) evening. . we had a.fine sail, tacking down the Medway with the tide in our favour. We were eraced with a fiery sunset, and the lights from the ‘navigation buoys and tankers at the refineries made a colourful picture. It was quite dark whom we anchored in the entrance to Stansgate Creek but by now I knew my. way around the deck well enough to avoid tripping over the umpteen bits and pieces that are oe i make ra barge gow were Hs ete me tere one mF

Next — Chumeden, was our last= and we had to be at Southend . Pier by“the afternoon to change’-places with the next charter party:
Marjorie was to Stay in the Thames as she was to sail in the Surbhend Barge Match the following weekend, Thursday morning we up-anchored (a back breaking bu siness, by far the worst job on the barge).,.‘and oo headed back into the Thames. Once clear of the Medway I got my ¢hance 4 to take the wheel under the guidance of a watchful barge skipper. This indeed was sailing in grand style as we tacked our way down river just off the Kent coast. The sea was choppy and the “breeze fresh, and the wheel kicked like a mule. I soon found it was better
to le 4 her have’ her own way” whom‘she kicked making alterations in|
between times. I continually cast anxious glances from the bob th the sails, ever conscious of the gaze of the crew. Putting the barge about was certainly different to tacking my GP 14, but the principle
appeared
to: be much the’ same. A Héarty "Leé-Oh' to warn the crew tending the foresail bowline, then helm hard down and around she goes. The foresail is backed by means of a bowline which pushes the- barge S
bows cleanly through the wind. Once on the new tack the bowline is |
let go and the foresail whips across the horse and away she goes. 411 good things must come to an end and the barge was handed back to her crew and course set for Southend Pier via the South Shoebury - buoy and the Essex coast. The holiday was. over when the. barge. dinghy landed us on Southend Pier with all our gear, 4 days and 60 colour- slides after leaving Maldon. ‘

If my tale has whetted anybody ' S appetite and tempted them to organise ‘a charter party, I would ‘itdke the following suggestions, one is to book early as chartcring is very popular and the second is
to be sure of your party and see the colour of their money before you commit yourself. Being left with half your planned-for party can be very expensive.

In the early summer of 1973, an increasing diserchantment with dinghy racing '( perhaps not unconnected with a conspicuous lack of success Since 1972 ), together with crew problems, led me to consider wider sailing excursions in my GP 14, Lady Clare,

What follows has, I hope, sufficient of the characteristics
of
a log- to qualify it as a Mamgu Trophy entry,. but it is priorarily a pie of-ce’
personal writing.

The choice of crew presented a problem. Nik and I have in the .. past made several successful short sailing/camping trips, the most recent having been in 1971, when we. visited Burnham and Foulness island.But this year he was not available. The only other person ~With whom I have achieved that instinctive, intuitive, rapport in the boat which is essential was also not available, so I concluded that this trip would have to be single handed. .

The planned trip was.a five-day north easterly excursion up the issex coast. The first and last nights would be spent, sleeping in the boat in the general vicinity of Colne Point, and the other two farther North at pre-arranged accommodation ashore.

The planned times of departure, -passing and arrival, taking into account tidal flows were set down on paper in terms of High water rather than clock times in order to allow(prophetically, oe it turned out) for slippage of dates. Each day's sheet of paper also had a column in which I was to log the actual times. That column :
remains blank to this day- and the paper looks as though it had seen more sea water. than ink..

By converting the HWD based times to clock and calendar times, |
I found that.the only suitable dates when I could be free, were :
between the 6th and the 10th of August, and in mid-July I committed myself by giving to a somewhat incredulus wife and family a statement of my intention and to the Almighty a fervent prayer for good
weather, :

Because of the planned overnight stays in the boat, a sleeping bag, the boat cover, rudimentary cooking gear and two thermos flasks were to be taken. Food would include milk, coffee, sugar; soup, orange juice, biscuits, cheese, nuts and dried fruit. Each morning the flasks would be charged one with coffee, and the other with soup for consumption at the-end of the day. Midday food would be contained in a plastic airtight box and consist of biscuits, cheese, nuts and fruit. Brandy would also be. taken. :

I planned to take. extra sailinggear, including. the small |
headsail, a second anchor,.all the spare line I could find,’a small compassand my knife/marlin.spike which doubles as an identity disc. The latter two items were worn around my neck. I borrowed Clare's - M.W. transistpgr radio and took alist of BBC M.W. weather forecast (23.45 Radio is best
I also purchased
). a red hand flare. (Use when aireraft or vessel is sighted). It remains unused. I did not take the spinnaker..I wore my wet suit and bouyancy jacket all-the sailing time. I have included the foregoing details because they were the subject of much thought in the planning stage which absorbed
