In the event, most of this Logistic. planning was successful, but the one thing-I could not plan, of course, was the weather. Force 6 wind on Monday the 6th August, reinforced on the Tuesday by heavy rain made a start impossible; or at least foolhardy, By Tuesday. morning, with no comfort to be had from a telephone weather forecast . featuring force 5 to :7, I had decided to cut my losses and return to work on the following day, -unless there was a significant imp- rovement. A CRUISE TO KENT
by Andy & Sue Dixon. Sept.1973.

INTRODUCTION

This account.is constructed from the day-to-day working log of SUZANNE-MARIE, our Drascombe Lugger, and covers our holiday cruise from, 16th. June to 29th. June 1973. The aims of the cruise were to explore the Kent coast from the Downs to the Medway, and if circumstances permitted, to pop across the channel to Calais. The fact that these aims were not quite fully realised did not detract from a very enjoyable and successful cruise -.not the least because we actually. had some sun this year!

SATURDAY 16th. June.

The Sailing Club Open Day - also the first day of our holidays!
& fine morning gave promise to a successful Open Day, which indeed it was. We dutifully did our bit by taking prospective members for a spin in SUZANNE-MARIE but by 1630 we could dally no longer, and md slipped off downstream with a salty beat into the fresh easterly .. :
breeze. Our first night destination was only Tollesbury Fleet, so it-was not long before the Nass was rounded and we were running up to the Leavings, where we brought up at 1815.We were glad to get our tent strung up between the two masts, as the breeze and the thickening haze had made it decidedly chilly for the last hour-or- so,

SO we settled down to-our first night of the cruise - always, I
think, the most exciting whilst still getting accustomed to the motion of the boat again, and with the prospect of the holiday before you. And especially as tomorrow we were hoping th make the long haul down to Ramsgate, Also

SUNDAY 17th. JUNE.

Up at 0500 to be greeted by the first accident of the holidays — I had slept on my spectacles and broken one of the arms!. Luckily. I had actually thought to bring a spare pair with me- a thing I usually forget.

The day promised fair again, although the wind had veered SW overnight, and a lot of altocumulus cloud was in evidence. We set off at 0620 ghosting down Tollesbury Fleet whilst receiving a reassuring shipping forecast -—- S, F3-4, veering W.. Round the Nass we had a fresh sail in a strengthened breeze for a while,- until it dropped right off again. To maintain our schedule we had to start the motorw to take us over the young flood to the Spitway,, from whence we continued under sail again. At 1020 we rounded the Barrow Beacon and set off in the gentle SW breeze to crab across the channels and shoals that radiate out from the Thames. The sea was mori the sun was warm, not another boat in sight and life was
good

‘Inspite ofa developing haze pilotage was easy - a matter of--
buoy hopping, allowing for tidal drift by keeping two buoys in transit. However, as we were crossing the Black Deep, life became not so good! The wind had been falling steadily so we resorted to the motor again, but before -long it coughed and spluttered to a halt. Whilst I was effecting temporary repairs to a spark plug connector, a tanker loomed out of the haze towards us and caused us to heave ‘to and have lunch while it passed. All the time the cloud cover had been increasing, trapping a sultry atmosphere under it,

The last stretch was a pleasant close reach along the coast and _ at 1730 we motored through Ramsgate. harbour entrance with a feeling Sof achievement that ~is only possible with a small open boat, and were directed alongside an old fishing boat in. the outer harbour. After setting our clearance and paying our dues, we celebrated the successful voyage with a slap up meal ashore and a stroll.along the prom, in the evening sun, ( the clouds having cleared again!),.

Our first night in Ramsgate was not a success! Our little SUZANNE- MARIE was being smashed up against the rusty old fishing boat . outboard motor. It was ideal holiday weather - indeed so hot that

Having gone’ to bed early the evening before, our plan was to _ :

COMMODORES NOTE

Membership renewals have been coming in at a gratifyinz rate, and our foolish fears that the general alarm and despondancy . would extend to sailing appear to be groundless, thank goodness. Neverthe less, we are anxious to increase our ordinary membership, so do encourage your friends in the company to join us, even if they haven't a boat.
Many of you are aware of the enthusiasm and hard work that
Bruce Long has put into building and encouraging thé.development of the 18° Sydney Barbour Skiffs. However, you may not be aware that these boats are maintained in part by sponsorship, which involves advertising brand names on the sails. Bruce has applied for his boat to sail from the club, as an M.8.C. registered boat, but our club rule 24 states, 'Members shall not display gross forms of advertising at the club, or on or about boats registered with the club." Furthermors, the R.Y.4. have a similar rule, and we ave affiliated to the R.Y.A. We are informed by the Skiff Class that 7 the R.Y.a. are considering a change in their rules regarding sponsorship. Your committee have made the following decision. Bruce will be allowed to sail his boat from Stansgate for this season, without prejudice to future action. We will have to arrange an Extraordinary General Meeting (or at the 4.G.i.) to consider the clubs feeling regarding our own rule, and take action accordingly. Our action may be influenced by the R.Y.A. decision.
No doubt there will be plenty of discussions on this point during the season, but most of us felt our decision the best compromise in the circurstances.

THE "MALCOLM MILLER".

by
Andrew Dixon.

A grey friendless sky hung close over the London roof tops, and a chill February wind murmured through the rigging. The silent dockland wharves and cranes added a cheerless backdrop to the scene, and in all made the prospect of setting out for the open sea a little unwelcoming. I was standing on the deck of the schooner "Malcolm Miller", supposedly polishing a large brass winch, but in reality gazing on the latecomers straggling aboard, and meditating on the voyage in the week to come.

The "Malcolm Miller", 135'0.A., is a Topsail schooner belonging to the Sail Training Association, and sister ship of the famous "Sir Winston Churchill" which was at this moment in its own state of bustle just along the quay from us. She is very sturdily built of steel with a good draft of 15%', and can sport up to I4 sails on three masts. She has four headsails, three square sails on the foremast, gaff rigged fore and mainsails and a bermudan mizzen. In addition she can set topsails above the two gaffs, and a staysails between the masts. However, these latter sails are usually regarded as playthings, only to be set on calm Summer days when there is nothing much else to do, and at this time of the year (February) even the large mizzen sail has a permanent reef in it.

The schooners accommodate about 40 "trainees", usually I6 to 21
year olds from all walks of life, and the purpose is to give them a taste of adventure as well as to teach them responsibility, discipline and teamwork. A permanent crew of five runs each schooner with the help of adult volunteers to act as watch officers, purser etc.. What then was 1, a relative old timer doing aboard as a "trainee". The schooners had just finished their annual two month refit in the West India Docks, and the first cruise they under take is regarded as a "shakedown cruise". As new rigging, etc., is untried at this stage any thing can happen, and the ships are in a shambles after theib dockyard sojourn. So adults are taken on for the shakedown cruise to get the schooners in smart and Shipshape condition again and to meet any emergencies that might arise. Also, presumably, it is a good opportunity for the STA to select future watch officers etc.

So on a quiet Sunday afternoon we were being initiated in the ways of the "Malcolm Miller". A spell of cleaning, tidying and polishing under the critical eye of the bosun was followed by an instructional session, first to make sure we all knew the basic knots and sail terms, and then to introduce us to the ropes with which we were to become intimately familiar in the coming week. The foremast from which 60% of the sails are controlled, particularly had a veritable maze of halyards, buntlines and clewlines. In addition, there were the yard braces, downhauls and of course the runners. These adjustable backstays are operated by lever mechanism, which when slackened off, allowed a very heavy block to crash around at head level until captured. Controlling this in a bit of a gale struck me as a particularly hazardous operation so I gave it a wide berth! We were also initiated at this stage in the delights of crawling up the rigging and swinging out along the yards. It seemed easy enough with the Ship sitting quietly in dock but no doubt it will be a different matter out at sea, with a good heel and large waves to plough into!

After a well earned supper we had the evening off and the more royste rough
oy S Too b
Seb i company went off to explore the delichts of

9.

I decided to have a quiet evening aboard reading and chatting to my enforced companions for the next few days. Our ships company were as complete a mixture as one could wish for. Age groups ranged from the twenties to the sixties, with at least two retired people on board. An equally wide range of accents made communication diffichlt at times West country, Welsh, Irish, Scottish, Yorkshire, Lancashire, broad Geordie and Australian come to mind. Lass than I thought were active yachtsman, only about half having any recreational sailing experience at all, and only few actually possessing a boat of their own. The majority were there just a break in their workaGgy lives, others were ex-proffess- ional seamen and at least two were there "Spying out the land" for sponsoring their firm's apprentices on future crtises. The range of professional status again ranged widely, from bank clerk and artisan to company director and high up civil servants,; the general norm seemed to be professional engineer or equivalent, although we did have with us an author, a BBC radio reporter and an under-butler from Buckingham Pakace!
—

Monday dawned grey and drizzly and we were up at 06.30 as we had
a busy day ahead of us. Sleep had all but eluded me during the night due suppose to strange surrbndings, noises and hard bunks. We, trainees were all quartered in the one mess deck with pipe cot bunks lining the Sides and these squeak atrociously as one turns over. Some were sleeping weel though, if the walrus sounds that reverberated around the cabin were any thing to go by.

We were due to set off in the afternoon, so we were busy performing last minute tasks, and practising sail setting and furling drills. These latter have to be team efforts, co-ordinated by the watch leaders. Several hands are required on each halyard as the gear is of traditional nature and very heavy. This is purposely so to keep 40 odd lively youngsters busy and exercised. As an adult cruise we had a complement of only 24, so there were barely enough hands to go around in a complete sail setting drill.

At I3.15, the last warp was slipped and at last we were away, ~Allowing the "Sir Winston Churchill" through the lock gates. We were motoring, as the schooners always do in confined spaces— the first “aptain of the "Winston Churchill" did a lot of damage with the bowsprit +n his abhorrence of engines! Out in the Thames we met a fresh easterly breeze, which, though it didn't help up and down the Thames was a faar wind for our final destination of Portsmouth. If the easterly wind held, we should be able to get a visit to Cherbourg in between.

The hard work really began now. We got down to one of the more back-— breaking tasks to be done aboard, which was to scrub a layer of lime off the deck that had been put down to preserve the planking during the re-fit period. It had hardened like cement and was a real devil to get off. Taking a breather in the work, I saw the International Code flags "0 Q" flying from the yard arm, and the shore line describing dizzy circles round us, which reminded us that on this the first trip of the season, the compass adjuster was aboard doing his thing.

At 17.30 we went below for supper, after which I had to tog up in warm clothes and oil skins to stand the second Dog Watch. We were split into three watches—- I was in the forewatch, the others being Main and Mizzen watches, named after each of the masts. This meant that when all hands were required on deck I assembled with the rest of my watch in the area of the foremast. In such occasions(eg. setting off, bringing up under sail) my tasks were to help with the foresail of headsails, and the other watches to deal with their corresponding sails.

Io.

If only the duty watch is on deck though, this watch, which ever it is, maybe required to adjust or hand any sail on any mast. We followed a system of four hour duty watches, which in general meant four hours on and eight hours off. This arrangement is complicated by two dog watches of two hours
each, between 14.00 and 20.00 which are introduced so that one does not
keep the same duty watch each day. On coming on deck at I8.00 I was sur- prised to see the lights of Southend on our port beam and Sheerness away to our starboard. The mizzen and foresail had been set by the previous watch, but we were still under power as the wind was almost dead ahead. Visibility had improved and there was plenty of shipping to be seen about. I had plenty of time to look about for the first hour, as I was standby duty. Each duty watch was split into one hour tricks, and one alternated each hour between doing bridge duty and standby duty. On the bridge, as well as the helmsman, port and starboard lookouts are required as well as a messenger. The latter ran errands for the watch officer, and also maintained the rough log book. The standby duty at night had to remain geared up but could sit in the petty officer's mess in the deck cabin consuming coffee and bread and cheese in limitless quantities, unless required for trimming or changing a sail. During the day the standby duty merged with the genere off watch chores of cleaning up the vessel and getting her into ship shape condition. The second hour I was messenger duty, with not many messages to carry, but I was busy keeping the rough log book up to date, noting each change of course and each buoy we passed down the Yantlet Channel. Also each hour a note of windspeed and direction, shipspeed, weather, tempera- ture, etc. was recorded.

Coming off duty I was ready to go to bed, although again, sleep did not come easily. The sea was still calm, but the motion of the ship could now be felt below- a restful unhurried motion that befits the I00' water- line. However, the waves slopping against the steeel bows did give the
feeling of lying in a 500 gallon oil drum! At 22.30 the engines were stopped
and we were a sailing vessel at last. Presumably we had now rounded the North Foreland.

When woken at 03.30 on Tuesday I felt that I had just fallen asleep and it was a struggle to get up for the middle watch at 04.99. On deck we were bowling along with a F5 wind behind us, with mizzen foresail and stay sail set. Shipping twinkled all around us and Cap Gris Nez light house could be seen close to our port. I was on standby duty for the first hour and spent an interesting spell in the chart room where the navigator showed us a few of his navigational aids, such as the Decca Navigator and the Radar (Kelvin Hughes not Marconi!) Beind down below we missed a few interesting moments on deck, where the helmsman battling with his inexperience and a quartering sea, ended up by heading for the landward side of the Cap Gris Nez, now but two miles away! Frantic signalling from the light house, plus some hysterics from the watch officer, soon showed him the error of his ways. The following hour 1 was on messenger duty again, as Boulogne drew abeam. The captain decided it was too early to stop, so we set a course for Cherbourg, a further I40 miles. The third hour saw daylight come upon us, and with it, we set the square topsail to help get us to Cherbourg as quickly as possible. The mainsail was not set, but that only seems to be set when closehauled, or when the captain wants to make a pretty picture. For .v the forth hour I did my stint at the wheel, and found her much more responsive than the Thames barge, the only other sailing vessel of comparable size I've helmed!!! The temperature was 69C so I was very cold and glad of a good breakfast after coming off watch.

If.

However, there was no respite, for the fire alarm went off, and we all had to practice the fire drill. No sooner had we got back below, before the Abandon ship alarm went off, and we had to go through that drill! And then we were informed that "Happy Hour" had been declared. This is the name for an hour each day when everyone trots off to their assigned cleaning stations below decks and scrubs and polishes till the place Shines. My assignment was the chartroom, and I kept finding myself diverted by glances down to the chart, or navigational book, or listen- ing to the captain calling up the mainland on the radio.

Then at last we had a break till lunch. The afternoon was free as well, and as it was grey and cold on deck, I lay on my bunk reading and writing most of the time. We were not likely to arrive at Cherburg before midnight, and we might have to stooge around outside the harbour till the morning, so there was the prospect of a busy night ahead.

Back on watch at 16.00, and a definate change in conditions could be seen. Gales had been mentioned in the weather forecast, and the anemo- “neter was now gusting over 40 knots.Black squalls came blinding down on us, and the lee rails were right under water, but still we forged on at II or more knots, with all sail, including the square topsail, set! Howerer, after an hour of port lookout duty I had to help hand the inner jib- out on the bowsprit lashing the sail down, I was fervently hoping my insurance policies were all 0O.K.!!

Fried liver and, onions were very welcome after a chilly watch on deck, although at 36° heel, even the fiddle rails failed to keep the plates in place, so the food had an equal probability of landing in one's lap as down the throat. The dinner table was quite deserted that evening- Why no-one felt hungry, I'm sure I don't know! While eating the ship jibed (on purpose I presume!) and that posed me with a probelm when it came to sleeping, as my bunk was now on the weather side. A canvas lee- board had to be strapped up to stop me from rolling out.

On deck again for the midnight watch, and it was a surprise to see _the French coast close by again and the stars out abowe. The loom 6f Jherbourg was approaching, and we were going to run straight in for shelter, After handing the stay we jibed again, and then the square top- sail brailed up andthe foresail lowered. Even so we seemed to tear past the harbour lights till we rounded up and dropped the anchor. After battling with the big mizzen sail, we retird below for some welcome rest.

I awoke at 2.30- still fully dressed- after the soundest sleep so far and found it to be a fine sunny day, but cold on deck. We had a busy day before we were allowed ashore to scour the fleshpots of Cherbourg. Actually there was not much chance of that, as the captain wanted to be away again by 14.00hours. After mooring alongside the quay we had another work session on board and got ashore, just as every where closed down for lunch. Perhaps it was as well, after working out a few of the prices in the shops. After a call at a bar or two and a patisserie we were too tired to do much else but take a short stroll round the town and then back to the ship to rest.

When we left at 16.00 hrs, the gale had dropped to a light air so although we proudly left harbour whth all plainsail set, we had to use the engines to give us any headway. Fore watch was bn duty again at 20.00,

Tz.

Once we crossed the shipping lanes the engines were stopped, making it wost enjoyable as we slipped through the water at a couple of knots. Visibility was good, so on lookout duty I kept a careful watch on the multitude of navigation lights twinkling around us. Before going off watch at midnight, St. Catherines Head, I.0.W., had been sighted. We were due at Cowes the next day, so we were to potter up and down the coast till dawn.

A mad scramble for breakfast, as the last watch had neglected to rouse us, and then on deck for 08.00 watch. The Nab tower was ahead, peering through a grey murky haze. We were attempting to tack up the Solent in a light fickle breeze, but when the tide turned against us as well, we had to resort to the engines. In time the hazw melted to let the
Sun seep through, and the breeze strengthened, so that we were trickling
along nicely under sail, as Portsmouth drew abeam. We ploughed right through a naval exercise which expressed its annoyance by letting off a depth charge. The water pressure waves hit us some seconds before the sound waves, and it really sounded as if we had struck a rock!

Soon after lunch we approached Cowes and rounded up to anchor in grand manner. The same second as the anchor hit the water, all sails except the mizzen came rattling down. Of course, the only hitch up had to be the jib halyards, I was stationed at! Another afternoon of scrubbing and cleaning followed, by which time the "Malcolm Miller"was beginning to look quite shipshape, after which we spent ams evening doing our best to "live it up" in wintertime Cowes.

Friday morning was greeted with a rude arousal at 06.00hours-—
extra early because it was my alloted day as galley worker. This meant I was relieved of ordinary watch duty for the day, but instead spent it, spudbashing, dishwashing and serving up food. One is on the gp all day, but the work is not strenuous and it is nice to lean out of the galley door watching someone else heaving on the braces. Unfortunately us galley workers (one from each watch) missed another fine manoeuvre as we left Cowes. The sails, including square topsail, were hoisted before the anche. was weighed, and as the anchor broke free the topsail was caught aback to bring the head off the wind so that we could bear away with the fair wind (now southwesterly) for Portsmouth, our final destination. The engines were not used for this manoeuvre in fairly cramped quarters.

We had to enter Portsmouth harbour at 14.00 precisely so the morning was spent out to the Nab tower and back, trying sail manoeuvres and generally showing off the schooner to all and sundry. The day started fine, but as we approached Portsmouth again a black squall came over and we fairly sizzled past the Round Tower into the harbour. A hundred yards off
H.M.S.Dolphin we rounded up, there was another dramatic all-sail-—down
together drill, synchronised this time with the start of the engine, which gently edged us into our berth. The captain certainly knows how to handle his vessel. The Royal Navy always offers the schooner an honorary berth in H.M.S.Dolphin- the submarine depot when visiting Portsmouth. However this means that we couldn't just wander ashore, but had to wait for a special ferry to take us to Portmouth for a last nights revelling.

The galley work was hurriedly finished that evening so that we could catch the ferry and a brief tour of the town night spots was followed by a spontaneous congregation of the ship's company in the Keppels Head pub by the Hard as we all had a last drink with the friends we'd made during the week but whom we'd probably never meet again.

I3.

Struggling back on board at 23.30 I found I was "volunteered" for harbour watch duty, which meant standing around on the bridge from midnight till 02.00 in near frezing temperatures, drinking mug upon mug of coffee to keep me warm. What we were to guard against, I'm sure I don't know, aS an armed security guard was patrolling the pontoon beside us. Relieved at last, sleep was very welcome, but not for long, as we were all roused at 05.30 for the final clear up below decks before our departure. There was a bustle of washing and scrubbing till 07.00 when we stopped for breakfast. Then at last we signed off and lowered our kit bags into the ferry waiting alongside. As we drew out amongst the silent black submarines around us, we said farewell to the "Malcolm Miller" and hoped that the next occupants of our bunks have as memorable time as we have.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

Our members can indeed be proud of the club's efforts in presenting the 1974 Regatta. Many visitors came up to me to congratulate us on the Organization and to thank us for a most enjoyable weekend. It was particularly encouraging that nearly 40 of our own members took part in the races including some up to their necks in the organizing!
Occasionally, one hears some complaint that the Regatta disrupts our club. This is true of course, but it is our only open event, and our chance to repay the hospitality of other clubs who entertain our own helmsmen at their open meetings throughout the year. In all, 43 clubs were repre- sented at the Regatta.
It would be inappropriate to single out individual efforts-— everyone at the Regatta must be aware of the hard work put in by those responsible for the sailing programme, the racing and rescue, the social events including the refreshments and bar, and the organization of boats and
vehicles.
Many people commented on the well groomed appearance of the club, a tribute to the working parties and Claude.
Our visitors co-operated handsomely in keeping it that way.
I think the thing that impressed me most was the number of people, both club members and visitors, who came up and offered to help, making the chores almost a pleasure!
We had a few panics of course, like blocked loos, but "modified" drainage arrangements and having the changing rooms in the new club house garages, helped enormously. A few stalwarts stayed on for a few days after the Regatta to clean up the site and by the following weekend the club showed no sign of the massive invasion.
We had another record entry, 235 dinghies took part in the points series— quite a spectacle at the start line!
I must admit that the weather helped, although we had a range of conditions from a fresh northerly on Saturday, through a flat calm and abandonment on Sunday morning to ideal conditions of sun and breeze on
Monday.
However, I feel we must be reaching saturation. I hope we don't get another 25% increase next year in spite of the fabulous bar sales.
You cannot have failed to notice the rapid growth of our new club- house -— it must be well ahead ofschedule. We are certainly lucky in hav:
on the front cover enjoying a little relaxation) who is not only a first class builder but also has the a great interest in the Club's
activities.

DENNIS BYATT. Commodre.

P.S. Thanks to Harry Holts offer to visit the Cambridge Agricultural Sales
we now have a brand new rotary mower at a second hand price.

NAVIGANS CONSUMER SERVICE........"WHICH BOAT",

There has been much discussion within the club as to whether or not we should have and race another dinghy class.To help anybody thinking of buying a new dinghy, I have asked four club members, with individual dinghies to do a "Which" report on their boats. Editor.

Let's have a Lark.

The Lark racing dinghy with its fast round bilges and flat after sections is moulded entirely in GRP and can be bought with wooden decks. The only other wooden features are the main thwart and rudder assembly, the centreboard being aluminium, as are the Proctor spars. Designed by Micheal Jackson of National 12 fame and first sailed in 1967, it is moulded by John Baker in Devon. The Lark can be obtained from several South Coast or Midlands builders who will also supply the boat in kit form.
This dinghy is 13'4" L.0.4., 5'53" beam and the hull weighs a
convenient 185lbs. The mainsail is 75 square feet, the jib 30 square fee. and the spinnaker is 80 square feet. All this adds up to a two man racer with a P.Y. of 93 (which may go down to 94). There is built in buoyancy below the foredeck and the side benches and transom flaps and auto bailers are allowed. There is a ggod deal of freedom allowed in the internal lay- out to suit the owner and sheeting can be centre-main or transom with sliding horse.
At the January 1973 count there were 1,250 boats registered, some of
these going to the U.S.A. where they are very popular,as they seem to be
in U.K. Universities. The 1972 National Championship attracted 105 boats.

Eddie Edwards.

CHOOSING A SINGLE HANDER- THE LASER.

My first consideration when choosing a single hander was low main- tenance, which menat fibre glass construction and from past experience with other classes, equally important a boat designed for this material. A boat designed for wood and later built in fibre glass is not competitive as there is a weight probelm that can only be overcome by reducing the thickness of the fibre glass, which makes the boat less rigid than the wooden predecessor. This has an adverse effect, particularly in choppy waters and I completely rejected all boats initially designed in wood. A very strict one design was a must as after the initial purchase I did not want to find drastic ‘improvements' allowed that would create expense in keeping the boat up to date. This feature would also ensure a good re-sale value as an old boat would basically the same as one newly
produced.

Capsizes are inevitable and I required a boat that could be quickly righted with the minimum of effort. In addition when the correct way up I did not want a boat that held water like a gold fish bowl, as so many do. A dry cockpit and ready to sail away was what I was looking for.
I found all these features in a sleek contemporary boat named the
‘Laser'. It is without - doubt the fastest growing Single handed dinghy in
England and ati least 14,000 have been registered Internationally. The dinghy is extermely simple, light and easy to handle with a most exhiler— rating performance.

This is not just a fun boat and once the beginner has mastered the basics, racing competition can be found practically anywhere in the world. Many local clubs have adopted the class and transport is no probelm as the boat can easily be car topped for holidays and open meetings.

THE BONITO

The Bonito has been designed by the British builders of the Finn to provide a 14'6" G.R.P. single-hander of considerable speed combined with stability, the hull shape bearing comparision with that of a Hornet. Although designed as a single handed racer, it will also carry one or two passengers and therefore has a considerable appeal to the family man. It has a simple cat rig sail of 88 square feet sleeved on to a jointed aluminium mast, making it possible to prepare the boat for sailing in under ‘Ye minutes.
The Bonito weighs only 120lbs and is easily car topped for holidays; I have taken one to Syke for the last two summers for family: sailing. A new Bonito cost approximately £250 but can be bought for as little as £120 second hand, and as the boat requires virtually no maintenance, it IMakes a relatively inexpensive second boat to buy and keep up. Sailing at the moment off a Portsmouth No of 104, the Bonito may well prove to be under handicapped when sailed skilfully against the more established Solo and Laser.
There are already three Bonitos at Marconi and one or two more would give this promising boat a competitive cnace to show its considerable pace. How about it!

THE SOLO

I suppose that we all have our problems at some time or other. In 1972 I was sailing my Mirror with son Mark, then aged 8, as crew. He seemed to enjoy sailing, particularly racing, but after the National Championships at Liandudno he started to rebel. This may have been due to the fact that club racing seemed tame after the Nationals or perhaps he wanted to stay ashore with the non-sailing kids, not seen for some time due to over—lapping
holidays.

6.

Of course, he may have finally got fed up with being blamd for my mistakes. Before that season ended we did have some very good and enjoyable racing, however, it was obvious to me that he did not wish to race all the
time.
My solution to this probelm was to find some alternative and I set about finding a second boat, a single hander.
Choosing the Mirror in 1970 was simple. Sailing was something I wanted to try and I had no interest in racing. I wanted a cheap boat with good second hand potential. It had to be new becuase I usually do very badly when I try to buy second hand. A Mirror kit seemed the obvious choice, and the fact that the Club reorganized the Mirror Class played little or no part in the decision.
With the new boat the problems were not the same. I was now interest- ed in racing and had there been a singlehanded club class I would almost certainly joined that.
Factors that I considered important included:-—
A Portsmouth number between 95 and 105 i.e. not to hairy.
A reasonably well established boat with good second hand potential. Enough of a boat to cruise with the family occasionally.
A boat that would give me some close racing locally i.e. in the range of the Blackwater and Thames.
A boat that other typical club members might possibly buy in the future. I decided that a Solo best met my requirements mainly because in 1973 there were twoopen meetings planned on the Blackwater for Solo's. In addition Solo's did in fact sail at our Regatta as a class and also at Stone for the Blackwater and Colne Championships. Boats that I rejected after careful consideration included the Laser, Bonito and the Moth, but of course it would take to long to give all my reasons.
As for price, in 73 I paid just under £320 for a G.R.P. boat with better than average sails and spars. Although at the same time Don Claydon purchased a wooden boat second hand which I thought was very good value at
&170.
At the start of the 73 season my new boat took me round the course, but after awhile I felt that I was slowly gaining the upper hand.I enjoyed the larger club handicap events and my cruising extended from Maldon to Bradwell. I was particularly pleased to come fourth out of twenty-one in two of the races at the Harlow Open meeting.
Crew problems! Yes, I still have crew problems, son Mark now complai that the Mirror is not raced enough!

MY ADVENTURe IN THE SOLENT

by
@ very amateur "SAILOR".

It was Easter Monday, and we were "parked", sorry moored in Ports- mouth harbour. The weather was perfect when we boarded the boat at 8.30am Every where was calm and peaceful and hardly a soul to be seen.
An hour later we were on our way, or is it underway, and quite an experience for me- a novice— squirming my way through the hatch with instructions (shouted by my husband) to 2ix the front sail. It wasn't ay fault i put it on up side down=— or was it!
By this time quite a breeze was blowing and we wended our way in and out and around the other boats, had a good look at all the R.N. cruisers etc. anchored around and sailed out of the harbour with me trying to look as experienced as my husband.
Suddenly we were rocking from side to side and I take a quick look at my mate expecting to hear the command "Get ready to jump". His face is as immobile as ever,however, on seeing my stricken look he mutters "Just the swell of the ferry". In the distance the Hydrofoil is bearing down upon us with a roar, but with a flashy glow passes by without causing much disturbance. Then the Hovercraft looms into view and what a beauti- full thing it is and gone by in a flash. Beginning to wish there was just a little rowing boat about, which we could overtake. The old Forts are in sight and soon passed and the navigator:has his charts out and can tell . me the names of all the buoys as we reach them. One of these had a bell inside tolling.
To the left of us is the Isle of Wright and at this time I suggest having our coffee and sandwiches. Unseasoned sailor that I am I travel on all fours to get in the cabin for the lunch bag and out again, and sit with coffee in one hand and a sandwich in the other and wish I had a Spare one to hang on with as we are travelling at a good speed. My first bite of the sandwich is taken while I am low in the water, then whoops I am on high.my food has gone down with a big clunk, leaving me feeling quite uncomfortable. Another thing I must learn- How to eat with the boat in motion.
Osbourne House, Queen Victoria's favourite home is to the left of us. and Cowes Castle, and at last we are sailing just oft Cowes. More coffee etc. well masticated this time, we decide after three to four hours sail-- ing to make our return journey, which my Captain says will take much longer because of the tide. We turn tail, or is it sail — and head for
home.
Across the water I think I can see one of the "Around the World Yachts", returning but cannot quite make out the name through the binocu-
lars.
At great speed now, we are tacking across the water and I begin to feel a bit uneasy again. The water looks very close to me so I crawl across to the seat opposite and hang on for dear life.
Ryde Pier is in sight and we see the train coming out to pick up passengers. The Ferry, Hydrofoil and Hovercraft are still in action, all doing good business that day.
Portsmouth harbour is before us, but we are having a little diffi- culty getting in, after much tacking we make it. Halfway back to the moor- ing a large motor boat roars straight at us, and then we notice someone taking our photograph. The name of a well known Yachting book was written on the side, so who knows we may have our picture in the paper.
Finally we reach the mooring about 7.30pm feeling tired and cold. Get everything shipshape, jump in the dinghy and my sturdy shipmate rows me to the shore. He considers we have sailed thirty miles that day.

9.

Crouching in the dinghy ready to jump out I catch my foot in something and there I am flat on my face on the hard with my face in about two inches of water. What an inglorious end toa most exciting day.
My legs are badly bruised and my knee cap still hurts, so would all lady members of the club please walk with a limp for a while. I should hate being identified as the biggest nit on and off the water.

EDITORIAL

Come one, come all, is our motto on Open Day and they did, including the Sanitary Department, who proceeded to empty the cess pit, adding that extra spice to the wind!! Snowgoose was busy- she is always a favourite for "sixpenny trips around the bay", and it was very nice to see Ian and Frances taking a busman's holiday.
As it was Mid-Summer's Day, we celebrated by dining on cold Christmas Pudding and custard and then joined the 18 footer's for an impromtu barbecue on the beach, Since they are all qualified "cordon noir" bonfire chefs, there was only a minimal risk of food poisQning!! The combined dinghy/cruiser cruise to Brightlingsea, unfortunately clashed with a visit from Marconi/Elliot's, from the Medway and also we didn't have very good weather. However, five cruisers and three dinghies, the Enterprise Up and Over, Dave Polley and son and F. Partlett's Mirror 16 went down to the Colne. All except F. Partlett stayed the night, Colin and Mike even refused berths on Snowgoose and pitched their tent on the saltings. We all had an enjoyable weekend despite the rain.
DON'T FORGET, to buy your Barbecue tickets for July 19th.

Brenda Tate.

COMMODORE'S NOTES

I hear the Open Day on 22nd June was well enjoyed and we were lucky with the weather again. I missed it as I had the opportunity of a few days holiday and John Witter, with a band of helpers, kindly took
over.
At least six new Marconi membership applications were received and we hear that many of our club members and their families also enjoyed the day, especially the boat trips. There is a suggestion that we change the format next year, and pay more attention to events for our own members- as well as inviting other Marconi people who we hope will join. Any ideas!
Sunday July 14th is an important day for the club -— it is our turn
to run the Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championships at Stone. The turn of each club comes every 13 years or so; about 150 dinghied take part, so it is almost as exciting as our regatta.
We would be especially grateful of help with Spotting as this is one of the most important factors in ensuring a smooth running race programme. So please, if you can possibly come along by about 9.a.m. at Stone you will be most welcome. It would be useful, but not essential, if you would let John Weedon, or any committee member know beforehand.
It looks as if the new clubhouse will soon be finished at least as far as the building is concerned. The present suggestion is that the formal opening will be coupled with the "Fitting Out Party" in March 1975. However, before then, there will be plenty of chores —- fittings for the changing rooms, curtains, site clearing , paths to be laid and grass to be sown, so we hope that you will all be making a mental note to reserve a day or two during the winter to join in one or other of these
activities.
Turning to be serious matters, I must remind boat owners that it is their duty to inform the owner of any boat that they damage or even just hit. In the case of boats under sail, this is not a probelm, but there have been one or two cases recently where moored cruisers have been hit and there have been delays in reporting. Unless the owners are informed as soon as possible, even more damage could ensue. Names of owners are in the clubhouse, but in case of difficulties the Mooring Secretary, Vic Tate will help. ,
A number of members have asked if the proposed Ramsey Wick Marina will seriously affect the club. We knew, of course, that outline planning approval had been given for the Marina long before we bought the site. However, we must be alert to any aspects which could be detrimental to our facilities, and to this end we are in communication with the owners agent, making sure that our well established usage of moorings, hard, access etc are in no way degraded.
Incidentally, may I remind you that the minutes of Committee meetings are put up in the Clubhouse in order to keep members informed of the business of the club, so please read them from time to time, as there is usually some reference to these things.
Lastly some bad news. I sec that V.A.T. is payable on hard fees and moorings as from Warch 1lst., 1974!!- so thats another 80p to pay next year. I hear that a tax on the wind is being prepared for 1976, at a rate proportional to the Beaufort scale, divided by amount of rainfall multi- plied by hours of sunshine!!

D. Byatt, Commodore.

T.W.HALLAM Esq decd.

On the first day of July 1974 a Sailor and a Gentleman hy the name of Terence Walter Hallam died at the early age of 54.
He leaves a Wife, Children and Grandchildren to whom deep sympathy is extended on your behalf in their sad loss.
Simple and true words and facts behind which lie a great human struggle against a long illness.He suffered and died bravely and this last great quality was typical of the boldness with which he lived and which this brief obituary will attempt to portray. Many others are more qualified than I to write of Terry but this account is of a man known to me first as an acquaintance in business and then as a friend — over more than two decades.
Vy very first sailing experience was on a converted 'smack' which he then owned. We were sailing on a very enjoyable reach down the Black- water when he suggested that 1 take a look forward. This I did, only to turn and find him approaching me with no-one at the helm. To say I felt concerned would be an understatement. Recognising my concern and with "that's all right, mate" he continued his walk around the decks, return- ing to the stern of the boat reaching the helm in time to correct our course and so avoid another boat beating across our bows.
He loved the sea and boats, and , as an expert and audacious sailor would have been in his element in the old days of the buccaneers. Many splendid and sometimes infuriating episodes form the backcloth of my memories of Terry but- at the front of the stage stands the man so many of us admired and will continue to remember with much pleasure and a little sadness.
As a founder member of The Marconi Sailing Club he will be remembered for his organising ability and participation. He was a man of
vision, a builder, a scrounger (in the nicest, legitimate way - let me
hastily add) the latter characteristic being very necessary in the earlier years of a struggling Club. The qualities and Individualism needed to assist in the building of our Club were found by Terry for besides holding many other offices he served as Commodore on two separate occasions each lasting 3 or 4 years. His last period in Office covered the time when vital decisions affecting the club's future were
made and the barge "Mamgu" -—- then our headquarters at Heybridge - was
sold and we moved to Stansgate.
Here under his leadership the present clubhouse was erected and the site opened up with high hopes for the future. His experience and success will never be equalled in the Club, for he lead during the days of "do it yourself" when each member contributed to its work and growth, when unity and friendships were taken for granted.
He was a great ambassador and as a member of other well known clubs and associations on the river brought great credit to both himself and us. His popularity, without question, was well deserved for he was known and :
admired by sailors and friends connected with the sea in all the Essex and Suffolk rivers and many elsewhere.
A happy man, generous to his companions, a man of compassion, young at heart and appreciative of the good things in life, who was devoted to his wife and family.
His cheery "Hello mate" will be sadly missed for he nows sails the seas of tranquility. Some of us will perhaps hear that same creating as the wind billows our sails for a long time to come; and that same wind will bring water briefly to our eyes.
Such was the man.
Farewell Terry - mate.

Stan Allerton

1974 Police Regatta

The annual Police Regatta this year was again held at Stansgate on
Monday lOth June, when 30 dinghies attended, some coming from as far away
as Hampshire, Sussex, Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire, London and Southend. The weather was not brilliant and there were some showers but not enough to damp the proceedings and the visitors had plenty of good sail- ing and altogether, a most enjoyable day. Calm conditions prevailed in the morning, exept for one unexpected squall, which sent the dinghies flying with several capsizes, and the morning race lasted over four hours necessitating the postponement of the afternoon race, Eileen Hodges and Robina Boswell did stalwart duties as race officers in fact, they were in the race box all day and even worked out the results; Crystal was on the flags.
The police launch Watchful moored off the club and served as rescue boat for the racing, helping to bring back the capsized dingies to the hard, the crew coming ashore for refreshments between the races. Malcolm Moore was in charge of the proceedings and attended to the
booking-in.
George Charlton did a brisk business in the bar and Margaret Cottam was in attendance in the galley, and Alf had a swim!
Wireless communication between Watchful, the clubhouse and the race box was continuous and the equipment seemed to function perfectly - probably the police have a depot at their headquarters, which is constantly overhauling the equipment.
It had already been decided to hold next year's Regatta at Thorpe Bay because more over-night accommodation for the visiting crews would be available in that district, but Dennis Byatt, in his address of welcome to the visitors, predicted that they would soon tire of the mud and limited sailing time there and would be back at Stansgate before long. The Chief Constable's Trophy for the best performance by an Essex helmsman was won by Arthur Hodges.
Our Commodore and Vice-Commodore arrived in time to see the Chief Constable, John Nightingale present the prizes and he thanked the Marconi Sailing Club for their hospitality and making their premises available to them.
The organization was superb and the discipline of such a high standard that my duties as 0.0.D. were light, in fact, my wife and I passed a most res tful and enjoyable day.

Eric Payne

Arising on Saturday morning, it was disappointing to find that the rain was still with us, neverthe less the boat was made ready and sails hoisted just in time to prevent the receding tide leaving "Jo" stuck

The bad weather we've been having makes it seem all the more fortunate that we did so well with our major events earlier in the season. We appear to have suffered little damage in the recent gales.
The final stages of work are being carried out on the new clu house- interior fittings, main supplies, decorating etc., but we are not pressing to use it this season.

Vic Tate, Ron Rider and myself had a meeting with Bidwells, who are the agents for the new Marina developement. Il have been known to flood the kitchen out by leaving the plug in the sink and the tap running, over-flowing the washing machine, but never before have I flooded our boat "Carasou".
It all happened on the last leg of our holiday. We had said cheerio to Tony and Wendy Cherry and their family in Brightlingsea and set off a day earlier for our Stansgate mooring, as we were due at a weddings on the
Saturday.
It was a lovely sunny afternoon with a good breeze as we tacked up the River Colne. As we passed the wreck buoy off East Mersea the sky look- ed very ominous ahead. A great black mirk lay right across the horizon. I told Ken, my husband, I didn't like the look of the weather ahead, his only comment being,"We'll just get the edge of it". What a hope, as we discovered later.
The wind got up and I still wasn't happy about the weather around us, so Ken went up and reefed the mainsail, while I took the helm. Then it all happened, the storm broke right over us, lightning flashing, thunder and howling wind. Poor "Carasou" was toboggoning down the waves with their saps being blown off at great speed. All sails were then dropped.
I then got the instruction to go down below and turn off the sea- cocks. (It was all rushing around as far as I was concerned). I managed to do the 'loo' by lying flat on my stomach because of the movement of the boat, and then I thought of the sink. As I turned the sea-cock it didn't seem to be going home, so I turned it the other way, then to my amazement it came away in my hand and the water started to pour in. I grabbed the tea cloth and pushed it into the hole, and then held up the sea-cock to show Ken what I had done. Poor devil went white, and shouted something like "you bloody fool, we'll sink!" (I'm sure I'm not the only crew member that has ever been called a 'b' fool).
All hell was then let loose!! I was put on the helm, (storm still going and wind howling) whilst Ken went below to try to do something to stop the boat filling up. It was no good, turn round and run for Bright- lingsea were my instructions, which I duly carried out. It took all my strength to hold "Carasou" at that time. My only thought was, I think he is trying to get rid of me. This must be why the insurance man called by appointment the other week, Ken knew this was going to happen. I just sat rigid with fright. It was hard to believe that the river had ever been so calm as we sailed up to the wreck buoy.
A minor repair done, ken came back on the helm again and I spent the rest of the journey to Brightlingsea on my knees with my hand over the pipe to stop any further water pouring in.
Back in Brightlingsea we saw the Cherry family. They weren't surprised to see us back: again. We told them about our sea-cock drama. I was immediately taken onto "Ace" by Tony and Wendy’ had a tot of brandy at the ready. She also had the kettle on. Was I pleased to be on "Ace" with Wendy again who was a great help. Tony then helped Ken to mend the sea-cock and mop up.
That night it was decided that I should be sent home before I did any more damage. John Smith was telephoned and asked to come and pick me up, which he duly did. Isn't it nice to have such good friends. On leaving Ken was trying to explain to me how to get the hot water on at home. Tony's comment was, "I wouldn't bother, you'll probably go home and find her sai!- ing around the bungalow in a wooden box".
The irony of the tale is that it wasn't necessary to put the sea-cock under the sink off in any case, as the pipework had been diverted somehow, to prevent water from coming up into the sink.
"Carasou" was taken back to her mooring by Ken the next day, but on coming out of Brightlingsea, he left the helm, to go below for a his sweat- er and ran aground. The boat then lay over for 24 hours, but to make it look deliberate he spent his time over the side cleaning "Carasou's" bottom,

4.

Good thing I wasn't on board, it would have probably been my fault!!!

Avril Stephens.

P.S. By the way we made the wedding after all.

ROULETTE = EAST COAST LOG 26TH JULY - 11TH AUGUST 1974

Friday evening saw us all at Stansgate where the trip was started in true
cruiser style within the clubhouse drinking to its success. It was a perfect evening and we reminisced over the fateful start of last year's Calais trip. However this definitely felt different and the weather forecast certainly sounded
hopeful.

Despite the fact we had stocked up Roulette with stores to avoid delay on the
Friday evening we still managed to fill our dinghy to capacity without taking any
of the crew aboard!! We were to be five on this trip and I must say I looked on the fortnight confined on a 21' boat with mixed feelings! Last year only three of us attempted the full trip with two extra for the last five days. Also at least three of us had grown since last year. Roulettes water line was well down as ve had taken enough tinned food for a siege and toys to amuse. These had to be cut rather drastically after foolishly telling the children to pack a few things they would like to take! "No not your badminton set Tim or the entire contents of your bookshelves Carol."

After drinking to a successful trip it was moorings away and down to Bradwell to anchor within the barrier and bed by 10.30 p.m. in anticipation of an early start. Peter says he didn't sleep much that night but it did not stop him having to be woken by the alarm set for 04.15. As you may remember from last years log Roulette though a stalwart sailor before the wind does need a bit of waxing to keep up with the fleet which means we usually get two hours less sleep than the others en route. We set out at 04.50 and were pleased to see one other person awake, Stan waved us off dressed for the occasion in his pyjamas. It was quite light with a Westerly force 3-4 blowing as predicted. We watched a superb sunrise at 05.15, one of the bonuses of an early start.

04.50 Motor sailed close to Bradwell bank following 8 knot buoys until we took course 85 M.

05.15 St.Peters Chapel due South, altered course to 115°M for approx. 1] hour.

06.10 Changed course to 95°M, with a good swell running.

06.30 Weather forecast W.5.

06.35 North Eagle abeam. On time, engine cut.

08.10 Gun fleet old Lighthouse and the Red Cliffs of Holland on Sea in line. We were therefore twenty minutes ahead of our calculated minimum speed and on a gorgeous broad reach. We really had to make sure we kept our pace up to make the passage and ensure arrival at the Ore entrance an hour after low water when the flow out of the river would have ceased.
The following sea certainly affected the crew, two breakfasts were cooked but only one eaten and that with great difficulty! The children were still asleep, another bonus when we are aboard they always sleep late.

08.45 Passed Walton Pier, Medusa dead ahead 55°M.

09.05 Passed Medusa fair eddy behind the buoy with the tide sweeping. Wind freshening but the sea still flat, crew feeling less queasy. We were able to lash the tiller and set course 30°M and it was at least an hour before we came to the Harwich Channel.

09.20 Large ferry came by us.

09.40 Chris awoke and decided to get up!

09.45 Carol, reading as usual in her bunk, Tim writing his log.

10.15 North Cork, we had made 5° of leeway from Medusa, so steered 20°M to compensate to Orford Haven.

11.15 Off the entrance to the River Ore, much earlier than expected, really too early, the last thing we had dreamed of. However, the wind had been an ideal one for the boat and for once the rest of the fleet hadn't overtaken us. We had also stood well out to sea in the strongest tide and wind. We had to motor sail against the tide up the river, now with the rest of the fleet, and turned into Butley Creek and anchored together, eleven boats in all, just South of Boyton Dock where once barges collected bricks from the local works. The children were soc ashore, making a camp in the derelict brick barn by the dock. After lunch we went aboard Tijo for a drink and natter and after a short "kip" we went ashore with the Cherry family to explore. Later the younger members provided plenty of spectator sport for us with water fichts in the dinghies. Perhaps J enjoyed it better because my children were not involved and I didn't have to hang out all their clothes to dry on the stays!! Luckily it was a warm dry evening. We were exhausted by this time but could hardly believe our luck at being at our chosen destination on the first night of the trip, ensuring maximum time to explore down the coast. At this time we didn't realise how fortunate we really were for Avril and Ken Stevens couldn't make the passage until the following Thursday!

Sunday 28th July

Sunny morning but very windy, possibly 5-6 W, certainly glad we made our passage yesterday. The Butley proved a very pleasant anchorage and was sheltered enough for the younger ones to sail around in the dinghies to their hearts content which we left Tim doing as we made our way towards the village of Boyton after breakfast. The store, though marked on the map was not there any more, the village comprised only a few houses of various ages and a pub. En route up the farm track and along the lane we saw hundreds of rabbit holes and a lizard, a beautiful pale green, basking in the sun. Carol and Chris were left on the village green to play
on the swings while we continued our walk - they are lazy types - on our return they
had made friends with the 'natives' and Chris had acquired a large pram wheel. We
hopefully tried to dissuade him from carting it back aboard - yet another space
filler - but the locals insisted most generously that he take it. We met a local
retired farmhand on our way back to the boat who told us that once sheep and pigs were the money makers in this area but now everything was being ploughed up and mens work being taken over by machinery. "Brainless lot" he concluded "send out the hedge trimmers immediately the blackberries are ripe!" We lunched in true Ploughmans style on beer, bread and cheese and lovely local timatoes. We loved the atmosphere here so decided to stay on for a while longer when the others set off towards Orford. Je agreed to meet up later. That afternoon all five of us decided to take the dinghy to the head of Butley River and we made good way with the wind behind us. The saltings were swarming with birds, oyster catches, black headed gulls, terns shelduck, heron and many we could not identify. Their cries followed us up the river and we seemed to be the only people around. We went around several times and waited for the tide to rise to carry us farther on our way. We carefully avoided the oyster beds which in recent years have been restocked by the Butley Orford Oysterage and are now yielding a million oysters 4 year. Oyster beds existed here from Roman times until the 1920s.

Having decided we had had enough of the cramped conditions Carol and I wisely chose to walk back to the boat, exploring the countryside around Butley Low Corner farm, and seeing the ruins of Butley Abbey founded in 1171. Tt now stands back from the river but evidently when it was built a fleet of barges were able to bring the stone for its erection to a quay beside it. Records show there was a constant struggle to hold the tides at bay but little by little the marsh land was reclaimed and in 1500 the Priory scribe wrote that the newly walled marshes were only drowned by the occasional high tide.

We came over the hill above Butley Ferry to see the others fighting the tide back. They were tacking, rowing one leg and sailing the other and getting nowhere. We sat on the hill and watched them be rescued by a chap in a motor boat who gave them a tow. We were back to the boat by 6 p.m. and off to Orford and in half an hour were directed by a local boatman onto a mooring opposite the hard. This was 30p well spent for the tide really races up and down this river and we tried to avoid rowing across at other than slack high or low water. It is definitely an advantage to have an outboard motor for a dinghy on this trip.

Monday 29th July

We awoke to a gorgeous clear blue sky behind Orford Castle, a beautiful sicht and we were ashore by nine o'clock. We walked up the pretty main street with cottages to either side but not a sign of life and what peace. The shops seemed hidden too until we found milk and papers in a cottage sitting room and a general stores tucked around a side turning. we finished our shopping and then explored the Castle which is extremely well preserved. It stands high on a hill and commands an excellent view across the river and countryside. Before the lighthouse was built iron baskets with lighted beacons were set up upon Orford Castle. Tradition says that the port was thriving in the 9th century when the town was said to extend far beyond the castle where there are now green fields. The then castle was not built but Orford haven was a snug anchorage and trade and fishing flourished. A fleet of ships brought stone for the new castle in 1165 and berthed at the newly built quays below it.

The children were delighted to explore the dungeons and we saw the banquet hall with its stone ovens and the earliest equivalent of wash hand basins with tunnels behind to shoot the water out, the 'loos' worked on a similar shute principle. The view from the top of the keep was marvellous both out to the river and inland, we could see Sizewell Power Station clearly. We lazed and sunbathed out of the wind all day and enjoyed the local Admams beer pumped by an old fashioned lift pump. We bought smoked salmon from the Orford Oysterage, but did not try the oysters whose beds we had drifted over the previous day. At 4.20 p.m. we left the mooring under motor but soon set two foresails and mizzen and cut the engine. Later we needed the mainsail as the wind appeared to drop. Actually we found we were hammering along so made good time.

17.15 Martello Tower at Slaughden Quay abeanm.

18.30 Joined the "fleet" at "The Oaks" and went ashore for a beach barbecue. Ropes had been attached to the huge trees on the shore line and by the end of the evening it wasn't only the children that were samplin; the swings! We lit a huge fire and cooked sausages and beans and concluded the evening sitting on the hill above in full song!

Tuesday July 30th

The "fleet" was on its way but we chose to make our way by dinghy towards Snape Maltings at the head of the river. The route was very twisting and shallow and one could not help wondering how the schooners of the 1800's with their 10 foot draughts navigated the fortuous channel to Snape Bridge. All these vessels were engaged in the coal and corn trade berthing at Iken Cliff where the firm had its coat yard and voyaging as far as Rotterdam, London, Famersham and Chatham. About 1860 ketch barges or "boomies" appeared and replaced the schooners because of their lichtness of draught and smaller crew. They traded between the Snape Maltings and Cardiff with Welsh coal. Sprit sail barges used the river in large numbers during the last century, probably some of them carried the bricks for building the Martello Towers at Shingle Street about 1810. The Snape granaries were built by Newson Garrett a merchant and ship owner of Aldeburgh in the middle of the century. The last sprittles are said to have been seen in Snape in 1928. However we were able to pull up beside the barge "Redoubtable" after negotiating the red can, black flasged Channel, and climbed up the quayside to view the lovely Malting buildings now the centre of the Aldeburgh Festival. We browsed around the craft centre and had a snack at the "Plough & Sail". Peter and the children set sail again for the 'Oaks' and I.walked across the cornfields beside the marshy land. It was very picturesqu but I could hardly be described in the same way once I had waded through thigh high mud to get aboard Routlette! This was one of the hazards of the "Oaks", it is extremely unpleasant at low tide.

15.30 saw us leaving the anchorage, having lost the dinghy off the back of the
boat - who had tied it on! - and regained it, thanks to the rapid action of
a fellow boat owner with an outboard motor! It started to rain as soon as we left the mooring but we negotiated the narrow passage and with a fair wind only had to motor for a short time. However it died again in Short Reach and we just made it onto a mooring above Aldeburgh when a sudden squall came and it poured.

17.20 Cosy on board cooking up meal, Roulette's smallness is an asset on these occasions. By the time the meal was finished it had turned into a lovely
evening.

18.30 Tim rowed across to Jappa to find Ian had gone with a crowd to see "The Three Muskateers" at the local cinema.
Ten minutes later we were all on our way! The walk to the cinema seemed endless with the children clamourix.
to know if they were going to miss the beginning! The cinema was housed in a Tudor styled building reminiscent of a centile tea house and at a price unheard of in most places Peter plus three children saw the film, the combined price was 65p! I refused to sit in a cinema on a nice evening so met up with some more of our party coming ashore and walked en masse to the lifeboat, the loot Hall and coastguard look out post. It must be noted that on this occasion we walked for nearly two hours and passed every pub! The others told us of their dire experience when trying to anchor earlier in the day. They apparently set out 10 fathoms of chain in 3 fathoms of water but the wind and current sailed the boats around so that they all went adrift amongst the moorings, all nine of them! So the moral of the tale is don't anchor at Slaughden the round is not suitable.

The weather looked a little threatening so I hitched a ride aboard Routlette and was asleep when Peter returned at around eleven o'clock. They had enjoyed tlhe film - which I had already been assured of when others of our party arrived from an earlier showing saying 'We heard Peter enjoying himself’. I wonder how they knew he was there! The phosphorescence on this night was marvellous with orange, purple and kingfisher blue light from the water as we sped across the water with the motor on.

Commodore's Notes

In these my first notes as your Commodore and in succeeding notes I will try to continue the policy, so well establish by Dennis, of keeping you as much informed on club affairs as possible. First, however, it is my pleasant duty to say thank you for the hard work done by the members of last years main and sub-committees and particularly those who did not seek re-election at the A.G.M, after several years service, It was a real pleasure to work with you all and I look forward to what I hope will be a successful year with a new Committee on which there are both new and familiar faces and a new Club home,

The first major item of news is that the Clubhouse has now been handed over and has become the property of the M.A.S.C,. and we the Sailing Club members are the custodians of the property and responsible for its management. This event actually took place on Wednesday 27th November.

This custodianship is something your committee takes very seriously and much discussion has taken place on methods of providing the maximum deterent to unwanted guests at Stansgate while still providing the greatest possible freedom for bona fide members of the Club within the constraints imposed by these two aims. As reported at the A.G.M. enquiries have been made to establish the suitability of magnetic locks for use at Stansgate and at the Committee Meeting on December 2nd full discussion was allowed and some conclusions reached, To recap a bit, many of you will know that at least 5 rubber dinghies were stolen from the site during last Season and it is confidently thought that these left by road. Also almost every occasion when members go down outside the usual sailing times strangers are found on the site, ranging from Gypsies trying to find what they can, to picnickers from as far away as London, to Essex residents who claim a right to play in our garden, I have twice in the last two weeks been to Stansgate on business only to find others there uninvited. As you may imagine this gave rise to lively discussion and it was eventually agreed that the only way to keep vehicular traffic off the site (there is public FOOTPATH through the site) and discourage intruders would be to lock the gate, The only practical way to lock the gate and still to provide access to all members arriving by car is to fit a magnetic lock operated by a keycard which is coded, can be produced in large quantities, is uncopyable and returnable if lost without identifying the property to which it gives access. Consideration was then given to access to the Clubhouse and it became obvious that it was desirable to make the same "key" fit the door. It was, therefore, proposed and agreed by the Committee that in the interests of protecting members and club property as far as practical, without placing unacceptable restrictions On members movements, magnetic locks would be fitted to both the gate and Clubhouse and that for this year all members paying a parking fee would be issued with a key which fitted both locks. These locks are expensive and will cost approximately
£325 including installation with a further charge of about £175 for the first batch
of 400 keycards. (There are at present approaching 200 official keys for the old
club in circulation.) This expense will only be justified if members show the necessary sense of responsibility and always lock the Club and gate after them as there will now be no need for members to leave it open for other members without keys, as has been the practice in the past, which lead to the Club being left completely unlocked and unattended for long periods. Further discussion will take place during the year on the methods of issuing keys for future years, the frequency at which all keys need to be changed and the method of covering the cost of these keys.

3.

This is seen as a radical departure from our previous rather lax methods of giving access but it must be remembered that there is not a very large investment in Stansgate made for MSC members and this demands much stricter discipline than previously imposed, and your Committee look for the support and co-operation of all members in making this an effective deterent to our light fingered friends,

Now on to the subject of fitting out the new Clubhouse. The planning sub-committee has now been reformed and will be meeting shortly to continue the process and finalise the plans, so if any of you have ideas about requirements for the club please either drop Ron Greygoose a line or get in touch with your local committee member who will pass on your ideas.

I look forward to seeing many of you at the Christmas Dance on Lecember 14th as I hear the tickets are selling very well. I will close these notes by wishing you all on behalf of the Committee a Very Happy and Merry
Christmas.

John Witter, Commodore.
