THE MARCONI SAILING CLUB — ANNUAL GENERAL WEETING 1974

COMMODORE'S REPORT

It seems no time at all since we met here at the last A.G.M. The object of these reorts must be to highlight the major events of the year and give members some impression of the way the club is developing. We hope you will express your views freely, because the committee are very anxious to take note of members interests,
I recall that last year, 1 was a little disappointed having to tell you that formal planning permission had not yet been received for the new clubhouse. This year I am, of course, delighted to report that the club- house is complete, and is to be formerly handed over this week.
There is no doubt in my mind that the club did the right thing in voting fot the new clubhouse two years ago. No one could have foreseen the fantastic rise in costs that have occurred in the last year or so- I'm sure we would have been very worried about starting to plan for the new clubhouse now, for completion in two years hence.
Ron Rider has continued to be a great help with his advice, and Bernard Lee has acted as Clerk of Works for the M.A.S.C. throughout the construction. Our grateful thanks to them both. Mick Taylor, as all can gee, has done a grand job, not only with the structure, but also with advice and help with those inevitable associated problems which always seem to crop up.
During the year, your committee took several decisions which we felt cure would be in the long term interest of the club. One of these was to avoid, if at all possible, any change of plans which would increase costs and be unfair to the M.A.S.C.However, it became evident that it would be inconvenient, uneconomic and possibly unsafe to use the existing mains cable for the new clubhouse, so we purchased a new cable and Mick put it in for us. He also equipped the galley and improved some of the electrical services, particularly in the garages. The concrete paths were also extended. We considered these extras to be part of fitting out, and legitimate expenses from the clubhouse and precincts account. The bar has been furnished, including the grill, by courtesy of the brewers.
Several of you have commented about the calor gas cylinder, which we agree is rather an eyesore. This had to be a specified distance from the drains, the main building and be accessible from the road so the choice of position was very limited. We hope to camouflage it in due course with fencing and shrubs.
It is intended to make the Fitting Out party next Spring coincide with the opening of the new clubhouse. I think we should have a small formal ceremony for this milestone, and again your comments would be
helpful.
Now to Sailing - I don't want to steal the thunder of our Sailing
Secretary - but after all, sailing is what it's all about. We can't really
say the weather has been up to much, although none of our events were seriously interrupted. The Regatta was another record — 250 boats this time! Thanks to the most generous hard work put in by the committee and many members, it all went well, and the club received a number of compliments, both at the time and since. At least next year there won't be so much queueing for the essential services.
The management of the 1974 Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Handicaps and Cock of the River, by the Marconi Sailing Club was also most gratify- ing, as not only were we praised for the organisation of the races, but we inherited the event with a deficit and handed over to Dabchicks in credit!

De
Our own race programme has been well :@&pported and our sailing secretary will be reporting on this.
The cruiser fleet has been very active, no doubt their regular social gatherings have done much to create a fleet spirit. Certainly the armada which sailed on the East Coast Cruise was pretty impressive and the trip throughly enjoyed by all.
A probelm was raised at the beginning of the season by a request from the Sidney Harbour 18 footers for permission to sail from the club. One of our rules prohibits advertising but we decided to waive this for one year, and you have a proposition to modify that rule tonight.
We have, as you know, been somewhat concerned this year about the possible effects on our club of the new Marina in Ramsey Wick, particularly regarding the sea access and its influence on moorings. We have maintained quite a lot of correspondence on this subject and the developers have taken note of our concern. I think that the last letter I received from Bidwells is as much as we can hope for at the present, bearing in mind that as part of the purchase agreement for our own site, the club agreed not to object to planning permission being given for the lWarina.
a I must now
say a few words about subscriptions. When we asked for hese to be raised two years ago we said we hoped no further increases would be necessary for some time, and this has been so. We could not have foreseen V.A.T. of course although this was luckily minimised last year by virtue of our separate club and hard fees. I'm afraid that from now on though, V.A.T. is payable on the full subscription. Neither could we have foreseen the rapid inflation and so it may not be possible to hold fees at the present level for many more years.
Nevertheless, as you can see from the accounts, we still have a good reserve, in spite of spending on some fitting out for the new clubhouse, the rates, @ new mower, anothe: van etc. We agreed to pay the rates, at least for this year, in lieu of increasing the rent to the M.A.S.C. even though they had to start funding the new clubhouse when building commenced.
Incidentally, the rates have risen from £40 to «150 to £660 over the last
few years. We are negotiating with the valuation officer for a re-assessment and are hopeful of getting a significant reduction, although this may be somewhat negated by the new clubhouse. The exact contribution we shall pay to the M.A.S.C. for the new clubhouse has still to be fixed, although we have discussed this with them fully and the estimated sum was used to -~alculate the increased subs two years ago.
One topic of increasing concern is the security of the site and the new clubhouse. As you may know, several inflatable dinghies have been stolen this year, and I'm afraid quite a few people enjoy the benifits of Stansgate without being members. If we are to protect our personal and club property, we must be prepared to accept some small inconviences. The favoured solution at present is toprovide magnetic locks for the main gate and the clubhouse, and for each member to be issued with a key card, the code for which could be changed each year. This would be expensive, but I'm Sure worthwhile, as it could also affect the insurance premium for the clubhouse and possibly our own boats if the pilfering is not stopped.
Last year the proposal to hold the Laying - Up Supper at the M.A.S.C.
was rejected, but I'm afraid the attendance at the Chancellor Hall this year was not as high as we had hoped. Although the evening was most enjoyable we are worried that the cost for a family is high, and will probably be higher still next year. The final decision for next year's venue must come from the committee but again your opinions will be most welcome.
After sailing, the main activities next year will be fitting out the clubhouse and surronds, and a new planning sub-committee has been set up to tackle this.
Before 1 close my report, 1 would like to remind you that this very successful year has been made possible by the hard work and enthusiasm of & magnificient committee and help from many members.

I am sorry that i cannot manage my third year, due to several unavoidable factors, but I am very happy to give my wholehearted support to the excellent committee proposed for next year.

SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT 1974

The first part of this report covers the club's organised sailing activities, which of course was the published sailing programme. The weather was reasonable kind to us, causing only one occassion when the whole day's racing was cancelled, and even then scratch races were arranged. On the whole the programme was well supported, with the Mirrors emmerging as the largest racing fleet, in fact their summer series had an average entry of over 10 boats. 1t was pleasing to see big turnouts in the Ladies and Cadets Series. The Handicap fleet had regular racing support this season, which should encourage more boats next year. The Enterprises had Similar turnouts to last year and the Hornets slightly fewer. The G.P.14 racing however, was very poorly supported. The Helmsman of the Year final attracted all 10 qualifliers and was won decisively by Julian Bigden.
The more informal events - pursuit races and Wednesday evening races
were very popular. Cruiser racing(Barnacle Points) was disappointing, probably due to some bad race management. On the bright side, however, the cruises in company were successful including a fortnight's Hast Coast cruise with 14 Marconi boats enjoying mixed weather.
Our open events began with the traditional Spring Bank holiday Regatta, which was again blessed with good conditions, had an even larger entry than before. The Blackwater and Colne Dinghy Championships held at Stone, was organised by ourselves, as it was ourturn, ran smoothly and for that I would like to thank all the helpers, particularly the Ladies. The Marconi Dinghy Challenge Cup was again won by our visitors.

At National and international level the Hornets, bnterprises and liirrors were in attendance with Marconi Enterprises again amongst the leaders. The rescue and Race Officer duties on the whole were efficent and it
is up to us all to assit when required - one only gets out of the club
what is put into it.
Your comments would be welcome on any club matters as it is important that the activities are run for the benéfit of our members and they will therefore, be fully supported in return.

I find myself writing this article in my new capacity as cruiser captain- a position 1 attained in circumstances noneto clear to me, but which reminds me of the soldier left standing when the rest of the troops step backwards on hearing the call for volunteers. The cruiser fleet gathered again in strength at the General's Arms, Little Baddow on Thursday 5th December, and amidst the beer and the laughter, had a most interesting discussion with Gordon Swift, the owner and skipper of the stackie barge "Dawn".
Gordon brought along a photograph of Dawn converted to a sailing hay- stack and described the trip to London- the need to dig a trench through the stack in order to lower the mast- the return journey loaded with manure- and back to London again with flour. No wonder our bread no longer has character! Gordon very kindly gave an open invitation to visit Dawn tn Maldon- or whilst on the River, and of course would welcome any charter
arties.
I was sad to read the following article in "Yachting Monthly":- "While at Ibiza --- --- was joined by another ex-West Mersea craft, the Baltic ketch "Soloeig". Later "Soloeig" sailed to the near by island of Formentera prior to setting sail for South America. The day before her departure she dragged her anchor in a westerly gale and went on the rocks;
within twenty-four hours she was a total loss" - a sad way to go.
liany thanks are due to Vic Tate for producing yet another winch from the company archives. Bigger and better than the last, we hope this will reduce the knocking knees and shaky hands of extreme exhaustion from hauling out.
Finally a Merry Christmas to you all, and may your new year be filled with the petrol of your dreams.

Brian Bowsher, Cruiser Captain.

In my last notes I wished you all a happy Christmas and I forgot that the next issue of Navigans would not appear uhtil the New Year and omitted to wish you all a very happy and successful 1975, an omission which I hope I have now rectified.

The process of moving into the new clubhouse has now started, and there will be working parties each Sunday, between now and the beginning of the season to do the physical work of moving equipment and fitting out. Each Sunday some members of the committee will be present and some help each week from members, spread over this period, would be very useful; so if you want a breath of fresh Stansgate air, why not come down and give us a hand, and the benefit of your company. Elsewhere in this issue, you will see a letter to the Editor from Alf Cottam, in which he endorses my comments in the last issue on the footpath through the site. The existence of the footpath has always been weoegnised and was the reason for providing **e kissing gate, when the main gate was installed at the entrance to our premises. What ix perhaps overlowked, by those that want to use the footpath, is the fact that it joins our road near the Eagle gates, and that there is no right of way for vehicles to drive to our boundaries near the farm entrance. (The latest issue of the Ordnance Survey shows the path joining the road at the right hand bend after you pass through the Eagle Gates). Some of you may have noticed that this fact was endorsed in the Daily Telegraph of 6th December, 1974, under the heading, "Wedgie's wailing wall stops riverside stroll". Many of you who are already members of the R.Y.A. will have received the discussion ocument on the proposals for raising money and levying subscriptions, and may have already given it some thought. Your committee, at present, has this under consideration and will be discussing at the next meeting the merits of being either a fully Affiliated club or merely an Affiliated club. Briefly the revised membership proposals are as follows. There will be two types of individual member:-
a) Personal Members paying an annual subscription of £5 (of. present £3).
b) Affiliated Members paying through their club, an annual subscription of &1.
This type of member would be contacted by the R.Y.A. through the club.
c) Fully Affiliated Clubs will collect the £1 R.Y.A. subscription from all their
members, except personal members of the R.Y.A., and forwards their fee to the R.Y.A. The club then pays no annual subscription itself.
do) Affiliated Clubs will pay an annual subscription of 4% of the agreed membership income with a min. of £10 and a max. of £300. For the M.S.C. this would be about the same total as we are currently paying.
Both types of Club membership receive the same benefit, so if you have any views on these proposals, and which type of membership the club should take up, please express them to a committee member.

6.

The log of "Roulette" continued.

Wedn ist Jul

The wind was blowing strongly when we awoke, and we were not at all surprised the others had previously gone adrift for we had sailed around the mooring all night long. Peter had tied the dinghy alongside in desperation for despite a bucket anchor she had bumped for an hour or so earlier. A campaign was mounted after breakfast to get ashore with the minimum effort. We have no motor and the tide was very strong and also we were a good way from the quay. Finally we calculated that we could go over to the nearby saltings and walk along the sea wall to town. We had a very smooth passage ashore and tied the dinghy up. A pleasant half hour walk found us in Aldeburgh and we got all our supplies in a super delicatessen shop and had time to browse in the many lovely bookshops before early closing. Unfortunately by the time we got to the Moot House Museum it too was shut. Obviously another reason to return again in the future. The other reason was the delicious local caught fish and chips which we consummed on the beach in true tradition straight out of the paper, only to be greeted by a past member of E.E.V. staff. He remarked "You certainly look the part, one would never have taken you for an employee of EEV" True praise we felt!

We arrived to collect the dinghy to find we had left it a little late! We hTM* to negotiate three feet of mud to reach the dinghy! But with an assortment of dra.t wood, boxes and planks we achieved our end and it was a much smoother operation than expected! Luck was on our side again for no sooner were we aboard and brewing up a cup of tea when another squall hit us! We had planned to drop down to Butley River but on seeing the Cherry's return to their mooring after setting out half an hour before,we stayed where we were and Peter rowed over to hear how they had got on. They had taken water over the deck in the first leg of the trip with 5 rolls in the main and a storm job! We settled down for a cosy evening and heard on the weather forecast that the winds were force 7-8!

Thurs August lst

The alarm went off at five o'clock and it was very much less windy but still about force 4. We set out for Butley at 5.30 a.m. motoring all the way as the wind was dead on the nose. The sunrise was gorgeous,and made us feel better about getting up so early.

06.30 Listened to the weather forecast off Orford. Gales forecast for Thames
SW5-7, Gale 8 dropping to W4 but increasing later SW5-7. Gallope SW5.
We found the rest of the fleet moored off Orford.

06.50 Pulled alongside Jappa because Jack was on deck. Had a cup of tea and chat. It was hard to believe the gale warnings it was such a pleasant morning but still too late to change our plan and leave for the Deben.

08.10 Left Jappa and though the tide was now reasonably strong against us we managed to make Butley River by 08.50 where we anchored with trip and buoy. We found out unwittingly how they all went adrift at Aldeburgh. We set the tiller to hold towards the bank but in actual fact it enabled the boat to sail. She rode over the trip, trapped it in the propellor or rudder and away we went! Luckily we realised the buoy had disappeared and got worried. Released fairly easily.We sent the children ashore and I tidied up while Peter mended the mizzen where a runner had come adrift. The sun came out and Tim and Chris went swimming, the latter with a life jacket and line on him. After lunch Ace of Diamonds and Whimbrel crews came aboard for a cup of tea. We heard shouting on short and looked out to see Lyn, Dave, Louise and Ian sitting on the bank. They had walked from Orford. They wallowed through the mud and Tim picked them up and with very little free board made their way to Roulette with legs over the side to clean off! Soon the boats appeared and we all went

aboard Jappa.

Friday August 2nd

Peter awoke at 2 a.m. and on glancing out of the porthole found we were alongside Tijo, having drifted downstream past two boats en route! He'd only put out 5 fathoms instead of 8!

Up at 5 a.m. - very misty.

05.40 Left the mooring, motored down on the ebb, very little wind until we were into the main channel of Ore. We put up a mainsail and two foresails but kept the motor going to head better. We found the leading marks hard to see as we were low in the water and the shingle banks were high. However we found them once they were in line, which we felt was a bit late! The course was roughly S.E. with a fair swell coming in the channel. We started to punch the first of the flood which was quite vigorous.

06.20 Passed Ore Channel Buoy and headed down the coast, the wind was on the beam about 3-4. Sea calm with a gentle swell. Cut motor. Woodbridge Haven buoy very easy to distinguish, we aimed for it until the Bar Buoy sighted. We had previously spotted the red can buoy close to shore. Went about almost on top of Woodbridge Buoy. We found we could not hold our heading under sail alone so switched on motor. The course from the Bar Buoy to the Red Can, magnetic North, leading marks dead in line, though we did not realise at first. The A has been replaced by two spades Ww which is orange not black.

This is not an easy river to enter and to be on the correct course one must pass through the roughest water close to the shingle bank. We headed for the red and white chequered buoy on the Horse Shoe Shoal, which becomes very shallow (7 feet) just before it one turns leaving the buoy to port. This despite the fact that the buoy is marked as a middle channel buoy. The shoal was very clearly visible even when we came in 2 hours after low water. We decided that the sails were of no help whatsoever so we motored up on the flood. Just below Ramsholt we spotted a dinghy on the mud, just about to go adrift. There was no sign of a rope anchor or yet footprints away from it, so we pulled up on a nearby mooring and rowed over to investigate. It was just in time because as we took her in tow she floated off the mud. Set off to take her to the nearest yacht club up the river passing Segla and Carasou at Rams Holt. The Stevens hadn't been able to leave Brightlingsea until the previous day. Towing the dinghy was a lark, it scudded from side to side, later Nick Tovey told us we should have dropped the centre plate a little and set the rudder central. We made it up to the Rocks, where the others, who had overtaken us while on our rescue mission, were anchored. We in turn anchored and put out 8 fathoms of chain in 5 feet of water. It was abeautifulmorning and we sunbathed on deck, the children playing happily on shore with ropes on the trees and a sand slide down the steep bank. Most people had a swim. After lunch it clouded over so Peter and I went for a walk to stock up on supplies. We decided we couldn't get to Waldringhamfield, as the path on the 0.S. map didn't look complete so we set out for Shottisham, and were able to do a circular route of approx. 6 miles! The rabbits appeared very tame at first and didn't attempt to run from us, then we realised they were almost blind with bulging eyes, they seemed diseased possibly with myxomatosis.

8.

Partridges by the score flew low out of cornfields or ran under the drops. The farms seemed to specialise in pigs and root crops and we passed a beautiful old tithe barn with grown timbers for the angle beams of the roof. Shottisham was a quiet village with an old church dating from the 135th century. The tower was in need of repair and an elderly lady busy polishing the brass said the population was depleted as the old were dying off and no young families were moving in.

We wanted sausages for our barbecue that evening so bought the store out of them, 8 in all! On the way back we saw hatcheries for the partridges and passed a huge Manor House which caters for shooting parties. Once back at the "Rocks" we collected wood and moved a huge treeroot and trunk in preparation for our bonfire. Meanwhile Roulette went aground and to our horror we found our anchor laid on its side on hard rock, certainly not suitable for anchoring especially near in.
Fortunately we hadn't chosen the bit that shelved steeply to 12', Stan apparently did this one year and landed up at a ridiculous angle. We ate supper and moved to a deeper anchorage with enough anchor chain for a battleship. We rowed ashore at dusk, with a full moon coming up and a huge fire glowing on the beach. What a sight. We once again cooked sausages and also potatoes in the fire and a good time was had by all.

Saturday August 3rd ~Y

After breakfast we set off by dinghy to Waldringhamfield. Jack gave us a tow after we set out trying to sail! We had a drink at the pub and then walked to the Yacht Club to enquire about friends of ours from Woodbridge who were competing in the Deben Week races being held there. Almost immediately Sid appeared and in no time he and Maureen, plus her brother and wife had joined us over another pint at the pub! We told them of our trip but they capped it all by saying they had been out ina Wayfarer outside the bar on Sunday in force 6-7 negotiating a buoy in the middle of the bar! They decided they would like to join us at the Rocks and come to the barbecue so we promised to fetch them that night on Roulette. We sailed and rowed back to the boat with the tide and after lunch Peter went ashore to wash some of the Alde mud off the dinghy. I stayed aboard to do likewise to Roulette ready for the invasion. That evening there was a beautiful wind so we set 2 foresails and a mizzen and did not need any more despite the last of the spring ebb.

We drifted upstream with Carol at the helm and picked up a mooring 20-30 yds off the Maybush Inn. Tim went ashore for water and then ferried our 6 visitors aboard, four adults plus 2 children. They were settled either below or in the cock-— pit and with the main sail hoisted we set off downstream once again. On landing a’ the Rocks we were later told that our party were taken for Pakistani refugees coming ashore! The huge fire was beautiful, someone had even found a hollow trunk to act as a chimney. The only disadvantage on this occasion was the acrid smoke from a
fellow picknickers bonfire - they were burning new wood. At 10.15 p.m. we once again
ferried our party aboard with the kind help of Stan and motored up river, navigating in pitch dark with no moon until we reached a mooring once more off the Maybush Inn. Having ferried our party ashore we were soon in bed with the promise of meeting up with them again in the morning.

Winter Meeting :- Two speakers gave interesting and entertaining talks to about 70 people at our first meeting of 1975.
Sam Poulton from Maldon drew on his great depth of knowledge and experience of the Spritsail barges, that often sail past Stansgate, and gave us a glimpse of the characters who sailed and worked them over the years. Sam owned and raced his own barge some years ago. This was brought for the princely sum of £90 (current selling price £6,000), but because of high maintenance costs, he had to have her broken up; a fate which Sam sadly predicts will overtake many of the present barges on the river. He also showed a film of barge races giving a magnificent view of the massed fleets, and incidentally a glimpse of the virile bargeman's dreams- also magnificent.
John Jowers, a fisherman from Mersea, gave the second talk of the evening. John, formerly a University lecturer turned to full time fishing 2 or 3 years ago, I believe. It was something of e surprise to find that this is an expanding business along the Essex Coast. The theme of the talk was that fishermen and yachtsmen can co-exist without undue fricton on the same waters given common sense, and an understanding of the others man's problems. Drifters apparently, shoot out up to one mile of nets and then drift up the Blackwater with the tide. Here the fishing boat can't get out of the way, the drag of
“= mile of net prohibits any manoeuvre. Pair trawling - that‘is two boats sailing abeam
vc. each other with a massive trawl] net in between, is also carried out on the Blackwater - get caught between those and the chances of losing mast, boat and finishing up on a slab at Billingsgate isn't right out of the question it seems.
Our thanks go to Sam Poulton and John Jowers for an evening well spent.

There now follows the third and final part of Gill Foreman's log of "Roulette".

Sunday August 4th

Peter awoke at 5.30 a.m. and in pouring rain put the tent over our cockpit up. By & o'clock there was a gale blowing so we lazed in, had a late breakfast watching Ace and Segla going upstream. We set out at noon and in really heavy rain, thunder and lightning we made for Woodbridge. Tim and Peter suitably dressed in all their oilies were in charge and we watched the storm from below. One huge flash we found later had put the O'Hara's (the friends we were meeting again) electricity off. We entered the marina quite well but once in, it becomes very narrow and we made a complete hash=-up of getting into a berth, the wind, which was very strong, kept blowing us into the boats while we were trying to turn round. Luckily, Snowgoose, Carasou and Whimbrels crews were at hand to help us! Once in we packed up the boat, collected towels and clean clothes and made our way to meet Sid who had gallantly offered us all showers. Perhaps that was a condition of going to stay with them on second thoughts, we had been afloat for over a week! We had a wonderful day with them, reliving all our times together in the States, where we had originally met. They too are now happily settled in this country and we couldn't blame them liking their setting in Woodbridge. Perhaps I shouldn't mention our evenings entertainment
in what is meant to be a seamans log - Shush!! We went bowling!! On our return it
was damp and cold and we gladly took up their offer of a bed on the floor for the nighy instead of negotiating the damp, dark reaches of Woodbridge Marina.

Monday August 5th

We slept very well and after breakfast took Neil, our friends offspring, in exchange for Carol, swimming. She envisaged a day on terra firma and Neil certainly seemed to like sailing round the Marina and river with Tin. I went in search of stores again and Peter, and the boys braved the outdoor swimming pool. Rack to the boat for lunch after a drink aboard.

Carasou with Ken and Avril, Peter, Neil and Tim went exploring the other side of the river in the grounds of Sutton Hoo. Chris played with Mary beside the boat most of the afternoon, while I read. Maureen arrived with Carol to swop children again and we had a cup of tea aboard, at 7 p.m. we saw them off as we planned to move on once more tomorrow. They promised to come and explore 'our'river next year. We had supper and went to admire the mullet, a 4 1b one, caught by Dave (Starlight). By the end of the holiday he speared one fish for each boat on the trip and they made a lovely meal.

Chris and Tim went to bed and we left Carol with Ian (Jappa) and Peter and I went for a long walk along the river bank. We came back at ten o'clock to find a party in full swing on Tijo and Thundercloud to meet John Swintons arrival, and a hilarious evening was had by all. Luckily there was no one sleeping aboard the boats in the her vicinity!

Tuesday August 6th

Woke about 9 a.m. to a lovely sunny morning and breakfasted on kippers. After lunch we set out for Ramsholt after watching a hair washing ceremony with hoses on the pontoons? We moored at the Tips, just above Waldringfield. It had been recommended by Sid and Maureen. Peter sailed the children ashore to swim and I sunbathed, it was really hot out of the wind, which was bitter. We went down to Ramsholt later and found Carasou, Ace, Segla and Snowgoose. It was a most beautiful evening and sunset. It was Our turn for the mullet that night and it went down a treat with a bottle of wine. The children sailed themselves ashore while I wrote the log and read, Peter plotted our trip for tomorrow, though the weather forecast at 17.55 was not favourable.

Wednesday August 7th

Woke before 6.30 a.m., the weather forecast was still force 4, rising to 5-6. Decided at least to try to go to Bawdsey and as we only have a 1+ hr passage down the coast we shall probably chance it before the 5-6's set in.

08. 30 Left mooring following Snowgoose, with Segla right behind. As we approached
the bar a chap who had just come in remarked that it was pretty rough but it didn't look too bad. With the wind at a maximum force 3 we gauged it was safe to go. There was quite a swell, with waves of two to three feet. The minimum depth on the echo sounder reached 4', In fact with each wave it was 4 foot, seven foot, 4 foot again in rapid succession. Once we were out to sea the waves levelled off and we set course 180°M for Wadgate Ledge. Segla soon overtook us on a close haul. Felixstowe Pier in sight, a really beautifully clear morning.

10.00 Being swept down the coast decided to head straight down 230°M.

0.05 Felixstowe Pier in line.

10.15 Went over the Platters, it showed up as a line of smooth, then rough water,
dropped from 16' - 7' very quickly. Platters Bell could be clearly heard.
We aimed straight for the Rolling Ground buoy, course still 210°-220°M. At this point we took a photograph of a large coaster going out from Harwich. Another boat, probably a dredger came out but did not keep to the channel. Peter jibbedto avoid and at that moment the wake from the other hit us broadside. We then had to jib again because he headed determinedly across our bow. We passed inside the N.W. Beach and on a beautiful reach with a smooth water roared up Harwich Channel. We noted how attractive Harwich Church looked.

11.00 Entered the R.Orwell approx. hr ahead of schedule. A coaster overtook with no trouble at all.

Off Cullimer Point turned for a dead run and poled out roller jib as a huge ferry came by en route between Ipswich and Rotterdam.

2015 Turned on the motor to head into the wind and picked up a mooring 100 yds
from Boat hard beacon.

13.00 Ashore at Pin Mill after srounding in the dinghy by the barges off the "Butt and Oyster". We enjoyed a drink here for they have a side room where children are welcome and one can buy cold snacks. Here we met up with Snowgoose and Segla crew and after a meal we set out to walk up the lane to Chelmondiston to get stores. We returned to sit on the quay while Chris and Mary played in the Mill stream. The Mill itself is no longer standing, the name however goes back as far as the 14 when the old mill with its millpond or pynd stood in the valley a little way back from the river, where the grass grown banks can still be seen.

8.

Ipswich townsmen used to have their ‘main water' supply in the form of a "yenmnd" from a neighbouring brook flowing into their gardens. Although we no longer use this old word for the stream at Pin Mill, it is still called the Grindle, which is another old Suffolk word meaning the same thing.

The Butt and Oyster is probably 16 and was an ale house and reputed to be a smugglers haunt, it may have been a ferryhouse too. Later when the tide went down we walked in the woods alongside the shore and returned via the shore beneath the huge barges. We found a sandy beach with grass banks and a beautiful view over moored boats on the river to the parkland and manor house opposite. We saw a strange bamboo like growth which I had never come across before and evidently it is a very ancient plant called Horse tails or Equistales and dates from the very early days of the swamplands.

18.30 Back on board Snowgoose and Segla were moving on to the marina at Levinton and told us dire tales of being moored very near the main channel. Peter stubbornly refused to move and after a very bumpy hour or so, once the tide changed, the mooring was very comfortable. We weren't aware of any commercial traffic overnight and after all what the eye don't see the heart don't grieve over! We slept well!

Thursday August 8th

We woke early to continuous rain and it was very overcast. We were undecided what to do. After listening to the weather at 7.55 a.m. which was a bit more favourable decided to up anchor and go down river. ve had thought of going up to Ipswich but the large commercial traffic put us off a little.

08.40 Left the mooring and sailed in a light S.W. which developed into a good force 3-4 after Levington which carried us on a nice broad reach down river. It started to rain again. A huge dredger came up behind us and passed down the channel. Ye noted that Levington Marina had a lightship for her
clubhouse.

10.55 Passed Parkeston Quay. Lovely w/SW blowing taking us on long tacks up river, half a mile each tack. We passed Galloper light vessel plus three others which pleased the children. Many of the large liners were loading so it was a very interesting voyage. Luckily none were moving.

11.45 Recognised Ken Bevin's boat heading up for Pin Mill. We had a lovely wind, still 3-4 S.W.

12.15 list rolled up and made visibility pretty bad so we decided to pick up a mooring off Wrabness Point and have lunch.

13.15 Mist lifting,on up to Mistley on motor with sprit sail and mizzen set.

13.45 Alongside quay at Nistley beside the warehouses and maltings. We walked into Manningtree passing the remaining two towers of Robert Adam's Mansion built for Richard Rigby, grandson of a linen draper and son of a father who made a great fortune ouf of the South Sea Company and had enormous funds to spend on the liistley Hall Estate. He became .P. and Paymaster General of the Forces. The port, which his father had already begun, laid out a shipyard, stone built quays, a timber yard, warehouses, maltings and limekiln together with the amenities of a fashionable watering place, bathing pavilions, swan pool, fountains and a new church.

9.

The swans are still there as we found to our cost. They stood on the only footpath in their dozens and refused to move, so we took our lives in our hands and walked on the road! As we walked a huge black cloud appeared before us so Peter, Chris and Tim turned back and Carol and I went into Manningtree for shopping. "More shopping", was Feter's comment!

14.55 Peter and the boys arrived back at the boat to find it had risen three feet in an hour, no wonder it sluices out on the first of the ebb.

Meanwhile loaded with provisions and wet to the skin, Carol and I saw a neighbour from our estate driving through. They enquired if we were enjoying our holiday afloat! We must have looked the part with oilskins and sou'westers. We hot footed it back to the boat in the midst of the thunder storm.

16.00 Left Mistley, motored off until we picked up the wind off Waift fleet Creek, leaded on broad reach towards Wrabness. It brightened up and we debated going on down to Walton immediately, until we saw the thunder clouds gathering behind us. We were just about to pick up the mooring as the storm broke with hail, heavy rain, thunder and lightning. We decided to stay for the night on a large moorings. The storm lasted for two hours but we were quite content reading and playing cards aboard.

Friday August 9th

09.05 Left the mooring, little wind. The forecast at 06.30 had predicted W.4.

09.45 Passed the Sir Alan herbert, a Thames Barge, anchored a mile up stream from Erwarton Ness in line with Beaumont Hall. The sun was shining and the wind a steady 2-3.

10.30 Passed Parkeston Quay, the wind was freshening in gusts. Ve took down the
washing - drying from the storm the previous day - to improve visibility!

11.40 Passed the Pye End Buoy. We motored for 35 mins until we turned into Walton channel. The wind had veered 5.W. making sailing impossible.

12.40 On a mooring in the Twizzle, having passed Tijo and Jappa on our way in. Once again we tried to sail the dinghy ashore and started off well but it turned into a close haul so took a little longer than expected! One doesn't feel very seamanlike with 5 in a small dinghy, sailing one tack and rowing the other! ve walked into ‘lalton and bought fish and chips to consume on the beach as usual. We then made for the Pier and spent the afternoon with the children on the amusements. This was intended as a treat for them alone but Peter used up a lot of the tickets on the bumper cars and I even braved the big wheel! The
sea looked fairly calm from the top of the wheel, but at ground level there was quite a swell. We realised that we were also sheltered by the headland. We returned Ian to Jappa and had a council of war to decide whether to venture home.

The weather forecast was predicting Force 6-7 so it looked as if we were going to be holed up after all. Planned to listen to the 6.30 a.m. weather in the morning before making any decisions.

10.

Saturday August 10th

se woke during the night to hear the wind and rain lashing down. On
awakening for the 6.30 a.m. weather we turned over and went back to sleep - it was
not at all favourable, with W. Gales all around the coast. Peter and Tim went ashore to get supplies and were not back until one o'clock! They had to walk miles because they landed at Foundry Creek hard instead of Colonels dard nearby. This was a big mistake because they found a dinghy adrift and walked miles to a boat builders to report it. It turned out that they owned the mooring we had taken in the Twizzle and we were advised to move because it hadn't a very heavy anchor. We couldn't help thinking that if it had stood up to the previous nights storm it was pretty safe! Peter returned and looked at the other mooring he had advised and found it had an appallingly thin chain! We decided that the £5.5 fee in the manna would be well worth it if we had to desert the boat. The whole afternoon and evening was interspersed with heavy squalls and we stayed aboard. However by the evening the wind had swung round !!.W. which was a favourable wind for the return journey should it die down a bit. To bed to await the morning forecast, though very doubtful we wovld take the boat home that weekend.

Sunday August llth

we heard the 6.30 a.m. weather forecast, gales all up the coast, so the decision was obvious, despite the fact that conditions in the river at that time looked favourable. We dropped down to confer with Jappa. Vic Tate was already there, he was wondering whether to take Snowgoose down with Kobert aboard sending the others by train. We stated we were going into the Marina to leave the boat to return when conditions were more favourable, probably next weekend. It was a very easy Marina to enter and moor, plenty of room, unlike that at Woodbridge. We left Roulette alongside Segla, Dennis had left the previous day, and set off towards the station, two miles away, looking like refugees with pillow cases of dirty washing over our shoulders! I wasn't leaving that aboard for a week! Once at the station we were lucky to catch the 11.45 a.m. train which was running late and were home in Chelmsford by 1.15 p.n. It is a very easy journey from Walton and I would never
worry about leaving the boat there should we need to in the future - very different
from the journey home from Brightlingsea when we got holed up there - but thats
another story! -

There was still a question mark over our decision as the weather both en route and in Chelmsford looked very suitable for a passage. However later Vic confirmed that conditions had been pretty hairy.

It was disappointing to have to leave Roulette on Walton but why spoil what had been a superb holiday when there was always another weekend to collect her.

CRUISER HANDICAPS 1975

At a Cruiser Handicap meeting of the Blackwater Joint Racing Committee (B.J.R.C.) in February, the method of handicapping for 1975 was agreed.
They will keep strictly to the procedure for allocating and re-rating cruiser handicaps as laid out in the R.Y.A. publication YR2/74, with the exception that yachts with established handicaps will only be re-rated twice a year; once in the winter, and again in mid-season. (This year after the Smith's Cup.)
Yachts without established handicaps,i.e. neither a previous B.J.R.C. handicap nor a R.Y.A. primary or secondary yardstick will be re-rated after each of their first three B.J.R.C. races in accordance with the R.Y.A. procedure which bases their handicap on their average performance so far. After the third race the handicap becomes B.J.R.C. established, and will only be changed twice a year. This adjustment each half-season will be the sum of the differences in performance in the races completed, divided by the number of races completed plus three.
This adjustment will apply to all handicaps, including those of yachts with primary and secondary yardsticks. However, the yardsticks will be maintained for those yachts solely for the purpose of calculating the standard time for each race. (The standard time is the corrected time of the centre-placed yardstick yacht in the race, using her yardstick number, not the handicap.)
This year the B.J.R.C. races are :-

July 6th Blackwater Cup

Brute force, maybe; but ignorance none. An account of the ist British crew, Alf Reynolds, Bruce Long and Brian Elry, to participate in the 18' skiff Worlds (Sydney 18's).

"Hello there", typical Aussie greeting we thought, must be in the right place. "Your on tele, Channel 9's midday sports program —- at eleven".
"Yes, that figures ", we thought, "Aussie logic at its best".
This was the way that three superb weeks of sailing, sun, swimming and sightseeing
began. (You'll notice no sex - after all, we are British). Suffering from too much
British Airways booze and food, we emerged into the Sydney sunshine, pale and forlor, to be immediately surrounded by brown and brawny bodies, ever had that slightly inferior
feeling?
Apres the television, we were whisked away to the New South Wales 18 footers league club, snatched a quick bite to eat in the club's restaurant and joined a private boat loaded to the gunwales with grog ready to watch the opposition performing in Sydney Harbour. Being Saturday, the racing was organised by the Sydney Flying Squadron and this was the last heat, but one, for the Australian titles, so all the big names were on th. water. It didn't take long to appreciate the standard was high, very high, and that the new Bruce Farr designs are in a class of their own. Bruce, a young New Zealander, has developed the 18's over the past five years from relative heavyweights to featherweights. Modern hulls rarely weigh more than 160lbs equipped with their basic gear,this added to highly developed rigs, related to crew weight had made the 18's absolutely untouchable in the dinghy field. The new hulls feature a relatively narrow entry in the first six feet, but are formed in quite a pronounce 'U' section to prevent nosedipping. Having kept the entry narrow, the sides then rapidly flare outwards to the gunwales. This is the final stopgap which prevents the boat completely submarining in a big sea. The aft sections run out fairly flat, with a nearly straight chine the length of the boat. The amount of bottom round and thus the amount of buoyancy available in the hull is once again geared to crew weight.
For instance, a light weight crew say 32 stone, will use a design which is considerably narrower in the chine beam and which is slightly flatter all round, than one for a crew of 39 to 40 stone. Science is the new keyword, KB for instance, have a paid aeronautics expert at hand to advise on sail shape etc. and to keep a weekly watch on strech and warping etc. which may affect their performance. Incidently, the KB crew quite happily sail for 2 hours a weekend and devote 25 hours during the week in mainte see
and improvement - carefully photographing each stage as they change gear.
The racing on Sydney Harbour used to be followed by five ferries - now only two remain
old age having claimed the others but racing is followed more enthusiastically than eve by a huge fleet of private yachts and motor boats.
Our week was spent alternatively working on the new Kwikasair -— which we'd borrowed from Phil O'Donnel, sunbathing, surfing and stuffing ourselves with the biggest steaks on earth. "Kwikasair" had been plagued by ill luck since her completion 2 months previously - this we felt was because the builder hadn't followed Bruce Farr's plans. Try as we might there were some aspects which we couldn't rectify or improve, and instinctively felt would be troublesome later on.
The following weekend we flew Ansett to Brisbane, where Jane joined us, leaving Phil to tow the boat up for us. The Brisbane river was our first shock, Horneteers will when I say a "super Shoreham harbour". Filthy with cromate from the tanning factory and blood from the abattoirs it takes on a light brown tinge which is tidal and runs out at about 2 knots. The banks are crowded with docks, a power station, the previously mentioned abattoirs and tanning factory and finally a huge petrol storage area streching either side of the river. However, to compensate the Brisbane 18 footers club was super. One

We were made particularly welcome and eventually stayed with the Commodore in a caravan situated in his back garden. He was also putting up twothirds of the New Zealand team. I think this all got too much for him towards the end of the series— particularly as he'd two young attractive daughters, who were making the most of their ten days of good fortune. There were to be six races —- the first was an allcomers invitation with a handicap (pursuit) start.

Kwikasair was favourite to win as we'd obtained a very early getaway but inspite of an excellent windward leg our spinnaker work was shoddy and we eventually went swimming. At the commencement of the series proper, we had to say goodbye to Phil, who was flying to America for his firm, and in his place acquireda proper team coach, Wally Web - complete with speed boat to follow our motley performance. After our first two races Wally was fit to blow a gasket — he'd stand in his little yellow boat shouting and waving his arms, we weren't flat enough, our tacking was too slow, and worst of all —- he was right. We had 16th and 13th to our credit and determined to do better in the 3rd race.
Suddenly we seemed to hit the go button - the boat came alive to windward and amazed at
its performance — wrong selection of kite got us only 14th, but we were improving and beginning to see the light. The fourthrace was frankly a disaster from start to finish. A poor windward leg and the eventual loss of the spinnaker halyard, which meant a capsize to retrieve it put us fair and square at the back. Determined we carried on and started making good ground on the second beat, very flat and fast when an LIYE bailer disappeared clean out the bottom leaving a gaping hole into which the water gushed with “She ferocity of Trafalgar. It was sink or swim. so with Brian's foot square over the aole we sailed for home. If the fourth race was disheartening the fifth was a tragedy. _ The wind came up to 25 knots gusting 35, by far the strongest breeze all week. We equipped ‘Kwikasair with her smallest rig, knowing this would deliver more power than we could cope with. We were all conscious of the boat's weak points and the fact that it didn't belong
to us, any damage wouldn't be popular, but Wally said, "Sail like....... and never mind
the consequences", so we did just that. From the gun we flew, Kwikasair felt as if she had a rocket under her, hard on the wind we couldn't stop her planeing, not ideal as we thought it would go faster if we could keep more hull in the water. With the wind shrieking and the main 90% backwinded, we corrected from none to none, with one particular hard fall into a trough and the three of us hard on the wire, Kwikasair gave a grunt and then the tearing of timber was all we heard as the plate case collapsed.
Wally, all this time had been dancing with glee, as we were lying 7th and whilst not front runners, this promised to be our best result of the week — but alas Kwickasair UK and its three occupants was now sadly settling in the water. Thus ended the series not quite as successful as we'd hoped but packed with valuable experience.
KB won the series with precision power sailing that was totally faultless. We watched awestruck as she deliberately gave up 1st position to the close second runner as she set a 75 square foot extra. For the first half mile afer this manouvre it was too close to se — and her crew let it flog. The competition now were robbed of their opportunity to
hoist anything quickly - requiring all their weight outside the boat. As the wind eased
~at a bend the nearer KB sheeted this sail and powered through, never to be seen again.
Well who knows— a british champion in five years - I think it quite possible.

Bruce Long.

For those who are mentally on the way to Holland, there was an amusing article in February's Yachting Monthly, covering the negotiation of the Great Zeeland Bridge on ti — Easter Scheldt by the yacht Tandala from Pin Mill. The lifting section of the bridge has apparently been broken by a giant crane, and this necessitated a crew member standing on his bosun's chair with his eyes level with the top of the mast in order to check whether the calculated 14cm. clearance was correct, (and we do this for relaxation?) EDITORIAL

That old saying that the man who goes sailing for pleasure will go to hell fora pastime can certainly be applied to some club members, who braved the elements and were sailing in a snowstorm on Easter Sunday.
We have however, enjoyed a few days of sunshine and the Handicap fleet have been the first to take advantage of racing in decent weather. After the discussions about a new class dinghy last year, the problem seems to have resolved itself and we have an increased handicap fleet with everyone "doing their own thing".
A few cruisers have appeared back on their moorings although those in the dinghy park maybe able to sail out shortly, the ground is so waterlogged. Let us hope that the Gods will smile upon us and give us the usual good weather we enjoy for the Regatta.

Brenda Tate.

COMMODORES NOTES
The Fitting Out Party on March 22nd was a great success, if the reports and comments I have heard are any thing to go by; and I would like to thank you all for coming and converting our new building into a lively Sailing Club clubhouse. A more formal occasion is being planned for the evening of Saturday May 17th, when our President, Sir Eric Eastwood, the Officers and Committee will be hosts to invited guests, who have sailing connections with the club or have helped with the planning and building.The evening will be a club function and members who also wish to attend should complete the tear-off slip at the end of this issue, as soon as possible, so that we will have an idea of the numbers wanting to come.
There are still a large number of small jobs to be done in and around the clubhouse to complete the fitting out,and if there are members coming down who would like to lend a hand, for a short period, please, find either Ron Greygoose,
Vic Tate or myself for details of what is to be done.
It was a very pleasant surprise to find that many of the holes in the road had been filled and we are all very grateful to be relieved of this task, by the thoughtful gesture of Mike Taylor, who had some spare material.

John Witter, Commodore.

ASSOCIATE MEMBERSHIP

Bach year we take on a limited number of new Associate members who, by virtue of their connections with the club, the Committee feel are eligible for membership. There are still a few vacancies for the year and while not wishing to have applications from total strangers members are invited to propose for membership friends who already have strong connections with the club, or attend as the guests or crews for members and are already using the club. Application forms are available from the secretary or committee members and if you want to make proposals I suggest this is done quickly.
The fees applicable to Associate Members arei-

Husband and Wife £12.96 including M.A.S.C. fees.
Hard fee for boat owners £8.64. Joining fee £5.40. All fees include V.A.T. at 8%.

OLD CLUBHOUSE —- MEMBERS PROPERTY

The old clubhouse is now in the process of being cleared of all club property and ~—sembers are asked to ensure that all personal property is removed from it byApril 30th. she clubhouse and sheds are due for demolition shortly as part of the conditions of our planning approval. Property remaining there after that date will be considered unwanted and will be disposed of as neccessary.

DISPOSAL OF OLD CLUBHOUSE

The committee is anxious to find a buyer for the old clubhouse, which has served us so well for the last 12 years and if any members know of any organisation that are looking for a structure of this type I should be pleased to hear from them. The only condition placed on the disposal of the building is that the purchaser dismantles and removes, and that the removal is carried out against a time scale acceptable to the committee.

WATER ECONOMY

Although we now have a large cesspool, we seem to be using far more water than we used to. Please, try to be economical and have quick showers and flush the toilets only when necessary as emptying the cesspool costs money.
The drains leading away from the clubhouse were rather unpleasantly blocked because paper towels and other waste, that isn't very soluble in large quantities had been flushed down the lavatories.

John Witter, Commodore.

3.

SOCIAL SCREED

About 50 to 60 people came along to the 3rd Winter Meeting and thanks to Vic Tate, who obtained the films and acted as projectionist, we saw two R.N.L.I. films and a colour film about Chichester's Round the World Voyage.
Although the official unveiling of the new clubhouse has yet to take place,
Saturday 22nd March saw the influx of about 150 Fitting Out Partygoers, who in the confines
of the clubhouse produced, as someone there commented, just about the right amount of overcrowding. It was a good party enjoyed by most, including for some the return coach trip to Baddow. The food arrangements worked very well and I would like to thank all those ladies who made such a fine contribution to the work in planning, preparing and serving. The next social event is the Young People's Party, again at Stansgate on May 3rd. For this there will be taped music plus the added attraction of a live group, "The Andromeda" This group of young men featured recently in the local press and have performed successfully at a number of functions in the area. We are looking forward to a good attendance from all
age groups - after all, parents are needed to provide transport and provided they stay
in the background will be very welcome. Transport may be a problem, so if there are any
young people without transport, let me know and I'll try to arrange for lifts - offers of
Spare seats would be welcome. As on previous years, all parents are asked to supply a
little food on the night, the usual cold buffet type stuff - if it's edible I'm sure it
will be eaten.

Roy Battye, Social Secretary.
'D' Bldg. Basildon, Int. 460 or Chelm. [redacted].

CLUBHOUSE

Considerable sums of money have been spent on new furniture and fittings, approx. £1,000 on tables, chairs and curtains alone.
Your co-operation is requested to help maintain our investment in good condition. In this direction will you please help by not using the soft chairs while wearing wet clothes and to keep the hard polypropylene chairs away from the heater units.
There is also some concern that due to the low level windows, there is danger to small children, who could fall some 10' -— 15' to the ground. Consideration is being given to all safety measures, however, you will appreciate it is difficult for the committee to cover every aspect and we consider it to be the responsibility of parents to keep a watchful eye on children to ensure that a serious accident does not occur. Obviously, t’ committee will endeavour to reduce hazards if possible.
The treads of the main stairs leading to the lounge will be treated to provide a non slip surface and modification to the construction of the fire escape stairway at the end of the building is being examined.

David Harper, Clubhouse Secretary.

NAVIGANS DISTRIBUTION

The costsof printing and distribution are substantial, and it is therefore important that we keep the number of copies to a minimum and use the company's postal service wherever possible. Would any families receiving two copies where One would suffice, or anyone receiving their copy by G.P.0O. where a company postal route is avadleble, please contact:- M.J.Gray, End. B Baddow. Int. 461 or [redacted], Gt. Baddow.
Chelmsford .

CRUISER NEWS

Well, here I am with the boat almost ready, and it's snowing every other day, and cold enough to freeze the whatsits off a thing umajig. Not only that but the dinghy park is so wet that I am thinking of sliding the boat on to the road. However, we were lucky last weekend and had some splendid weather on the Sunday, and it was pleasing to see how a few hours of sunshine improved the situation.
So many people turned up at the last cruiser meet that the evening was punctuated
by cries of "Move that car ". The film of the Round -the - World Race was superb and left
one with a tremendous feeling of speed. It is strange how a mundane speed of 20mph in everyday life seems so specta@gmlar on the water. The shots of the Burton Cutter tearing down wind for long periods at 20 knots was something to be savoured —- as were the aerial shots at Cape Horn showing how a 70” yacht can be- tossed around.
Last Sunday a water-skier on a kite was going up and down on the Blackwater, and gliding quite some distance in free flight. Very spectacular and I suppose I have a sub-conscious desire to try; and yet it is so far removed from what the River and sailing mean to me that I find the whole antic irritating, and a potential threat. _ In April's Yachting Monthly, (I don't in fact get paid commission, but I do think it _3 a damn good magazine) there is a thought provoking article on safety. Shouldn't we all have some form of home-made buoy and drogue attached to our lifebuoy?
Thanks to Vic Tate for obtaining the largest pair of toe-nail clippers I have seen
for a long while - they are not bad on chain either. See you on the water/bogged down in
the dinghy park(delete which is inapplicable).

Brian Bowsher, Cruiser Captain.
New St. Int. 9261 Ext. 376 or [redacted].

HANDICAP FLEET NEWS.

There was an encouraging turn-out on Sunday 6th April with five of the Handicap fleet competing in tune-up races. Robert Tate pipped Frank Savill to win by 10 secs. in the gmoating race. In the afternoon they were joined by two Mirrors and an Enterprise and Robert once again took first place. On the whole it was a good days racing with plenty of sunshine, and we look forward to many more with plenty of contenders.

Tony Drury, Handicap Fleet Captain.

CADET PROGRAMME

The programme will start on Saturday April 19th with a meeting at M.A.S.C. Beehive Lane when all Cudets will learn how to rig a dinghy and be familiar with its use and purpose. (I will contact all Cadets prior to this date). The Saturday tuition from Stansgate in dinghys will commence Saturday May 3rd., when we hope the weather has improved. The early tuition will indicate which cadets are competent to compete on Sundays, but as the season progresses then more cadets will be expected to participate (weather permitting). An approach is being made to obtain adequate Insurance cover for both Saturday and
Sunday sailing.
It looks as if Stephen Perkins will be racing in the point series and Chris Weedon together with Colin Harper will sail when John and David have weekend duties. Robert Tate will be competing whenever possible and it is hoped that we will see many more cadets on the water on Sundays. When it comes to racing, Cadets are free to beat everybody except me. It is my intention to have one more Mirror available for Sundays, which I hope will be released by other helmsmen who have Sunday duties.
N.B. Would the cadets who kindly returned the application forms and phoned me with the
exceptions of the following:—- Chris Robert and Roland Weedon, Colin Harper, Karen Stuart, Stephen Perkins, Andrew and Susan Barclay and Mark Savill.PLEASE CONTACT ME AGAIN, After carefully making out a directory of all the applications — my wife has carefully gone and handed it to the dustmen along with many other items.

Rick Anstey, Cadet Captain.

GOSSIP

The Sailing Club membership is on the increase} Leonie and Gordon Golding became the proud parents of Stuart Gordon 71b 110zs on Good Friday. Leonie's ex-crew, Noreen, says that the baby has masses of black hair and looks like Gordon. Noreen is expecting her second baby in May.
Gill and Julian Bigden's new baby is Victoria Lucy, who made her first appearance at Stansgate at the ripe old age of 9 days.
The cruiser fleet wives are expecting some new members too. Our good wishes and congratulations go to Rebecca and Walter Standing, Dave Lawson and his wife and John and Diana Rogers.
Simon Darney and Susan Christiansen surprised everyone when they brought their wedding day forward several weeks. Congratulations Simon.
We are all delighted to congratulate Geoff and Jennifer White on their recent marriage on Kaster Saturday.

The Cruiser fleet has made a few changes during the winter months and there are several boats with new owners this season. Freddie Harrison has sold "Avalon" to David Sheppard and become the proud owner of Dick Weaver's old ballerina "Giselle". Dick has

bought John Swinton's Macwester 27 "Thundercloud", and his brother Sidney aquired John Selby's Westerly Centuar "Whimbrel", now renamed "Weaver bird". Albert Pearce has sold "Starlight" and now has a Macwester 26, just like Stan's.
The swing to wooden boats continues,John Swinton has replaced "Thundercloud" with the magnificent "Bettine", from Mersea. Peter Foreman is working hard on his Sea King, "Jestabei", and John Smith has put a lot of very hard work into his Dauntless and hopes to have her launch soon. Ken Stevens sold "Carasou" this weekend and is hoping to buy a wooden boat too. Avril says that after twelve years she can't imagene life without a
boat.
The cruiser man who must have worked hardest this winter is Andrew Dixon. "Mayleaf" is fitted out to perfection and a joy to behold. These chaps from Appledore certainly know all about boats/

PLEASE TAKE NOTE

The death of yet another man while rowing out to a moored boat at night is a very solemn reminder of the follies of overloading small dinghies and of not wearing life jackets. The accidents of this nature that I can remember have been at night so we must all remember to bring our life jackets ashore before a sociable evening in the club and-~— WEAR LIFE JACKETS when going back to our cruisers.

COMMODORES NOTES

Clubhouse Opening Arrangements are now almost finalised for the formal opening on May 17, of the new clubhouse by our President. The programme for the evening is that there will be one or two speeches during which the plaque will be unveiled by the President. The remainder of the evening will provide an opportunity for the guests to look around and for members and guests to mix. During this time the bar will be open and light refreshments will be available. It is not intended that the evening should become a party and members are asked not to attend unless they have previously advised me, as requested in last month's Navigans, that they wish to come. About 100 guests have been invited and the unscheduled appearance of a large number of members would upset all the plans and create an extremely embarrassing situation for the Club.
Gate Lock The installation problems which have caused the delay in fitting the lock to the gate have now been overcome and the work is expected to be completed shortly. It is proposed to bring the lock into operation on June 1st. by which time all outside organisations needing access to the site should have keys. After that date, members will require their keys to get into the site and I would remind you that you will also require your key to get out again. The practice we adopted, at the end of last year, of shutting the gate after each car, has been conscientiously observed and I would like to thank yo all for your co-operation and ask you to continue this discipline.
25% VAT. I cannot imagine that any member of the Club missed the budget announcement of the 25% VAT rate on boats and sailing equipment. This will undoubtedly increase the cost of sailing to all members at a time when it is already hard to make ends meet. This high rate seems particularly unfair, as our type of sailing is quite definitely a sport, an active participating sport, in fact, which is no way different to other sports which are not penalised in the same way. The only way to try to improve the situation is to make your voice heard as an individual by writing to your M.P., to the Chancellor or to anyone who you feel can influence this illogical decision.
The R.Y.A. are already making representations on our behalf and if we are to get the best value for our affiliation fee we should follow suit. If all else fails we shall have made same contribution to the economy in that we shall have helped to keep down the loss now sustained by the Post Office, as a result of increasing postage out of all proportion to the value of the service. ( That's provided you put a stamp on it, of course..)

John Witter, Commodore.

Lost Property Members are reminded that they should not leave sailing gear and clothes in the changing rooms after the weekend. At present a substantial collection of lost property is being collected each weekend and put away for safe keeping. This may be ; recovered by the owner on request to the 0.0.D. and by payment of the appropriate fee(15p) which will be put into club funds as a donation. See Clubhouse Bye Law No.6.

Anchors in Dinghies

Rule 5 of our sailinys instructions makes the carrying of an anchor obligatory. This rule has been discussed on several occasions in committee but has been retained on the grounds of safety.
Arguments for carrying an anchor include:-
1. If the boat becomes disabled the anchor can be used to limit the drift which should
shorten the rescue operation.
2. If the weather conditions are such that the rescue service has been stretched it may
“only be possible to recover the crews initially, and if the dinghy is left anchored the chance of damawe or loss is reduced.
The above is supported by certain insurance pvlicies and championship sailing instructions, which require an anchor to be carried by dinghies in tidal waters, and there have been a few occassions when this has been proved justified.
The arguments against carrying an anchor have been:-
1. An additional expense which does not have any berefit as the anchors are too small to
grip. This has not been bourne out in practise as however small the anchor, the rate of the drift will be reduced.
2. It may not be possible to stow it in some boats due to the construction of the boat
or the class rules do not allow it. A little ingenuity would get over the first problem and it would be irresponsible of a class association to disallow a possible item of safety. I should be pleased to hear from any members with information to support either argument to enable us to come to a satisfactory conclusion.
Note -— Although the sailing instructions Rules can only be enforced during racing, it would seem even more important to carry an anchor when pottering and cruising.

CRUISER NEWS

On the water at last, and we have spent one weekend away down at Mersea, moored between the new iron posts in the Ray Channel, (Ian Tate territory). Be warned however, that it is a formidable job fitting your own mooring ropes, if you are not able to pick
up any existing ones. These are normally tied together and left floating between the posts, but of course, the owner may well return and one should try not to inconvenience anyone, It is very pleasant being able to stop at Mersea again, as moorings have been so tight to get there, and it is quite impossible to ride to an anchor.
For those who wish to secure their dinghies at the club, I have laid about 50' of chain along the base of the sea wall. This is fastened to two metal fence posts knocked in
at 45 degrees to below the surface - so I defy anyone to get those out in a hurry. I
Suggest dinghies are attached by a 6' length of stainless steel rigging wire with an eyelet at each end for a padlock. On rubber dinghies the wire can be looped through the outboard bracket sockets. These could be cut by a thief, but the dinghy would not be saleable without repair. Obviously, it will not be possible to stop the determined thief, but the above precaution should stop the more casual thief.
In view of the water-logged state of the dinghy park, it is not surprising that many cruisers have been moved to the hard for final fitting out. However, for the sake of those who may wish to sit out on the sea wall, would those on the hard, please make every effort to launch as quickly as possible —- certainly before the Regatta, when the space will definitely be needed.
To get my boat out of the bog I was able to borrow a device called a Tirfor winch. This is a hand-carried winch, which can be hooked onto the appropriate tree, and by movement of a lever, hauls on a wire cable to the tune of 30 ewt. It is ideal for man- oevering trailers around the dinghy park, as with it one can get controlled power from any point. The lender is very willing for it to be used by the club, but has asked me to look after it. If anyone wished to borrow it, would they therefore, collect it from me.

Pleasant sailing to you all, and to those still on terra firma, may the sun shine on your
paintwork.
