MARCONI'S INVASION OF THE CONTINENT.

The aim of our holiday this year was an ambitious one - five Marconi boats were
bound for a cruise in company to Holland. On our boat 'Tijo' we had our family - Ian (the
writer), brother Jim, father Stan, mother liargaret plus Richard Swinton, who was to be with us for the first ten days. Early Friday night the crews of 'Tijo' ‘Snowgoose' and ‘Entrophy' mustered at Stansgate. 'Jappa' and ‘Janthina' were to join us in the morning.

Saturday July 26th. At 4.30a.m. all aboard 'Tijo' were awoken by the sound of giggling.
On peering out of the hatches we found that the source was 'Jappa’. Lynne and Lowtise Sianning had apparently brought her round from Mayland with Jack and Jackie and brother Ian below asleep. We beckoned them to come alongside as there were no deep water moorings available. This manouvre having been accomplished we all turned in again for another couple of hours sleep. We awoke to a morning that couldn't quite decide what it was going to be like. We listened to the Shipping Forecast which did nothing to clarify the situation and decided the we were all suffering from lack of sleep we would postpone our departure for Ostend until the following morning and see if by then we would get a better forecast. We decided ip=tead to make the short journey down river to Brightlingsea. On this spic voyage to Bi shtlingsea we spotted a whale that was stranded on Thirslet Spit. Vic closed the enormous mammal and managed to take some very good photographs.

Sunday July 27th. The early morning Shipping Forecast informed us that the weather was
greatly improved, wind force 1-3. We quietly slipped our moorings at 6.50a.m. In contrast to the previous day t)ere was almost no wind at all, and we were forced to start the engine to
maintain a constant speed. At 11.50 a.m. Barrow Deep Buoy is abeam and by 12.55 we had passed
barrow Deep No.6. At 15.35 p.m. we sighted South Knock, this being the last Buoy this side of the North Sea. We were making extremely good time although this was with the accompaniment of the constant chugg chugging of the engine. The wind showed no sign of increasing, our navigation proved to be almost perfect, and everything was going without a hitch. A good two hours was spent spinning for mackeral which certainly proved to be abundant in this part of the North Sea, for before long our cockpits were full. The darkness crept down upon us and it was decided that the crew should take half hourly stints on the helm, as longer than this would prove harder to concentrate.
This was carried out religiously with the exception of Mum, who was given the job of sitting in the cockpit talking to the helmsman to keep him aw. 3, a job at which she was quite accomplished. Fairy Banks was first spotted at 21.55 and before long the loom of the \est Hinder was visible dead ahead. The “West Hinder was abeam bo 23.25 35 miles from South Knock and dead on course. As the night progressed the wind fiually decided it was going to aid us on the last stretch of our journey, and for the first time in almost 19 hours we were able to switch off the engine and sail for a couple of hours. At first light we see Ostend and we are extremely proud of ourselves, not quite believing we had actually achieved what we had set out to do wothout any incidents whatever. jie entered Ostend Harbour at 5.20 and tied up quietly and got our heads down for a couple of hours much appreciated sleep. We were now &5 miles from base.

Monday July 28th. It was not until about 7.30 that Ostend began to wake, but the noise
gradually increased until it was almost impossible to sleep, but nobody was much both=red as we were all eager to explore the town. Duty Frees were ordered and promptly delivered, this liquid refreshment being gladly taken as the sun was now blazing down on us with all it's might and already our lily white bodies were beginning to turn a reddish brown. It was not long before we got chatting to some kids from another two boats, one was Dutch, the other German. One of the girls, Miriam, attracted the attention of both men and boys alike, but to the amazement of us all we learned she was only 14 years old. This friend- ship lasted the duration of our stay in Ostend.

Tuesday July 29th. All lack of sleep has now been made up, and today we were happy just
to split the day between explorin,; the town and swimming and sunbathing off the marvellous beach. The weather seemed even hotter than the previous day. A splendid lazy day was spent by
all.

8.

Wednesday July 30th. Once again its an early start. Dad, Richard and myself get up and
quietly weave our way through the tightly packed boats in the harbour, leaving mum and brother Jim fast asleep down below. Even at 7 o'clock in the morning it is quite hot enough to be dressed in shorts. We seemed to live in shorts and swimming truncks for almost the complete duration of our three weeks holiday. The wind had dropped once again and we were forced to motorsail up the Belgian coast. As we sailed across to Vlissingen we see a
familiar boat - Yes, it's John Hooper in Davalos 11. This is the second Marconi boat we have
seen already. Dave Seward having arrived in “stand whilst we were there. This made seven Marconi boats on the continent at one time. These Marconi people certainly get about. After shouting and waving to John we entered Vlissingen at 13.00hours and soon were snuggly tied up inside the Jachthaven. A few of us made our way up to the bridge that crossed the canal and made friends with the bridgekeeper, whom we found, like the majority of Dutch people spoke #nglish nearly as well as we did. He invited us inside to look at the workings this was the first of many examples of the friendliness of the Dutch people towards us. We also discovered that they are very trusting and it was common practice in the Clubhouse to help yourself to beer and put the money in a box. It is to be assumed that they are not let down too often. We made use of their very adequate washing facilities and felt very’ l to think that any Dutch boat visiting ingland would not find a public shower from Ramsgate to Stansgate.

Thursday July 3ist. At last we can leave at a more civilised hour as we are no longer
dependant on the tides now that we have locked into the canals. After a short journey up the Walchkeran Canal we approach Middleberg, the capital of Zeeland, and as it is market day we tied up alongside and went ashore to look around and make a few purchases. The most popular of thses being the traditional Dutch clogs, which can now be seen on various feet clomping around Stansgate in a variety of painted designs. It was here that we had our first problem. A large piece of net was fouling 'Tijo's' prop, so while about 20 people crowded onto her bows, Jimmy and Dave Pierce entered the water and freed it. In the afternoon we left for Veere. The sun was still blazing down relentlessly and soon after arrival people were jumping overboard for a quick dip to keep cool.

Friday August ist. We were all greatly impressed by the town of Veere and decided to stay
for a further day. After a swim in the morning the adults went to climb the very tall tower in Veere, whilst us kids decided to spend the afternoon just swimming and sunbathing. Apparently the view from the Tower was fantastic. That evening we split into two groups, one party staying to drink in the clubhouse and the remainder of us hunting for the local nirht- life which we tracked down and eventually found ourselves singing "Yellow Submarine" wit. the locals. I think we caused quite an impression in Veere that night.

Saturday August end. We left Veere again in blazing sunshine and no wind and we dropper
our anchors in the Veeresmere for a swim. The water was very clear and we all swam from boat to boat. This was perfect and definitely what hloidays are all about. tie locked out of the Veeresmere and into the Ousterschelte, where the dinghy sailors were in great evidence. It was the weekend and the Dutch were enjoying themselves. Wwe locked into the Goes Canal, what a pretty little canal this is, just as you imagine Holland should be. We arrived at the small Jachthaven at Goes at 6.30 p.m. in the evening though tiny there were still empty places for all five boats. That evening we went for a stroll around the town and acquired a self appointed guide in a Dutch boy called Dick. He wished to improve his inglish so became No. 23 in our crowd.

Sunday August 3rd. It was decided today should be a day of rest and I don't think any of
the adults did any thing but lay under the shade of the trees that Surroundedthe Jachthaven and were totally lazy. The kids, however, did go to the excellent swimming pool close by, where we were again joined by Dick.

Monday August 4th. ie returned along the Goes Canal and went out into the Osterschelte
again, this time our destination was Zeiriksee, just beyond the Zeeland bridge.
Everybody had been measuring masts to see if they would get under alright and it was decided tke only one who might have trouble would be 'Jappa’. However, we should not be there at the topof the tide so all should be well.

9.

dn and then ete ‘Signeliod to bear offs an che end ahoy Got tirugh witnoet savings tinie mast behind, for which I'm sure Jack was glad. On arriving in Zeiriksee, Richard and Lesley made preparations to leave us. They had come to the end of their part of the holiday and we were sorry to say goodbye. They were met by a friend who was taking them back to Rotterdam . and hence from there to England.

Tuesday August 5th. We left Zeiriksee at 9.30 a.m. and for once there was a good breeze
and we were able to sail without the accompaniment of the motor. We sailed back under the Zeeland bridge and had a fine sail in the Ousterschelde. Ne locked back into the Veeremere this was the start of our long journey home. We again stopped at one of the islands to swim and have lunch, and it seemed a great shame to us all that we had to leave this delightful place so soon. With great regret we lock out of the Veeremere and back into the Walcharen Canal and make our way back down to Middleberg where we had decided to spend the night. It was certainly not the quietest mooring of the holiday, on one side we had a bus stop and the other the railway station, but once you get used to the idea of being on public display, you realize you have a fine berth in the centre of the capital of Zeeland for nothing. Anyway, are soon to add some noise of our own as tonight we celebrate Fenella's 16 birthday. First a visit was made to the fair followed by a get-together on ‘Janthina' and 'Snowgoose' who “are laying side by side.

Wednesday August 6th. We awoke after an extremely hot night to the sounds of English
voices laughing at us asleep. However, if you sleep at a bus stop with all the hatches wide open, what more can you expect? Had the voices been Dutch we wouldn't have noticed — but
English tourists....... We left Middleberg at 11.0 a.m. and as we passed the Town gardens
there stood Dick, our friend from Goes waving goodbye to us. We knew he worked in Miidleberg, but did not expect to see him there to bid us ‘Ben Voyage’ or whatever in Dutch. We locked out of the Walcharen Canal at Vlissingen and are soon back at sea again. We cross the Kstuary in rather poor visibility and enter Breskins Marina at 2.30 p.m. This was to be our last day in Holland. It was still extremely hot and we amused ourselves by spraying cold water over each other and washing hair under the hoses.

Thursday August 7th. We left Breskins at 9.30 a.m. our aim being Neiuport in Belguim,
however, due to an error in our homework, we left at completely the wrong time ( six hours to be precise ) and found ourselves punching a strong tide down the coast. After a week of net having to bother about tides we shall have to be more careful than this. At 3.30 p.m. ws decided to put into Blankenberg instead. We had made very poor time. However, it was a happy diversion, we all immediately made for the beach and had a swim and a look around the wn. It's a bit like a continental Southend with the addition of fine sandy beaches, but we liked it even if it was an unscheduled stop.

Friday August Sth. We have now decided not to lose another day by going into Nieuport
but to make straight for Dunkerque. So it's now ‘Goodbye to Belguim'. This time no mistake is made in the times and we leave at 4.30 a.m. Wwe are back to early mornings again. Dad and I get up again leaving Jim and ium to sleep on almost till the time when we arrive at Dunkerque at 11.30 a.m. After the many places we have visited it seems very noisy and dirty, but we all get berths together again and it is a place we can replenish our Duty Frees again, which are now sadly de;leted. The adults take themselves off to find Dekkespotter and the rest of us make our way towards the beach. When we return we all sit outside the clubhouse awaiting the delivery of the Bonded Goods. After a false alarm when we all leapt up to welcome a van delivering electric light bulbs, much to the drivers amazement and our mirth, the right vehicle came with welcome nourishment.

Saturday Auyust 9th. We had a Violent storm in the night. I wonder is this the end of our
heatwave? However, the morning doesn't seem too bad, so up sa#ils and leave the harbour bound for Calias. As soon as we leave the shelter of the harbour we find there is a strong wind blowing against us totally unexpectedly and we realize we have a tough sail ahead of us. There is 4 nasty sea kicked up by the storm and in no time at all there is water everywhere. "Snowgoose’ and 'Janthina' both signal thumbs down and it is an unanimous decision to head back to Dunkerque again. After all we have plenty of time in hand to await for more favourable
conditions.

10.

Sunday August 10th. Yesterday's wind seemed to have abated but the sun has not come
back yet. We leave Dunkerque for a second time at 8.15 a.m. and head for Calais. About a mile off shore we bumped across the sands and shook ourselves a bit, however, we got off without too much trouble and came closer inshore where there was more water. Arrive Calais 1.0 p.m. It was just starting to rain, looked like our brilliant weather bad left us fora while. We are all pleased to be visiting Calais again, because we have spent some good times here in the past. ‘ie are soon off up the town to see all the familiar places and to have a go on the dodwems. We put up the cockpit tent and everybody comes on board for the evening. It's cosy and makes a change to be cool.

Monday August 11th. ie awoke relieved to find that the weather had not completely
broken and the sun was trying it's best to penetrate the low clouds. Various beach and walking parties set off and the day was spent in an idle manner, the evening was rounded off by a visit to the fair as this was to be our last night abroad. Kveryone was spending the rest of their foreign currency before returning to England.

Tuesday August 12th. Time to leave for Pngland and another early start. 4.30 a.m. DeTM
and me up again as we leave France regretfully for England. Visibility deteriorating and vy 5.30 a.m. is very poor and we lose sight of the other boats. We hope it's not like this a] the way across. Another hour and it has improved slightly, we are all in sight again toge car with another boat that obviously intends to stay with us for safety. We go north about the
Goodwins and make good time, we seem to be in Ramsgate quickly - 10.30 a.m. We are glad to be
in as the visibility was pretty poor all the way across. In Ramsgate the sun is shining brilliantly again. It seems strange to be back, as we have got used to the conveniences of the continental harbours with floating pontoons and all facilities and now we face reality again in the shape of that horrible wall with it's vertical ladders, no showers or toilets and a long walk for water. However, after theprices in the continental shops it made things seem relatively cheap in !ngland. We really felt we were back home when we met some girls we knew in Benfleet.

“ednesday August 13th. 'Ti jo', 'Snowgoose’ and 'Janthina' all left Kamsgate at 10.0 a.m. bound for Oare Creek. ‘Jappa' stays behind in Ramsgate as she is not happy about wetting a mud berth in the Ore as it dries out and ‘hbntrophy' stays behind with her. We arrange to meet them in Brightlingsea Thursday night. There is a pleasant breeze today and we able to sail. We take it in turns to be towed behind in the safety harness. When my turn arrived somebody decided to put the motor on and put 'Tijo' full ahead, and when I waved at then to slow down they had the cheek to wave back. I think they wanted to get rid of me. We arrived at Oare Creek at about 5.0 p.m. It's nice to be back in this pleasant lit*“e creek again. It's a place to which we have become quite attached to over the years and yo, are always sure of a good welcome in the ‘Shipwright 's Arms', It is a quiet peaceful mooring and the eveniny was spent over a drink in the bar.

Thursday Auvust 14th, Alas, another early start. Left Oare Creek 5.45 a.m. Visibilit
poor again. This seems to be our major hazard this holiday. 7.0 a.m. visibility worsening, lose sight of 'Snowgoose' and 'Janthina’. 7.55 a.m. visibility now very bad indeed. Hear foghorns all around us -— most unpleasant knowing we are approaching the Thames Estuary's busiest shipping lane. Dad is just working out a reciprocal course to take us back into the Oare when we see right on our bows the Red Sands Towers South Buoy. We circle it and decide our safest move is to get a line to it and wait for the fog to lift a bit. 8.0 a.m. we an safely tied on. It is very eerie, but feels much better. At this stage the fog is so thick we couldn't glimpse the towers in the murk. However, we are quite comfortable on our new mooring and mum cooked us all a good breakfast and I did a bit of fishing. Gradually we saw the towers emerge and they looked very interesting. We would very much have liked to explore them. We spend a while shouting loudly at them and getting beautiful echoes back. By 10.0 a.m the fog had lifted reasonably and Dad said we should be leaving, so we dropped the line and were off again. Visibility was still not good but we are ablw to pick out the buoys.

MUMBLES GRUMBLES

1974 Mirror Nationals were held at Mumbles near Swansea in Wales, supporting the k.S.C. were R.dattye, R.Anstey, J.Weedon and S.Oaker.
All it did was rain and poured, the highest wind was gale force 7, but it was just about as high as that every day, there were about 50 capsizes nearly everyday and about half of them were towed in. Before the start it was chaos and confusion boats were bumping into each other and capsizing. There was one 9 mile race everyday and I think that was a bit much for me and just about enough for my Dad.
The ums and my sisters were alright, most of the time sitting in the clubhouse with a pair of binoculars trying to see at least one Mirror through the mist, but the only ones they “aw were the ones that were towed in, and when they came in after a race. I suppose if you ~ad really good eyesight then perhaps you could see 300 little red things bumping into each
other.
We thought that the Welsh people had done their best to keep us all occupied and happy. One evening there was a wine and cheese party in the clubhouse, another party in a big hall in Swansea where all the women that worked preparing the food all day (voluntary) gave us some entertainment. Then t.ere was a Civic Reception and the last night the prize givings that were held in Swansea in a big posh place. reter Barrett won the whole event, but Marconi's hadn't done too bad, in one part of a race John Weedon was 2nd for a while. We were lucky for & place to stay because we hired a chalet, down near Caswell bay but the battye's were camping and at one point it was so terrible that Richard battye had to sleep in our chalet, otherwise he'd have got pneumonia with sleeping in a mud bath, because they were completely washed out. The Oakers and the Weedons camped as well, but I can't remember if they were quite as bad or not. The Heath's were alright they stayed at Ted's mothers but Ted didn't take place in the actual event.
I think it was just one day when there were two races and to give me a breather Colin Harper went out with my Dad, and that was the day he capsized. I wouldn't have liked to have been in that sea, the waves looked 10' high to me. The Harpers were just passing through on their way to Cornwall, they stayed about 3 or 4 days then continued heading for Cornwall. Despite all the bad weather we all enjoyed it thanks to the Mumbles Sailing Club who made us very welcome.

Sara Anstey.

To Rescue or be HKescued

Saturday, 5th July was the day of the Pilots Cup at Stansgate. The course was from
the club to a mark at the mouth of t:e river, then back to a buoy in the sialdon direction, finishing at the club. Starting at 14.00hrs., Dave, bob and I left in the Rescue Launch and followed the boats up to the first mark and watched them go round from the Bradwell side of the river. Attempting to go back up the river following the boats the engine would not go forward. As we were out of radio distance we could not get help. The tide was coming in 80 we were drifting homeward. The sailing season of 1975 started. This was the second season on the water for the boat. The previous year we did not do very well at all considering it was out first sailing and my sister did most of the crewing. But at the beginning of the 1975 season I started crewing for my dad and Hilary crewed for Hleanor Witter. Half-way through the 1975 season my dad and I were not doing to badly until one Wednesday evening race. My dad and I riged up the boat for the racr that evening. There was a fair wind blowing then and we moved away from the hard fairly fast. to had not gone far when there was a huge great crash and banging noise from underneath the boat. A’'minute later we felt our feet in some water 80 we looked at the bottom of the boat and there was water gushing into the boat, we then- had no choice but to head back to the hard. When we reached the hard we looked where the boat had been breaking and the centre board casing had been cracked in half and there was a whole in the bottom of the boat. So that definatly meant no sailing for a few weekends, Since then we have not done very well.
My dad orders me around a lot in the boat, but when I went in for the cadet races my dad crewed for me so then I had my chance to order him around for once. THAMES TRIP MAY 1975

Our coldest trip on the boat. We set off from Stansygate in the late afternoon, a little later than we had intended as the boat was firmly aground and remained so for an hour after we arrived. Dad's calculations again. fe sailed around to the River Roach that night where we anchored and were glad to hear the Northerly gales forecast had moved north of tke Humber. We awoke to a cold sunny morning and motored down narrow cut and went aground, Dad reached for his Cootes again and read more carefully that this passage was only passable at Springs. we were relieved to learn that these were springs so we sat and waited until Jestabel was lifted enough to carry on towards Haven Gore. The Had flay was still flying and we could hear guns booming as we approached, I think we had visions of cannon balls flying through he mainsail. Mum made coffee to ease the tension as it was now well into the alloted time to make the passage and we were being completely ignored. We peered hopefully at tke man in the bridge house but he looked straight through us. Just as we thought Dad's telephone call aad been in vain the man appeared, shut the gate and started to open the bridge. mum was alarmed because the red flag was still flying but the man beckoned us through and we motored past two uniformed gentlemen in state like royalty and waved in a dignified way. we had nine feet of water under us as we aimed out across the siaplin and by three o'clock we had pulled up on @ mooring in Ray Gut off Southend Pier, here disaster nearly hit again and we kept well out of the way while fumed and swore at Chris, who had accidently knocked over the spare battery in the 'loo' (he's always in trouble) acid was leaking and me and Dad got holes in our trousers from it, luckily we had salt on board and we went ashore for bicarbonate of soda we were relieved to find no hole in the bottom. wanted to run aground just in case” After breakfast on Saturday we upped anchor and headed for Gravesend. This was a super trip as we had loads of commercial traffic to avoid. Dad had thought of stopping off at Holehaven but he was looking at a 1957 Cootes and things have changed. The new Cootes we had left after buying it at John's in Mid)don. We swa dredgers, tankers and a super boat from Bergen carrying timber, we picked up a mooring at Gravesend Yacht Club and luckily I and Tim stayed behind with a friend while the others went shopping otherwise the dinghy would have been hanging by its painter over the quay as the tide drops a lot there.
On Sunday we were able to sail with a good wind past the ship ‘orcester at Gre-nhithe and Mum took loads of pictures instead off helping to go about. we only just made it ahead of the bowsprit. It was fun to sail over Dartford Tunnel for a chansze. 4ith such @ good wind behind us we made such good time that we passed both Grays Thurrock Sailing Club and Erith Yacht Club where there were spare moorings.

Dear Mr Weedon,

It occurred to me that there may be members of your club who would be considering the purchase of the National Squib keelboat but are put off as there is no class racing for them in your club. At Stone we have twelve squibs and would like to increase the size of our fleet but are restricted by lack of moorings.
The Squib Class at Stone would welcome any of your members with a Squib to come and race with us. We have a full programme of races and it is only a short sail from your moorings to our starting line.
If your club built up a fleet, our fleets might race together as a combined fleet as happens at Burnham with the Royal Corinthian and Royal Burnham Squib fleets. Racing could perhaps start at Stone one week and Marconi the next and so on.
I would be delighted to hear if any of your members are interested in this proposal as Squibs are eminently suited to the River Blackwater. Log of "Half-a-Sixpence", from Thursday 17th July 1975

The proposed itinerary was to make for Ostend, then head westwards along the French coast before returning home. Half-a-Sixpence ia s Vivacity 20 about 8 years old, with a Seagull 45 H.P. outboard. The crew on this occasion consisted of my father and myself. This was the longest trip we had attempted. Last year we went to Calais and back, stopping at Ramsgate for a night, both on the way to Calais and on the return journey. Due to other commitments this year we were unable to consider going to Holland with the rest of the Marconi fleet the following week.
The courses we intended to follow were all marked on charts in red pencil beforehand, with appropriate bearings. This did not mean we intended to stick rigidly to a pre-deter-
mined plan, but it did make life easier later - chart work on a 20 footer is not easy. All
charts are kept in 12" L.P. covers, the transparent plastic sort. By judicious folding of the charts the required 2 square feet can be made to show, and kept clean, dry and flat.
Chinagraph pencil is used for writing on the outside, drawing bearing lines etc. - this
can easily be removed with a damp cloth afterwards.
We took 3 hour spells at the helm - less than this does not allow the person off duty
to get much rest, more than this is too long at the helm, especially after the third or ‘yrth session. No doubt on a longer voyage this would have been modified, but it worked well on this occasion.
No attempt has been made, in this account, to cover up any mistakes we made.
Thursday evening saw our arrival at Stansgate, where all the gear and food was loaded
on board, and the Avon Redstart (hired from Lifecraft Hire Co. at Tiptree) lashed on the cabin top, after deflating the bow section. As there was no wind at all we motored down river, and dropped anchor just past Bradwell power station, fairly close to the shore, where we settled down for the night after hoisting a riding light, alarm clock set for 6.15am. There was a bit of a breeze during the night and as we grounded the noise of the water slopping about against the bottom of the boat between the bilge keels woke me. up and again when we lifted off.

Friday 18th July. Bradwell to Ostend H.T. Dover 07.33 (B.S.T.) 20.03 (B.S.T.)

06.33 Shipping forecast gave wind variable force 2, becoming southerly 3. Some showers.
Visibility moderate, some costal fog - patches at first.
After breakfast, one job had to be done before we left, attach the mounting plates for our newly-acquired Walker log. What a lovely instrument this is, with all the attachments fitting so neatly into the wooden case. Within a few short hours, we ndered how we have ever managed without it.

08.10 Up anchor and off we go, under main and genoa, against the last of the flood tide. Wind very light, s/w by w. Sky grey, with a few bits of blue showing through in places. N.B. Courses shown hereafter are courses steered, not necessarily to be made good.
09.10 Log reading 2.0 miles. Course set 108° M. to Bench Head Buoy.
09.40 Bench Head Buoy on port beam. Log reading 3.3 miles. Course set 135° M for Wallet
Spitway.
10.45 Wallet Spitway abeam. Log reading 5.5 miles. Course set 180° for Swin Spitway.
11.10 Swin Spitway abeam. Log reading 6.4 miles. Course set 80° M for Sunk Head Tower. Running goose-winged, or trying to, but combination of light following wind and favourable tide meant that sails were not pulling much. Shortly after this we noticed that the Red Duster had got wrapped up in the log line, which was coiling up like a spring. This was easily released, by pulling the flag, but how much it caused the log to under-register is not known.

12.25 West Gunfleet abeam. Log reading 9.1 miles.
13.55 Forecast gave W3/4, with showers at first, visibility mainly good.
14.00 Cup of tea and a snack. Wind by now very light, log hardly turning. We passed a large Panamanian cargo ship, the "Gardenia" while crawling down the Hast Swin.
(I say passed - in fact she was going in the opposite direction to us at the time).

15.00 Sunk Head Tower just visible on horizon, through haze.

6.

16.00 Sunk Head Tower abeam. What a load of old junk. All crumbling concrete with iron spikes sticking out all over the place. Log reading 17-1 miles. Wind getting up a bit now. At Sunk Head buoy altered course to 075 My, making for Long Sand Head.

16.45 Thundery rumbles coming up from behind, so waterproofs and wellies put on. A big, black storm following right on our tail. Shortly after this we had heavy rain accompanied by much thunder and lightning, which altogether lasted for about 1 hour, with squalls blowing frequently.

18.00 Long Sand Head abeam. Log reading 27.0. Course set 115° M for Galloper. Wind now
disappearing again, a heavy horrible swell remaining.

20.00 Galloper over to our port side. Dad comes up to start his next 3 hours spell at the helm, feeling rather queasy. Engine started.
20.15 Kentish Knock lightship noticed to West - still there then. Recent chart amendments
said it was to be replaced by a buoy on or about July 7th.
20.30 Course altered to 200° for awhile to let supertanker pass at a distance. When we first
saw it, it was pointing straight at us, but turning slowly to starboard. These monsters give no impression of movement at all, until you see the huge hump of water at the place where smaller ships have a bow wave.

20.45 Navigation lights on, then I went below for a rest of sorts.

I came up for my 3 hours session, also feeling queasy by now. The stretch from Galloper to West Hinder was a drag, as for most of the way we had no wind, and were motoring with a sickening swell on our beam — with no sails up to steady the boat we were rolling from side to side for hours on end. The course is 145° M on the chart, 27 miles in a straight line, and this we followed, reckoning on 12 hours for this stretch i.e. two tides, so overall no correction for tide necessary. We could have motored quicker than this, but this only made the motion worse. During the night several diversions had to be made for large ships, and also for a fishing boat
performing strange antics - whichever way we went, it seemed his lights always
looked the same. After these diversions we suspected our position somewhat so checked with the Seafix D.F. set on West Hinder and found to our satisfaction that it was in the right place, on our starboard bow, with the tide flooding to the s/w. The D.F. set is a very reassuring instrument to have around. We only use it as a navigational aid, not as our prime means of navigation. For one thing it would be wrong to rely wholly on it without any form of Dead Reckoning and another is that it is difficult on a small boat to get within 5°, unless you are very close to the radio beacon itself, or have lots of practice.

Saturday 19th July H.T. Dover 08.47 (B.S.T.)

07.00 Wind turned on very suddenly, so sails up — main and working jib.

West Hinder. Log reading 62.0 miles. Course set 100° M for S.W.Akkaert. Wind now a
good force 4, from the west. Long rolling waves coming up from behind, some breaking making boat very difficult to steer, constantly trying to broach broadside on. A buoy appeared on our port side, midway between West Hinder and S.W. Akkaert. Our charts showed a buoy "A" to starboard of our proposed course, which amendments have then shown to be removed. Because of the difficulty we were having in keeping the boat in a straight line we thought it a possibility that we were on the wrong track but couldn't believe we were that far out so decided to maintain course as best as possible. Shortly afterwards we spotted Kwinte Bank buoy in the right place. To the north of this stretch we could see thick clouds of smoke rolling along the horizon, emanating from an area designated for "Burning of Chemical Refuse." If there had been any north in the wind, we would have found ourselves sailing right through a dense chemical fog.
Kwinte Bank. Log reading 72.0 miles. At this point we could really see the strength of the tide so decided to head for Ostend from here rather than continue to the
S.W.Akkaert buoys - in fact we never sighted them. Course set 180° M.
Town of Ostend visible from here, but at a distance of 10 miles it was not possible
to pick out any landmarks. A check with the D.F. on Ostend Rear

made a positive identification.
It is surprising how difficult it is to make out a harbour entrance on one's
first visit, if there is anythirg but perfect visibility - we had spotted several
Sea link ferries seemingly steaming into blocks of flats, but did not see the actual entrance until less than a mile away, although compass bearings on the lighthouse showed we were heading straight for it.
Belgian flag and yellow "Q" flag hoisted when some way from harbour.

12.30 Sailing up between harbour walls, Log taken in, reading 83.9 miles. This was probably
due to flag getting caught up in the line several times - I'll have to re-locate one
or the other. We reckoned on a total distance of 90 miles, though overall we had a fair bit of help from the tide. Having learnt by heart the various combinations of spheres and cones that formed the harbour entrance signals, we were somewhat disconcerted to see only 4 black squares hoisted from the station on the eastern harbour wall. As nothing appeared to be in the way, we carried on in. We remembered afterwards that the squares were tidal height signs.
The North Sea Yacht Club was full, and we didn't fancy the Marina much, being in full view of all the crowds in the town, so made for the Royal Yacht Club of Ostend,
where on approach we were directed to a berth by loudhailer - all very friendly and
efficient. We were now motoring, having handed the sails once inside the harbour, and while pottering up to the pontoons putting fenders out, the engine stopped, and would not start for quite a few pulls on the cord —- visions of arriving at our berth or rather someone elses, sideways and out of control. One last pull before hastily setting some sail, and the engine fired.
Having said we would like to stay for three nights, leaving early on Tuesday, we were asked for 150 francs, and told to make ourselves at home, including the use of the shower. We were given a form to fill in, for the Mgrine Police, with all the usual immigration details. This we were asked to complete and post in the box by the clubhouse, together with passports and ship's registration papers. We did not fancy the idea of leaving all our documents lying in a post—box, so just posted the form to see what happened. Reaction from the Mjrine Police:- Zero. Just as well we had retained our passports as we were then visited by two gentlemen in khaki uniform, who introduced themselves as Customs Officers. Having been cleared, and apparently all formalities completed we hauled down the Q flag, and went over to the clubhouse for a quick wash and brush-up. Just above our names where we signed the visitors book we noticed "July 12th. Eric Taberly. Pen-Duick VI".
A telephone call was made home, connection arranged by the bar-steward, cost 25 francs per minute, followed by a walk into town. The R.Y.C.0O. is quite a distance from the town of Ostend and according to Delmar-Morgan it is possible to catch tram No. 3 or bus No. 9 to the station, though we always walked. The bus fare is 7 francs each way, or you can get a "season" ticket giving 10 journeys, for 60 francs. The main hazard to watch out for is the fact that one half of most pavements is set aside for cyclists and mopeds — we had several near misses. On our return back
from the town, came supper, hot showers and a very welcome long deep SLEWJEBE.....F.

Sunday July 20th At this stage we thought we had two days to be tourists so walked
into town to do the usual tourist things, having first rigged up a cover over the cockpit. First stop was the cathedral of St. Peter and St. Paul, whose twin spires can be seen some way out to sea. As we arrived a large congregation .as emerging and we went in to hear the great organ playing for a while, filling the whole cathedral with sound. It was all very impressive with the high roof and the stained
glass windows, and all very ornate - too much so for my taste.
A cup of coffee and a biscuit each cost us the equivalent of 65p, so we made the most of it and decided it would have to be tie last. While sitting in the open air enjoying our expensive coffee, we were engaged in conversation with two Belgians, one of whom belonged to the British Legion.
We decided not to look over the school ship "Mercator", a square-rigger per- manently moored in a dock near the town centre, as it would have made our 20-footer seem even smaller on our return.

Monday July 21st. While walking along the promenade I spotted a Marconi Sailing
Club pennant rising above the heads of the crowds. On going over to investigate we

Bie

saw Davolas II just going out of the lock from the marina. Monday afternoon was
spent doing mostly domestic chores, and preparing for Tuesday's sail - bought 10:1
petrol from the garage by the club, cleaned the plug and the fuel filter, and pumped up the Avon which had gone rather limp.
Monday saw the arrival of a new cleaning woman at the club, and a sign saying,
"Douches Vingt Francs". The arrival of these two items saw the departure of the hot water, so that was that. It was very difficult going to the loo or stripping down for a wash, as this wretched woman would stroll in with her bucket of water at any old time. My father said she even started polishing the mirror while he was trying
to shave - one felt like giving her a tip just to make her go away. Needless to say
a plate had appeared on the table by the door, and she always left a few francs in it to remind everybody of the purpose of this plate.
17-55 Forecast gave s/w 4, not very good for our proposed route. Soon after this we had supper, a short walk, and early to bed, with alarm set to wake us up for 00.33 forecast -— this was to be our routine for the rest of our stay in Ostend.

Tuesday July 22nd.
00.33 Forecast w/sw 5 to 7 - great.
Although I woke up for the 6.33 forecast, and turned on the radio, I fell asleep again and missed it, not that it made much difference. A Belgian on a big Finnsailei moored near us said he would listen to a local French forecast for us. On enquiring shortly afterwards, his wife told us that Hubby had heard the forecast, and the wind would be variable. Obviously we had got our wires crossed somewhere, as by now all the boats on the pontoons were shuffling about quite actively, and the wind was whistling through the rigging. To add insult to injury, the wind speed indicator in the clubhouse showed '1 knot' This is a Tannoy instrument, similar to the one at our own clubhouse — under-reading must b= a common fault with these.
We walked into town, mainly to see the sea, as if we did not see enough of it.
Very choppy, many white horses with wind blowing straight along the coast - dead
opposite the way we wanted to go. We did not stay to see it but the sea must have . become much rougher later on, when the tide turned to the west. On our way back to the moorings, we had to wait for a swing bridge over a lock to open and close, to enable a small coastal tanker through.
17-55 Forecast s/w 5 to 6, 8 later.
Wednesday July 23rd. A Radio Luxembourg outside broadcast van was parked near the
harbour, and we watched for a while —- a programme sponsored by a Children's Construction Toy firm was being made.
Shortly afterwards we witnessed a dramatic rescue scene, though we were too faz away to be of any assistance. A child swimming from the beach had got into difficulties, and was being swept out to sea. (Red flags were flying, and there were notices in umpteen languages saying "No Bathing"). Having seen the danger, a fellow who was obviously a good swimmer went out to her, but had trouble in getting back against the strong off shore current. He finally made it to a breakwater where they were both hauled out of tle water by many willing hands, the gallant rescuer collapsing onto a stretcher.
When it was all over, no less than three offshore rescue boats arrived on the scene. All this took place in seas thrown up by a force 7 wind. That afternoon we explored the possibilities of going by canal to Calais, via Nieuport and Dunkirk but found there were several snags, one of them being our mast. Also, on the French canals, a permit has to be obtained in advance. According to the Cruising Association Handbook, necessary equipment for passing through locks includes two 10' poles and a ladder. Now why didn't I think of bringing those with us when we set out?
I made a reverse charge ("P.C.V.") call home that evening, which the girl at the bar arranged for mes; The procedure is to dial 094 and give the operator all the details; the snag is that these particular operators will only speak Flemish. It was just as well I phoned as the folks at home were getting a bit anxious having heard the gale warnings.

17-55 Forecast, gale warnings, s/w 6 to 8, becoming W 5 later.

9.

Thursday 24th July
During our usual daily pilgrimage into town and up to the end of the harbour wall, we spotted a recent acquaintance of ours in his 35' motor cruiser attempting to leave -— like us he had been held up for some days. After a few minutes he was back
again. Back at the club, Marcel came round for his daily 50 francs - by now we were
nearly out of Belgian money. He informed us that we could change money at the bar, the rate being 75 francs, or if we cared to go to the station we could get 80 francs. We informed him that we preferred to get 83 francs from the souvenir shop by the harbour. A travel agent was also giving 83 franes.

17-55 Forecast s/w 6 to 7, becoming N/W.

Friday 25th July

Wind now in N/W, sea rough, and one or two boats out sailing, but nothing under 30' and all of them making heavy going of it. Very cold standing on end of harbour wall, as we watched one of the Sea link passenger ferries enter harbour. Even these conditions they turn round outside the harbour, and come in backwards at great speed. The car ferries come in forwards, but we never saw one leaving, so cannot say whether they depart forwards or backwards.
On our way back to the boat we called in at the supermarket for a few essential
supplies - staying in port all the time, we were getting through more food than we
would have done had we sailed earlier. DELHAIZE is a big supermarket, located opposite the school-ship Mercator, where prices are definitely cheaper than those in town. It was here that we bought bottles of wine for taking home. There was a large selection here, at reasonable prices. Some that we bought was only 30 francs, though at the time of writing this, we had not tried it.
17-55 Forecast NW/SW, 4 to 5.

Saturday 26th July H.T. Dover 01.37 (B.S.T.)
Ostend to Dunkirk 13.53 (B.S.T.)
06.00 Much quieter outside, so got up and dressed, ready to go if forecast satisfactory.

06.33 Forecast w/SW 2 to 3, possibly 4. No rain, visibility good to moderate.
06.45 Cast off from R.Y.C.0O.
07.05 Emerging from harbour entrance, log out. A gentle breeze, right on the nose, so did not attempt to put sails up. A clear blue sky, with haze at sea level.
8.05 Check log (3.25 miles) to give speed through water.
v8.20 Zuidstroombank buoy. Log 3.9 miles.
09.00 Westroombank buoy. Log 5.7 miles. Breeze a bit stronger by now, and some cloud forming. 09.25 Log 6.8 miles. In line with Nieuport harbour entrance.
09.55 Log 8.3 miles. Mid-way between yellow spoil ground buoy and green wreck buoy. 10.30 Log 9.9 miles. Between Trapegeer buoy and diminutive green wreck-—buoy. 11.00 Belgian flag down, French flag up.
11295 Log 11.5 miles. E2 buoy. Bear off to port for 3. Wind on our starboard bow for this
stretch, so main set, but motor kept running.
11.20 Log 12.4 miles. E3 buoy.
11.40 Log 13.5 miles. E5 buoy. Heading for E7, taking care not to stray north of line
between £5 and E7, which would take us over Banc Hills.
11.55 Log 14.3 miles. E7 buoy. Main taken down again.
12.35 Log 15-8 miles. E9 buoy. Tide now against us, running quite fast.
13.20 Log 17.6 miles. Floride buoy.
14.30 In Dunkirk harbour entrance, log taken in reading 20.9 miles, distance on chart about
25 miles. We had to motor in a large circle round the Event Port to let a cargo ship
by-
15.15 Tied up at Yacht Club de la Mer du Nord. The drill here is to moor bow on to pontoon (which makes getting ashore not so easy), and if you are lucky a buoy astern; if not ropes either side from both quarters to the pontoon to stop swinging. Fortunately there were plenty of rubber tyres available for bow fenders.
The Y.C.M.N. was dwarfed by a huge supertanker being fitted out opposite,

"EL PASA SONATRACH" - Liberian of course.

10.

17-55 Forecast s/w 3 to 4, becoming variable.
The charge for a one night stay was 10 francs. To wash your hands cost 40 cents,
and a shower 2 francs. A word of warning to those who intend to stay here - the loos
were locked up after 10pm and probably were not opened again until later next morning they were definitely shut at 6 a.m.

Sunday 27th July H.T.Dover 02.11 (B. S.T.)
14.27 (B (B.S.T
7 )
Dunkirk to Ramsgate

Forecast s/w 2 to 3, becoming variable.
06.40 Cast off from Y.C.M.N.
07-00 Log line streamed in the Event Port with the fishing fleet just coming in as we left. 07.05 Outside harbour, heading west for the buoyed channel. This particular stretch is very well marked, as clear as a road, with a pair of buoys about every mile. The first pair, DW 29/30, are just to the west of the harbour entrance. These tall French buoys are easy to locate from a distance, though they are harder to distinguish in terms of shape and colour, than the English can and conical buoys.
We tried putting up the sails but the wind was just a little too fine on the port bow, the mainsail flapping and the jib backing, so decided to wait until we left tr the buoyed channel.
07.25 DW27/28. Log 1.3 miles. A horrible coastline on our port side, just to the west of
the harbour - very much industrialised, with tall chimmneys belching out thick black
smoke.
07.40 DW 25/26. Log 2.1 miles.
07-55 DW 23/24. Log 2.8 miles. The beaches and sand dunes of Dunkirk about 1 mile away -
how easy the sailing was for us, compared with the hazards that faced the Armada of
small ships which rescued 345,000 English and French troops in 1940.
08.07 Dw 21/22. Log 3.5 miles.
08.20 DW 19/20. Log 4.2 miles.
08.33 DW 17/18. Log 4.9 miles.
08.45 DW 15/16. Log 5.5 miles. Course set 315°, due N/V.
09.30 Engine off, sailing under main and genoa, but not moving very fast.
10.30 Speed 2 knots in last hour, wind now dropping, so engine on again.
11.30 Passing through a veritable Sargasso Sea - propeller and log rotor caught up in thick
weed. This happened several times during the ensuing 1% hours, mostly seaweed, but once a polythene bag.
11.35 Outer Routinger Ouest. Sandettie lightship visible.
12.45 In between mid-channel buoys. Wind reasonable now, motor sailing well.
13-00 Sandettie due east, barely visible.
13.45 English coast just in sight - if we had realised we were going to be this far on, we
would have aimed further south, to go round the South Goodwin lightship, but on the other hand, we would not then have been able to motor-sail so well. Besides we have
been that way before - North Goodwin would be a change. By now, tide running strongly
N.E.
14.30 Turned engine off, for a bit of peace and quiet,yand just drifted with the tide - no
point in getting to North Goodwin much before tide started to ebb about 18.00. Log line hanging vertically. Sea like a mirror.
15.30 Engine on again.
East Goodwin lightship.
16.30 East Goodwin buoy, log 27-8 miles. Although we did not stray south of the line between
lightship and the buoy, there was one patch amongst all the calm, where sudden turbulence all round alarmed us considerably. A check on the echo sounder showed 5' when a minute previously it has been 50'. On occasions like this it is easy to see how
treacherous these sandbanks can be - just imagine what they are like in a stom.
17-55 Forecast s/w 3 to 4, becoming variable. Fair, visiblity good to moderate.
18.05 Gull buoy, log 33.5 miles - we had decided by now that there was no need to go right
up as far as the North Goodwin Lightship.
19.00 Q flag hoisted.
19.15 Motoring into Ramsgate Harbour, where we tied up alongside a Belgian boat. A quick visit was then made ashore, to phone our respective wives, and to try and obtain some fuel, but in this we were unsuccessful.

11.

22.15 Having scrambled, and consumed our last five eggs, we settled down for the night in readiness for an early start the next morning. The peace of this incredibly calm evening was then shattered as the life boat maroons were fired close by. Within minutes the crew members' cars were arriving at great speed along the eastern jetty, and the lifeboat left the harbour soon afterwards. We did not find out what the trouble was -— presumably some sort of power craft with engine trouble drifting onto the Goodwins.

Monday July 28th H.T.Dover 02.45 (B.S.T.)
15.00 (B.S. tT.)
Ramsgate to Stansgate

04.45 Departure from Ramsgate, absolute flat calm. Only four gallons of fuel left, and
reckoning 3 hours per gallon, we had enough for twelve hours running - we were
wondering at this stage whether we would have quite enough to get us back to Stansgate or not, should there be no wind. Lights on for a while, though dawn already creating a wedge on the eastern horizon, levering away the darkness. Between Ramsgate and North Foreland it is necessary to keep lookout for lobster pot floats trailing in long strings just below the surface, the only warning being a small flag at one end. Pockets of mist were forming at the base of the cliffs, making us wonder if visibility would be good enough. At this stage there was quite a chill in the air. 06.00 Long Nose buoy. Log 4.0 miles. A heavy tide swirling against the buoy, in a north - easterly direction. Course set due N/W.
06.33 Forecast. Winds variable - visibility good to moderate.
06.50 East Margate buoy abeam, about & mile away. Log 6.3 miles.
07.30 Very hazy, no buoys or land in sight.
07-40 Glanced up from compass, to see a seagull standing on the sand dead ahead. We had headed too far west in allowing for the beam tide, and had nearly grounded on Margate sand. The edge of the sandbank was clearly shown by a line of ripples and Wavelets. Turning 90 starboard with one eye on the edge of the sand, and the other on the echo—-sounder, we found our way round the eastern end of the sand-bank, and were back on course by 07.55. Tongue Sands Tower now in sight.
08.00 Boiling hot by now -— all oilies and woollies etc. put away, shorts being the only comfortable gear.
08.30 Started on last 3 gallons of fuel. Thinks: just about now I should have been back at work.
08.55 Tongue Sand Tower and buoys in line, to starboard. Log 12.5 miles.
99-15 Position fixing rather difficult now, with strong cross tide, and a haze reducing visibility to less than 1 mile — buoys disappearing before the next one in sight. 09.20 Edinburgh Fairway spotted, due N.
09.40 Edinburgh Fairway abeam log 14.5 miles.
10.00 Patch buoy. Log 15.0 miles.
10.10 N.Edinburgh No.2 Log 15.4 miles.
10.20 N.Edinburgh No.4 Log 16.0 miles.
10.35 N.Edinburgh No.7 Log 16.6 miles.
11.08 Black Deep No.12 Log 18.5 miles.
44517 Black Deep No 11 Log 19.0 miles.
11.45 Between Barrow No.8 and S.W.Sunk Beacon. Log 20.5 miles. Tide now flooding
strongly, giving us great difficulty in making any headway. Seagull now not labouring at all.
12.35 A breeze sprang up from the east whereupon we immediately set some sail. What _a
difference it made - the engine revs increased noticeably, the Seagull now not
labouring at all.
12.45 Barrow No. 7 Log 23.3 miles.
13.40 N.E.Middle, Log 27.0 miles.
13.55 Whitaker Log 27.4 miles, (after getting caught up in the Red Duster once again.)
14.10 Swin Spitway. Log 28.5 miles.
14.25 Wallet Spitway Log 29.4 miles.
15.10 Bench Head, Log 32.2 miles. The wind was now strong enough to push us along from
behind, and keep the sails filled even in the favourable tide, so we thankfully turned off the engine after 104 hours, keeping our last half-gallon of fuel in

12.

case it might be needed when the tide turned.
16.10 Bradwell Power Station. Log taken in reading 35.1 miles, as there was a danger of it
getting run down by the many small craft buzzing around. Tide just starting to ebb.

17.30 Arrived back at Stansgate, against a strong tide, after a very good sail from Bradwell, estimated log reading 40 miles for the days run.

Conclusion

We were of course glad to be back, yet settling down to normal routines would be difficult after 11 days on board Half-a-Sixpence. It was disappointing that we had suffered from either too much wind or not enough wind throughout the holiday, but that's sailing. Although we had not been able to make all the ports of call as originally planned, we had covered nearly 200 miles safely, and as always, bad learned a great deal. No doubt we could have taken some short cuts, and at other times took those we should have avoided but we did at least manage to keep out of trouble. The decision we have to make now is :- Where shall we go next year?

Peter Barker, 11th. September 1975.

ROUND THE IS RACE

Having decided to spend a week of our holiday sailing, and not wishing to travel far, the Mersea Sailing Week seemed ideally suitable for Stan Oaker, myself and supporting cast. This was held over the lst week in August and consisted of a pointsseries organised by the Dabchicks S.C. on Monday, Tuesday and Thursday, with separate races for Solos, Enterprises, Mirrors, Winklebrigs (traditional sailing workboats of about 15 foot length) and fast and slow handicap classes; Friday was the Dabchicks Regatta and Saturday the West Mersea Y.C. Regatta. The two Regattas included races for every type of sailing vessel from large ocean racers down to
dinghies even smaller than the Mirror - the Optimist!

What has all this got to do with Round the Island Race? You may well ask - well I am just
getting to that - on the Wednesday the West Mersea Y.C. ran this annual handicap race for
circumnavigating Mersea Island by sail. The rules stated that the start and finish line was off the W.Mersea Club House, the Island could be rounded in either direction and one's start time, which coujd be any time after 9-66 a.m., had to be stated on the entry form. Anyone
finishing after 5-30 p.m. would be disqualified, high tide being at 12-03. As entries had to
be in by the Thursday before, I rang Jackie Payne (The assistant Sailing Secretary of Dabchicks S.C. and well known helmswoman of the Enterprise "Jack Sprat" and as we subsequently found out 7 “yably the best cream sponge maker in Essex) to obtain advice on a good starting time and to huud in our entries and fees (50p) . After some discussion with Jackies father 11-55 was ~ecommended and a clockwise route around the island.

All those who have been to Mersea by road know that to get onto the island one has to cross a causeway, known locally as the Strood and although this can be under a few inches of water at extra high springs it was obvious that is was going to be impossible to sail across, to carrying or dragging ones boat was established as normal. The day before the race we walked to the Strood, about 13 miles from the West Mersea Y.C., to check out a suitable route across. The best plan seemed to be to land at a sandy slope which ran up to a gateway, across the main road which we were told would have a policeman on duty to stop the traffic and then down to the muddy banks of the other side. Not too difficult as long as it was around high water.

The day of the race began hot and calm as was common last Summer. we collected our race instructions, which included a chart of the island and a list of all the competitors, with their start times. Many dinghies seemed to be taking part, with 117 entries (40 of them mirrors) and
the majority starting between 11-00 and 11-45 and in fact only 8 boats starting after us. With
the promise of an Easterly sea breeze coming up after mid day, I thought our chances were good. The remainder of the family and friends had gone on to the Strood to assist in getting the boats yross. 20 minutes before our start time we launched and checked the position of the start line, checked the watch against a Unicorn starting 4 mins. before us and prepared for our start.

11-55 Bang: Our starting signal and we were off in company with 1 Enterprise, Jack Sprat, following the channel in a northerly direction. As the wind was easterly (about force 2) we hoisted the spinnaker and wondered whether we would reach the Strood before the water receeded or get across in one piece. As the channel turned to the N.E. the spinnaker had to be taken down and gradually the course became close hauled, the Enterprise slowly pulled away and then the Strood was in sight. The 11-58 Cherub just caught us up as we landed. Several pairs of hands helped the boats out of the water, up the slope, across the road to the other side, where the tidewas beginning to ebb —- we never even thought to look for road traffic. Settling down to a beat down the upper reaches of the Pyefleet Channel, which reminded me of the Norfolk Broads, we were overtaken by the 12-05 Flying Dutchman and eventuall by the remainder of the faster late starters but confidence was restored when we overhauled another Mirror, but maybe it was just pottering.- it was difficult to decide. As the ebb current increased and the clear wind (about force 4) was blowing directly up the channel we needed to sit right out while we tacked to and fro, keeping towards the centre of the 200 yd. wide unspoilt stretch of water so that we made the most of the ebb tide. We passed some fishermen and then overhauled another Mirror, eventually emerging into the wider waters of the Colne with Brightlingsea visible over on the far shore. A few more long tacks, during which we overtook a Cadet and we were round the Eastern end of the island, passing a friendly word with Jim French, the Dabchicks Commodore, who was on a moored committee boat checking off the competitors as they passed. Over half way round now and with a freer wind we kept close in shore as the tide was now against us, close enough in fact for some light-hearted advice to be exchanged between our boat and the bathers, because now we were passing the holiday beachea of E.Mersea. Stretching ahead several miles could be seen a procession of dinghy sails keeping about 200 yds. off shore. I am still not

4.

sure why as we were much oops: aground again ... perhaps thats why: Our next ai m
was to overtake the Optimist ahead and as the coast curved, up went the spinnaker. The next objective was to overtake a red sail in the distance but before that a swig of canned drink carried in case of emergency. Gradually we caught up the red sail and lo and behold not a Mirror but a Sea Ranger with a handicap of 128. This was quite a struggle to pass so I should
think it has a very favourable handicap. A large bunch of Red sails ahead - definitely Mirrors
this time as we were passing the more crowded W.Mersea beaches, but we could n ot quite catch them as we turned past the western end of the island and entered the crowded moorings in the sheltered channel gently gliding up to the finishing line off the Yacht Club 2 hours 26 mins.
after our departure - not bad for more than 11 miles in a Mirror. We wondered how the other
116 boats fared, some of them not as well as us but what about those who started earlier or the faster boats who disappeared over the horizon just after the start.

The results and prizegiving was announced for 7-00 p.m. that evening so with much trepidation we returned to the Yacht Club on that warm Summer evening and by 7-30 the officials
were at last preparing for the great announcements and presentations. lst ... Flying Dutchman,

Mirror - Stan, best capsize, etc.

COMMODORES NOTES

After not contributing to the last two issues of Navigans, I have taken up my pen again to report on the winter's activities. Following the magnificent effort on the Hard at Christmas we have not called formal Working Parties to prepare for the season but much has been going on behind the scenes by the band of dedicated workers. The winter and this coming season must be one of consolidation for the Club after two very eventful years with the building and commissioning of the Clubhouse. Some jobs were outstanding after the opening of the Club lust year and these are presently being tackled. In addition to the work on the Hard, winter hedging and ditching parties and our caretaker have done a great tidying up job. The septic tank has undergone further modification to prevent back filling from the ground water table when the level is up in the winter. Also, in the last week, with the generous help of our farmer neighbour Len Maclean, the area in front of the Club has been rotavated, levelled, sown and rolled and with a little bit of rain we should soon see it turning green. The area has been roped off and members are requested to keep off it and to ensure that their children and dogs are also prevented from going on it.
As you may remember it was agreed at the A.G.M. that we should permit some camping at Stansgate on selected weekends during the season. The dates have already been published and bye-laws have been posted at the Club for the guidance of members. It should be borne in mind that the facility is offered strictly for the benefit of Sailing Club members and their families and is not intended to create a situation where the Club becomes open to a and sundry for camping. The scheme is experimental and should it get out hand it will be necessary to consider whether to continue in future years. A very modest scale of charges is also published at the Club and all members availing themselves of the facility will be required to pay the appropriate fee.
The Committee were very pleased to hear from Jill Savill that she now has a good number of volunteers to help with the Galley this year. This is a major change in the organisation of one of the services of the Club after a number of years and it was encouraging to know that people had come forward and I would like to thank you all on behalf of the Committee. In conclusion may I wish you all a very happy and successful Sailing Season this year and I look forward to seeing you down at Stansgate.

Whatever happened to the Individualist?

Some ten or 80 years ago, the Sailing Club was caught up in the same discussions on class changes as it has been in recent months. It was then that the Hornet class emerged to fill the need. The reasons it was attractive then, are even more relevant today. The first of these reasons, must be that of cost. Even today, you can buy a fully equipped, competitive Hornet for as little as £150. I would think that this compares very favourably
with 420, 470 and 505's. In fact, my own boat, now two seasons old, was built for approx.
£450, about £550 at today's prices.
The Hornet has been sailed in many countries all over the world for twenty five years, but this does not mean that it is a staid design, as many developments have taken place over the years. These include fully optional deck layout within a one design hull, optional trapeze or sliding seat, genoas, and larger spinnakers. It is here that the individualist comes into his own, unlike many classes.
I cannot claim that the Hornet is the easiest boat to handle, but & boat to keep both helmsman and crew fully occupied and interested. In fact, a real team effort can be enjoyed. The Hornet is used in Poland, as the Olympic training dinghy. Self bailing cockpits help keep the beginner sailing, as most of you will have seen. The rig can be adapted to suit crews of all weights, shapes and sizes. Perhaps you can see from my description why I enjoy sailing a Hornet so much.
Our Club is fortunate in that there is a great deal of class competition available . our river and in the East Coast Area. This also helps to keep racing running costs down. In fact, all the top helms and crews in recent years have been local. Hornet sailors have most certainly gained a reputation for being a lively, friendly, helpful crowd. Why not come and join us and find out? Speak to Peter Clayton who is the Marconi Fleet Captain, or any Horneteer, who will be only too willing to give you a sail. (Pints most acceptable.)

Mike Turner, H1937.

Log of the "Barbara Star" from 15.8.75 — 25.8.75.

Friday 15.8.75. 21.00 hrs. Finds us in the dinghy motoring to the "Barbara Starr", clad
*n all our wet weather gear, I even have my umbrella up. The rain is pouring down as though ‘ishing us for the sins of our forefathers. This, after months of dry weather, when the avast godly of us have been praying for rain for our gardens. But why now? Just as we are about to go aboard. The devil's way of looking after his own I suppose. There was some consolation in the thought of the runner beans at home lapping up this lovely rain water. Later we discovered that Braintree hadn't had a drop.

Saturday 16.8.75. 09.29 hrs. Lovely sunny morning. Quietly we slip our mooring at an
unusually deserted looking Stansgate. The Hollanders are still at sea. Running on a port tack with the wind a moderate W.S.W.
On to Thirslet beacon with just a lonely cormorant flying low over the water keeping us company. Last night's wet clothes strewn around the cockpit drying out. Umbrella put away for a rainy day. The swell is high, but not, as yet uncomfortably so. Visibility good. St. Osyth trees quite easily discernible. Another addition to the layed up ships anchored at Bradwell. This one of british registration, namely "Salter's Gate" London. What a state the shipping world must be in with all these boats lying idle. Barrier wall alongside. Not much traffic about. Everyone's having a lay in. Being a nervous inexperienced sailor I'm getting the wind up. "Where's my life jacket?". Bench Head coming up. Interesting to see the new Radar reflector atop it. The boat is rolling, so is my tummy, but Cliff is enjoying it. It's all right for him, he can swin.
Still good visibility as we pass the N.W.knoll and Bar buoys. The radar masts at Foulness are quite clearly seen. Invaded by a huge bee in the cabin. I do wish it was in my garden pollinating the marrows or something.

Fighting the battle with the bee has upset my battle with the bulge. Some light refreshment is called for. Its very difficult though in these weather conditions wish I had another pair of hands to go with my two left feet. With one eye I spot the Knoll buoy in the distance and with the other I can see Clacton. No, I am not cross eyed. Just very observant. Walton looks pretty with the sun shining on it, but then so does everywhere when the sun's upon it. Tolling its message to all men andwomen of the sea we pass the Wallet Spitway, followed by the Swin Spitway buoy. Its just like being called to prayers with all these bells ringing. "Please God will you make the seas calmer".
We are now doing 6 knots which is supposed to be the potential of the “Barbara Starr”, but she will do a little more going down hill. Midday and we are in the East Swin channel on a close reach with a fort looming in sight to the south. West Hook Middle looking very colourful in mid ocean. We are riding high on a wave and catch the first glimpse of the Kentish coastline, and then tacked in sight of the Barrow Beacon. Log stopped working probably due to weed. If it doesn't clear Cliff will be over the side in snorkel and flippers as soon as we anchor. That's always good for a laugh. To starboard, Whittaker Beacon. Log cleared itself, what a shame. S.W.Middle, huge swell on. Apples and oranges rolling around the cabin floor. Bad housekeeping. I have a lot to learn if I survive this battering? Even the dinghy is trying to jump aboard. Overtaken by motor cruiser "Pepitor". Battling on between Maplin sands and edge buoys. Seas getting rougher, and I'm scared to death. Going to retire to my boudoir with a fit of the vapours for a while.
Tacked all the way up the Thames to Sheerness, avoiding the wreck of the old ammunition ship "Richard Montgomery", which has been laying near the entrance to the Medway since 1944. Rumour has it, that if it did blow up, half of Sheerness would go with it. Still forging ahead, all hands on deck. Passing Garrison Point. The roughest trip I've ever made. I'm seriously thinking of hitch hiking back. At last. Nicely anchored at Queenborough, Isle of Sheppy. Battered and bruised I quietly say a prayer for our safe arrival.

Sunday 17.8.75. 0O7.30hrs.

Rudely awakened by the raucous voices of two anchored boat owners shouting to each other across the water. They are re-enacting Treasure Island. Robert Newton surely gave that story the kiss of life when the film was made. For my part I wished "Me earties" had left me in peace for another hour.
We have a nice quiet days sailing locally with my sister and brother-in-law, who, (God help them) live on Sheppey. They ate all my home made scones and splits too Splite is the Cornish name for bread rolls, for the uninitiated. Naturally, to get the best flavour from them you smother them with home made jam and Cornish cheap.
It was nice to see me sister after two years. We'll call on them one day and eat the out of house and home.

Monday 18.8.75. 11.10 hrs.

As we leave Queenborough the wind is N.Hasterly. It's high water and lovely warm sunshine. Heading eastwards towards the Swin, tacking all the way.
11.32. Garrison Point on one side, the Isle of Grain on the other. Seastoo rough to make coffee. The Holland ferry is in the docks at Sheerness preparing for their trip to Flushing, which they do in seven hours. We passed under the bows of the cargo ship "Framcop" anchored at the More, and steadily forced our way through the rough seas until we reached Brightlingsea. (19.00) It was a very boisterous and "Moisterous" trip from Queenborough during which the decks were well washed with spray. I feel like a battered wife.

Tuesday 19.8.75 12.10 hrs

The Harbour Master slipped up here, as we slipped away without paying. Unintentionally. It must have been his day off.
Wind S.W. force 5. Seas again very choppy. Very few sailing vessels out.

COMMITTEE NOTES

Our Editor made an appeal to the last Committee meeting for the contributions to Navigans to be positive and encouraging, but as we progressed through the meeting we became aware that the things we needed to draw to your attention tended to appear restrictive. Unfortunately they must be said, so my notes this month are headed Committee notes. A number of incidents have been reported this season which have included infringements of the Club Rules and are therefore, of a serious nature. Rules have two main purposes, to provide guide lines for the Administration of the Club and to impose some discipline which is for the benefit of all. In the second case it is often also to protect members from themselves, as is the case with insurance. What people may not always remember is that, although they are Prepared to take risks with their property, in the event of an accident somebody could be seriously injured and if not adequately insured the party to blame could have a life long debt both financially and of guilt. We annually ask all boat owners to sign an undertaking that their boat is adequately insured before bringing it to Stansgate and this should not be done without being absolutely sure that there will be cover before bringing the boat.
Members are also reminded that the Club is there for the benefit of the members and — it has been observed that there have been a considerable number of non-members both visit. on shore and sailing and there appears to have been a marked reluctance for these guest's names to be entered in the visitor's book. Under the present rules there are two slightly different versions of rules relating to guests depending on the circumstances. To clarify the situation the Committee passed the following bye law.
"The names of all adult guests brought to the site shall be entered in the Visitor's Book by the introducing member".
Members are requested to observe this bye—law and to ensure that their friends only visit the site when properly accompanied.
We have already heard of anumber of items of members property disappearing since the start of the season. This we find both disturbing and distasteful. As you are aware a public footpath runs through the Club and members are urged to be careful with their property and not put temptation in the way of others. The Club cannot in any way be responsible for the safety of member's property.
I regret very much having to cover these topics in my notes but for a Club of our size to operate successfully on a fully voluntary basis it is essential that we all act with consideration for our fellow members and avoid where possible creating situations which put additional strain on others.

John Witter, Commodore.

SAILING SECRETARY'S NOTES

SAFETY IN DINGHIES A few notes about this subject are appropriate at this time of year when conditions can be cold and windy and most people are out of practice.
First of all pay attention to your equipment. The boat should be checked over to ensure that it is in a sound condition, worn halliards, fittings etc. should be replaced and the buoyancy verified. Clothing also is important and if conditions are such that a capsize is likely then a wet suit is recommended, especially with children who lose body heat quickly when immersed. A good fitting life jacket or buoyancy aid is essential, which must be worn at all times when afloat. (This is a club rule where under 18 year olds are concerned). When you do get into trouble however, keep calm and do not waste unnecessary energy but keep with the boat and try to recover the situation. If all else fails summon help. The universal distress signal of waving your arms up and down by your side may be useful. When there is a strong wind or tide an anchor should be used to prevent you drifting out of sight until help arrives.
Last but not least it is up to each person to decide whether they are capable of coping with the prevailing conditions, if in doubt ask and when the answer is "NO" —- don't go. Of course, if you are practiced at recovering from a capsize and have well found equipment, this will extend the range of conditions when the boat can be used safely.
