The Log of the "Barbara Starr" continued.
Our boat, a 23' Islander which we have just acquired is certainly being put to the test and so far coming up trumps. All that afternoon we sailed through heavy seas and high winds and arrived at Walton.
5.00pm. After rounding Pye-End buoy and tacking into Walton creek, 21 miles of sailing. Had a nice walk along the sea wall and found a fish and chip shop at the end of it. What ever would we do without this delectable meal? Got chatting to a family who were holidaying in @ caravan, very pleasant people, walking back we saw scores of sea cadets hurrying towards the town, couldn't get there fast enough to spend their money.

Wednesday 20.8.75. 9.50am. Raised anchor earlier than planned. We were getting
uncomfortably close to the boat next to us. Set off down the Walton channel, jib only. S.W.wind. 11.30am. Harwich harbour and the Guard buoy. To portside several red lightships are anchored. Tug XX12 passing. B.R. cross channel steamer leaving Parkeston Quay for the Hook of Holland. The tug "Egerton" crossing our stern and H.M.S.Ganges at Shotley is Sighted. Passing the Shotley Spit buoy to enter the river Orwell. Seas very rough as we pass the mouth of the Stow. The Ipswich Pioneer II car ferry is on its way to Rotterdam. ~Sontinue on our way to Collimer buoy with Suffolk Yacht Harbour to starboard.
-OOpm. In very calm waters we anchored at Pin Mill. Cliff went ashore for water, bread, etc, and I with an unusual spurt of energy did some cleaning up. A strange boat came in and used someone else's mooring, expecting to stay there all night. Later the owner returned asked him to move, and in doing so got himself tangled up with the buoys, with the other boat going round in circles watching every move and the squatter getting more and more tangled. Eventually, very red faced he managed to free himself. Motto, "Don't use other people's moorings without permission".
Later we spent a convivial couple of hours in the Butt and Oyster talking to an old salt (and soak) who had, at one time worked the barges. I do wish he had worn his teeth, I couldn't quite grasp all he was saying. On second thoughts I don't think he understood what I was talking about either. That's why we got on so well. Slept very soundly after a few gins and a jar of cockles. 10 miles sailing today.

Thursday 21.8.75. 08.30am. Still in bed I am viewing the panorama through the open
hatch. As yet no-one astir, except Cliff who is making a cup of tea, and a few squawking seagulls overhead. To port the smoking chimney of Ipswich power station dimly showing above the trees in the distance, with a line of colourful boats moored in the foreground, or foresea, or foreshore, or whatever. I'd be content to stay here all day, but Cliff has chy flippers, so I discard my night clothes for my day wear, which is less bulky, and we vontinue our way up the Orwell passing the Harwich Yacht Club en route. Winds very light. The Ipswich Pioneer II has returned during the night and is now on its way back again to Rotterdam. No time wasted there. (I bet they make a profit). Turn within sight of Cliff Quay Ipswich to take the tide down the Orwell.
16.47. Sailing past Felixstowe docks on our way to the mouth of the Deben. A beautiful evening with the sun brightly shining upon Felixstowe on our portside.
Suddenly and dramatically everything changes. The sky darkens, the heavens open and it rains cats and dogs. The thunder rumbles in the distance, our sails fill to bursting point. All this after a cloudless sunny day, very little wind, and within half an hours sailing time to the mouth of the river. Cliff loWered the mainsail, changed genoa for working jib and started the motor, and myself, knees quaking, at the tiller. In pouring rain, thunder and lightning bad visibility and everything else the heavens could throw at us we entered the mouth of the Deben safely, due entirely to Cliff's navigation. With rain on my spectacles I couldn't see a thing, I should have used my umbrella. Finally we found a safe anchorage opposite the Bawdsey Radar Station, which is, I believe, well known to Radar pioneers such as our own President, Sir Eric Eastwood and others.

Friday 22.8.75. 10.20am. Wind N.W. Lovely sunny morning. All craft anchored around us
have last night's wet clothing drying out on deck. Numerous boats moored outside the Ramsholt Arms. Very pretty, set in tall fir trees with fully ripe corn fields on either side. Convenient for the men who do the thirsty work of cutting the corn.

6.

Tacking quietly between the many boats moored at Waldrinfield, we were without warning assailed by an agressive pseudo Oxford accent coming from behind, "Get that bloody thing out of my way". Drawing myself up like a very large figurehead I called back in my broadest Cornish accent, "Have you read your little book about courtesy on the water". We then noticed that this individual was having a private race with one other yacht, so we unofficially joined in and led the way until just before reaching Woodbridge, when they overtook us, but they were bigger than us anyway, and also we were looking for a place to anchor. After anchoring in this very picturesque harbour with the town sitting amongst the trees, and St Mary's Church tower just showing itself above, we explored the town, purchased a few vittals and then sailed back to Shottisham woods and anchored for the night. Eventually four other boats joined us and , as usual in this particular spot a couple of families went ashore and had a barbecue. It was a lovely evening with the water as calm as as a lake. We did just 12 miles sailing that day.

Saturday 23.8.75. 8.30am. Found us up anchor and leaving with some regret this very
peaceful
and pleasant haven, with our neighbours cheerfully waving us on our way. A bright and sunny morning. Wind westerly. Temperature cooler.
10.45am. The coast line of Felixstowe abeam with its long row of beach huts. Viewed

from here they look like colourful tombstones standing on end. Sailed through Harwich harbour to the river Stour as far as Wrabness. Decided it was too rough for anchorage so we turned tail and anchored on the sheltered side of Shotley in the river Orwell. The
wind had dropped on us. Sh... had to use the motor to get there. We left a line out over-
night and found a hook gone in the morning, so we'll never know how big the one that got away was.

Sunday 24.8.75. 9.45am. Sailed from here on a fine morning but clouds were gathering
from the N.W. The wind is S.W. Intrigued by the old Harwich lighthouse which is surrounded by scaffolding. Presumably under repair. Also spot the old black shed where the ancient tread mill operated crane is preserved. We had a look at it some time ago. Apparently it was used in Nelson's time. It being Sunday, we clearly hear the church bells ringing their come hither message from the town centre.
12.15.pm. Sailing; past Walton-on-the-Naze with its cluster of beach huts, a feeling of nostalgia overcomes me for my native Cornish coastline. Its beautiful golden sands, and overhanging cliffs, and caves for shelter when the rains come, which they do, all too
frequently.
21.00 It was a long sail and at last we reached Burnham on the river Crouch. It was getting dimitty, as we say in Cornwall, so we put the navigation lights on, after fighting the tide. "The strong man", the locals call it. For our last night afloat we moored at . Wallasea. We had done 34 sailing miles, 5 motoring.
Although feeling very tired, we go ashore dressed in our usual shabby way and visit the Ward Room. “Ah, special dinner on tonight. &2 per head. Just what we need", and on entering the restaurant we spot an empty table. "Can we have this table"? I asked the lady in charge. With a withering up and down examination she answered, "Sorry madam, all tables are booked". Which, of course, could have been quite true, but I can't help feeling that if Cliff had taken his faded peaked cap off and I had worn my diamond tiara we would have managed to get our dinner. However, not to be out done we ordered an ‘open samdwich' at the bar, one of their culinary specialities, which consisted of a slice of toast, with & lump of grilled steak on the top and a salad. All for 55p. Fully recommended by us. After which we had a few drinks, a nice sing song, with a gentleman playing an organ like instrument and then made our unsoberly way back to our boat, along those bobbing pontoons. We slept like logs that night.

Monday 25.60.75. 8.14am. Up and away early. Unfortunately had to motor down the Spitway
against the tide. "We were getting nowhere fast". Plagued by flying ants as we left the mouth of the Crouch, and they stayed with us until we reached Bradwell. Became becalmed after passing the Bench Head so reluctantly we used the motor for a while. Called in the Bradwell Marina for petrol, after which we had a marvellous sail to Stansgate, where we moored up after a quietly satisfying exploration of water rather than land for ten wonderful unforgettable days.

Hileen M. Clarke.

Cleaning G.R.P. Hulls

. Many members whose yachts have plastic hulls will be distressed to find that their
»psides,
specially just above the waterline are becoming stained. Polishing has little effect, despite the maker's claims and some are resorting to painting.
These stains can however, be easily removed by painting with a solution of oxalic acid in water by brush. The drips which will inevitably run down on to the anti-fouling, do not appear to have any ill effect on the T.B.T. which was used in the case tested, although it is advisable to sponge off continually during application. The stain is removed like magic and after a good wash, it can be polished normally. The powdered oxalic acid can be bought from the chemist for 10 pence which is enough for several hulls.
NOTE It is poisonous and as well to use gloves when doing the job.

Eric Payne.

EDITORIAL

The Spring Bank Holiday was celebrated with the usual festivities. The Marquee Pole Climbing Contest was won by our own Hornet Fleet. The Lager Drinking Competition was, without any doubt won again by the Leigh S.C. with the Thames Estuary a close second; both teams competeing with the severe handicap of large amountsof froth and plastic mugs. Several G.P. 14's are on hit and run charges after the melee around Wedgie's summer retreat on Sunday afternoon. In fact, the Regatta went wonderfully well and in case you couldn't make it the sailing was superb.
Others have recorded their thanks to all those who helped elsewhere in this issue, but I feel a special thank you should be said to Ron and Mary Greygoose, who never seemed to be out of the marquee the whole weekend.
By the way, the M.A.S.C. are holding their own club Sport's Day and Fete on Saturday,

participation and static displays from various sections of the club. There are lots of prizes for races and a tug of war. If you would like to help in any way please, contact Jack Bigden or go along on the day.
Congratulations to Mick and Jenny Taylor, who have a new baby son that arrived very quickly, just before the midwife on Monday 24th May.

Brenda Tate.

(or Underwater Exploration part 3135)

The Regatta provided a good turnout for the Enterprises and again we were the largest fleet there, though only a few Marconi boats competed. We all seemed to enjoy the weekend, but next year I want to see more of you participating. You never know, if you sail enough this season and get in practice even YOU might win a prize next time. Some people have been saying that this column is almost amusing and they look forward to hearing of my adventures afloat, as well as my adventures when actually in a boat.
Yes, I did capsize at the regatta, twice, though I would like to believe that only one was really my fault. So for those of you who think this article is going to be funny too (especially young Weedons) here is an introductory discussion on Fluid Dynamics to help you understand the theory behind sailing.
In the 19th century a chap called Bernoulli investigated the phenomenon of fluid flow past an aerofoil section and proved that, within limits, the faster the fluid over the top surface moves the lower the pressure and hence the greater the lift force on the aerofoil. In a simple mathematical form, assuming partial (dv/dt)=0 Bernoulli derived the following 3rd dimensioral vectorial equation;- curl v x v = grad (ve /2 +h +Q) where Q is a potential function, h is the enthalpy and grad is not a boat but a vector operator. By considering streamlines and using very simple maths, the equation can be written in its well known form of 3s- intergral of ( “P/r + v°/2+Q)=C where p=pressure, r = density, and C is salty (or a constant).
You all with me so far? No, well then I will talk about the next fleet party instead. It will be held on Thursday 24th June at the General's Arms and I am asking anyone who wants to go to, or think they will be asked to go to, the Area Team Championships on
July 3rd, to come along - and bring crew/wife etc.

The Cadet week we held immediately after the Regatta was very successful. Out of 23 Cadets taking the Elementary Day Boat Certificate 15 passed and will be presented with certificates pasted in each Cadets log book. What is more encouraging is the fact that each Cadet took their practical test in very severe weather. Force 5 winds, heavy seas and very cold. A true test indeed. Of the 15 Cadets, 4 were ladies, I would add that I was one of the men. We will be arranging a day at Stansgate probably a Saturday so that Cadets who have to take certain tests a second time can have a further opportunity. I would like to take this opportunity to formally thank Colin Leveridge for his patient and persistent tuition and the time and trouble needed to secure success which was very evident.
If Colin and I can fit in the first of the Saturday tuition days in during June, I will ring everybody up in good time. I am sure everybody thoroughly enjoyed the Cadet week and hopefully we can repeat it again next year.

The end of the season is approaching faster than any of us would wish and with it the Laying Up Supper. Elsewhere Roy Battye has outlined the evening's programme so that you have good notice of the event. It is again at the M.A.S5.C. and as with other events during the year I am looking forward to a good turn out of members at our premier social function which sets the seal on a successful sailing season. I do hope lots of you will be able to come. Within a month of the Laying Up Supper we have the A.G.M. at which the new Committee is elected and as always there is room for an infusion of new blood into the body which reulates the life of the Club. Members who feel they would like to find out more about the Cogmittee should not hesitate to discuss it with any officer or Committee member. Next month we shall be asking for final nominations but in the meantime why not give some consideration to standing for election yourself.
During the last year a sub-committee has been meeting to review the Club's Constitution and Rules which were in need of updating to bring them in line with custom and practise and the changed situation resulting from the purchase of the land and the opening of the new clubhouse. The work of this comnsittee is almost complete and if we are not able to inclu¢s copies of the proposed rules with this Navigans we certainly will with the October issue — Fundamentally there are no major changes from the previous rules but for many of you it w:
be the first oppotunity to see a copy as the old ones have been out of print for some time. Adoption of these revised rules will be an item on the Agenda at the A.G.M. and to ensure that there are no misunderstandings at that time the Committee would ask you to read then through as quickly as possible after you receive them and to raise any queries with any Committee member at the earliest opportunity.
The Committee have also been giving some consideration to the state of the road and have obtained some estimates for the cost of essential repairs, which will have to be undertaken during the next few weeks if we are to avoid the risk of further deterioration over the winter. The cost is estimated at around £250 and this together with other large
expenditure on the Hard (£400), replacement of the workboat engine (£450) and repairs to the
Crecent engine (£100) will absorb more than the budgeted surplus for the year. We considered asking for volunteers to repair the road but concluded that, as at the time of year it needed to be done members would prefer to sail and professional equipment was required, we would have to pay for the work this time. On two occasions since the major repair and
resurfacing exercise some 9 years ago at a cost of £1,000 of which £450 was recovered from
member's donations, minor repairs have been conducted witb voluntary help.

John Witter, Commodore.

It was brought to the attention of the Kditor that a long standing member of the Sailing Club, Tom Patterson, Senior Froduction engineer, Marconi, Basildon, was retiring on September 30th after 23 years with the company. To "celebrate" this event Bruce Lony has magnificently illustrated our inside cover this month, and we received the following from John Taylor at Basildon.

I would be pleased if a mention of this laconic,cryptic, camera mad, boat "cat" mad otherwise agreeable Scot could be made in your September issue of Navigans. I don't know if this Scottish evolution business has anything to do with his leaving, but we have always maintained that had Hadrian's wall been another thirty feet higher Tom would not have suffered the ignominy of having his 'Supercat MK1 towed to a mud flat on Osea Island by a Mirror dinghy ably handled by Bruce Leggett and ddie Groves who, loath to administer the ‘kiss of life" brought Tom and Tony l’ssex back to life with a hot drink.
For a 'foreigner' say his associates he wasn't a bad ‘un. I have very pleasant memories of his performance on a fiddle with Sweet Georgia Brown. His performance wasn't with Sweet
( ‘rgia - he played the tune at our annual Christmas Party and Dinner at the iiasonic Hall
Shenfield - his supporting cast, or backing being a bottle of CLAYVA or Drambuie.
We shall certainly miss Tom whose all round knowledge of Electronic engineering techniques, "stickos", "goos", araldites, resins etc was invaluable —- especially when he was awake. MERSKA WEsK AND THe MARCONI SAILORS

At about 09.00hrs on Monday 9th August. 1976 about twelve people from Marconi Saili.
Club descended on Mersea Island. They took with them three Mirrors, one 420 followed by Frank Savill plus family plus Solo on Thursday and Friday. Not forgetting all the camping equipment. Apart from mud, mosquitoes and lack of wind at start times we all had an enjoyable week. The mud showed itself at low tide, (most days we launched at low tide), in the form of grey-black ooze, about a foot deep that spread everywhere. Feet sank in it, ropes trailed in it, sailing suits were covered in it, and launching trollies almost disappeared beneath it. By the time the race was over each day the tide was up and the mud was covered. The mud which had got into the boats was usually washed off during the race and disappeared through the self~bailers. The mosquitoes came out at dusk in their thousands. They must have been a special breed, they could sting even threwth thick clothing. Also they obviously enjoyed the finer things in life because they only seemed to bite the ladies. There were some very attractive ( and painful) pink and white mottled patterns on feminine legs the following
mornings. :
The wind wasabit late in getting up some mornin,s and on Thursday, Friday and Saturday the start line was out at the Nass Beacon, which meant paddling the boats for about a mile ( the blisters have almost healed now). Most days the wind did get up for start time and we had some good sailing.
On Saturday we launched extra early to allow plenty of time to get to the start, but the wind also came up early and we arrived at the start line about an hour early. Well one can't be right everytime, can one?
On the lighter side of the week, we had good weather, we won prizes, and had pleasant social gatherings in the evenings. One funny incident happened on Monday night, or was it the early hours of Tuesday morning, Pat? Pat was outside my tent calling, "Stan, something is wrong with my cooker".

Mersea Weekend the Marconi Sailors cont.

I still don't know what she was doing with her cooker at one o'clock in the morning - or what was wrong with it ( but Pat, I award you full marks for being original). A word of thanks to all our crews(especially Katie) and to the wives who got us all to
the starts on time, cheered us from the beach - fed us all, and were pleasant and attractive
company in the evenings.

THE MAwGU TROPHY

The MAMGU Trophy is a 12' to 1" model of Mamgu presented by Mr and Mrs A.M.Adams to the Marconi Sailing Club for two purposes:-
First, to commemorate the’ ship which for five vital years of the Club's growth served as our Clubhouse.
Second, to promote a wider interest in the sea and seamanship by encouraging members to go cruising and to share their experiences for the benifit of others.
The Trophy is to be awarded annually, and held by the winner for one year, for the best log and account of a cruise made in the preceding 12 months.
The cruise must be in a sailing or auxiliary yacht or dinghy, and should be generally of at “rast three day's duration, though a shorter passage of particular interest may be consiusved. Use of engine, if any, must be stated. The log may usefully include details of the yacht and any other interesting and relevant matter.
The author of the yacht must be a member or associate member of the Club; he/she must have taken an active part in sailing the yacht, but need not have been the owner, charterer or skipper.
A small panel shall be appointed by the Committee to judge the entries, the decisic— of the panel shall be final. The panel need not consist entirely of club members. Logs are to be judged on their interest and value for others who may attempt similar cruises, and on the seamanship and enterprise implied by the whole undertaking. Thus riding out a gale or @ passage in heavy weather, conducted in a safe and proper manner and described well enough to assist another mariner in a like situation, should score highly, whereas a colourful account of escapades arising out of gross ignorance or neglect of seamanlike prudence or out of sheer foolhardiness, may be placed lower than a cruise in which hazardous conditions were avoided by good planning. A copy of each log entered for the MAWGU shall be presented to the Club if the judges deem it worthy, to be kept for members to read, and to be published, if required in "Navigans".
The award of the WAMGU Trophy may he withheld in any year if the judges consider that no entries of sufficient merit have been received; but only after giving notice in "Navigans" at least two weeks before the closing date.

CRUISING PRIZES

Prizes will be awarded for member's first cruise, in the following categories:-
(a) For a cruise to a neighbouring estuary.
For a week's cruise away from home waters.
(c) For a cruise abroad.
For (a) a cruise to a neighbouring estuary, it must be a complete out and return trip in one's own boat, sleeping on board, or camping, using only gear that has been carried in the boat. (The neighbouring estuary to the Blackwater does NOT include the Colne, i.e. the Blackwater and Colne are regarded as one estuary).

For (b), a week's cruise away from home waters, the extremities of the cruise must be 40 miles apart, on a sea voyage. A chartered boat may be used as long as the entrant has complete charge of it.
For (c), @ cruise abroad, the boat can be one's own or a chartered one.
A brief written description will be required for all cruises, and these should be submitted to the Sailing Secretary.
It should be noted that anyone receiving outside assistance while sailing will not be eligible for a prize. All these rules are flexible and each cruise submitted will be judged on its own merits and with regard to the circumstances under which it was made.

COMMODORESS NOTES

One of the disadvantages of being Commodore is that one has to prepare a speech for the Laying-Up supper and an annual report for the A.G.ii., and 4s one has just taken place and the other is imminent, I will try to be brief this month.

The Laying-Up supper had some eleventh hour problems outside the control of either the M.A.S.C. or us but I think the evening was successful and enjoyed by the majority present. Each year we try to maintain a reasonable standard and keep the cost to members as low as possible but with inflation this is extremely difficult and unfortunately the price has to rise each year. There has been 4 steady decline in the numbers attending and if this trend continues it is inevitable that the price will rise or that the Club will have to meet the deficit. We are now at the point where the economies of holding the Laying-Up supper at the M.A.S.C. is in question and if there are not substantial numbers of members who wish to attend a Laying-Up supper then perhaps we have to move to a smaller venue to cater for those th.t want to come and limit the number of ticket s available. This is not a decision to be taken lightly and your views on thesubject woul¢~ be appreciated.

Last winter, with the exception of the repairs to the hard, members were not asked to undertake a great deal of work on the club or attend working parties. This year how- ever maintainance work and repairs will need to be done and your help would be appreciated by the working party organisers. Please try to spare some time over the winter as it is only by the use of voluntary labour th t we are able to avoid raising subscriptions mo-e frequently than we do.

Many of you will hsve seen or heard that Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, are offering their estate at Stansgate for sale on the open market. We are in touch with their agents 'Bidweils’ and have a clear understanding of the deal that is being offered. This varies very little from that under which they purchased the estate from the late Mr. Sparrow. It is also becoming clear that the chance of a Marina being developed is less of a possibility.

I look forward to seeing many of you at the A.G.M. at which you will have your opportunity to make suggestions and raise questions on the running of YOUR CLUB.

John Witter, Commodore

Are You Suffering From the "Itch"

There are, I understand, a number of people within the sailing club who have the "Itch". It is a condition which appears to affect members of all classes. The cause is hard to define, some of the afflicted claim that it is brought about by spending too much time in a trapeze belt, others claim that the conditions experienced in a amall two person dinghy on a hot windless summer day are certain to bring on an attack. Then again, conversely, I hear that others sufferers claim a few hours spent each week strapped into a trapeze belt would solve their problem — and single handed sailors sometimes see a small two person bo:it as an instant panacea. So as you can see one persons salvation is another persons itch.

I do not believe there is an easy solution to the problem but there may be one gleam of hope — group therapye Why not? It works for alcoholics, battered wives and compulsive flashers so why not for the poor oli itch sufferer. A friend of mine

i SGGee Care

belongs to a therapy group - for nervous twitchers - they meet at a "therapy centre"
called the Blue Lion. After an evening spent imbiding quantities of elixier and en- gaging in heart to heart talks my friend and his associates often find that their nerves are so steady that they can't move from their chairs let alone exhibit 4 nervous twitch, which demonstrates just how effective these groups are.

Anyway, I digress - back to the itch. Now this itch to change class buy
another boat -— or even build one is a dilema facing 4 number of us. Should we change to a class already existing in the club” or should we start a new one?

I have made a few enquiries among the afflicted and after a bit of scratching around have come up with the qualities thought to be most desirable in 4 new class racing boat at the Marconi Sailing Club. She should be constructed from G.R.P. and be about 13' to 14' long, she must carry 4 spinnaker, be well represented locally and an established class nationally and should rate somewhere between 96 and 19°, Cost and durability are also important. Now there must be lots of boats which
would fall into that loose description - one of which must fulfill all our require-
ments.

This is where the "group therapy" comes in. I suggest that all we who are seeking a new boat should meet at one of the local health centres to see if the spirit moves us — who knows we may 411 end up us part owners of a quarter topper!

COMMODORES REPORT 1976

1976 has, as I have seen it, been a year of consolidation for the Club during which we have been learning tolive with, and take advantage of, the splendid facilities we now have at Stansgate. The incredibly fine sunner brought members to the club by the hundreds and I would venture that more members enjoyed more hours at their club than in any previous year.

During the year a number of major repairs and improvements were undertaken and again a considerable amount of money has been invested for the future of the Club. Undoubtedly the major task of the year was the repair to the Hard last Christmas when many hundreds of hours of voluntary work were put in and with the generous help of friends of the Club, who provided machinery and plant, we were able to protect the launching facilities of the Club for the future. More recently we arranged for the repair of the road which provides our access to the site.

Our work last year to alter the drainage system was not so successful as we had hoped, due to the uncertain level of the water table on the site. To take advantage of the soak-away system we had installed, we were faced to introduce, during last spring an extra man hole and by purchasing a pump we have been able to pump over from the col- lection tank to the: dispersal system and in this way we have been able to cope with the continually increasing volume of largely fresh water waste created on the site. The pumping is normally carried out at times when there is little activity at the Club.

We have been fortunate again this year in having the continued services of Claud Emerson to look after our Clubhouse and its surrounds. He is often helped by his wife and between them they have done a magnificent job in keeping the Clubhouse in an almost continuous state of readiness for us. It would appear that the observations made last year on the general cleanliness of the Club did not go unheeded but we newer cease to be amazed by the amount of unclaimed lost property that accumulates and much of it not inexpensive clothing.

Financially we seem to be solvent still despite considerable expenses during the year and our Treasurer, Ted Barnes, has kept a close eye on our budgets, I am pleased to report that our contribution to the MASC for 1977 for the use of the site remains
_ unchanged.

During the year we experienced a break-in for the first time for 4 number of years but we were fortunate that our losses and cost of damage repairs was only £10. This does however highlight the need for constant vigilance and we are strongly of the opinion that our locked gate provides a major deterrent to the casual unwanted light fingered visitor and offers significant protection to both Club and personal property. While on the subject of g,to locks, many of you will have noticed the number of cars that accumulate outside our boundary and we are in discussion with the Tenant Farmer and the Owners of the adjacent sites on methods of discouraging the unauthorised usgof the approach road which is causing a4,:gravation to all the legitimate users.

Our sub-committee and volunteers have again worked extremely hard this year on all theactivities of the Club and many successes have been achieved.There is one area where a apecial mention is deserved and this is the Galley which has provided sustenance to many a cold and wet sailor throughout the year. Our thanks go to Jill Savill, who took this over when Margaret Cottam retired last year, and to her willing, cheerful and hard working band of ladies who have given a marvellous service which has been appreciated by 411 who use the Club, I am pleased to say she has volunteered to continue for another
year.

This year we say farewell to a few Main Committee members but I am pleased to say many others are offering themselves for re-election tonight. To those departing, Hric Royle our secretary for the last three years, Roger Durrant, Tony Cherry, Gerry Bamford

a

and Brenda Tate, Navigans Editor for the last three years, 1 would like to express my sincere thanks for the support they have given to me, to the Club and to past Officers during the time they have served the Club.

You may have noticed that one name has been left off the list. After 4 long and difficult search without much success among the members for a replacement Sailing Secretury John Weedon, who has already served four years and does not want to see the sailing activities decline in the Club, has offered to see us through another year. I am sure you will all want to thank him as I do for this act of generosity. There are also a number of new names on the nominations list who will be readily welcomed together with the appointed Officers onto the Committees for the coming year.

During the year a lot of work has gone into bringing the Club rules up to date and later we have the formal proposition to adopt these revised rules. SAILING SECRETARY'S REPORT 1976

The year began with the Cadet Fleet captain, Rick Anstey, organising and Colin Leveridge instructing about 30 cadets and a few adults in the RYA Elementary Day Boat Certificate, Later on in the year 16 of these passed the examination, which included capsize drill. This winter has seen the start of further courses.

Before the start of the season a new li¢htweightrace mast replaced the original one. Also an electronic clock was installed in the race bar, which included an auto- matic five minute hooter.

As for the Club sailing , the mid-week races were very well supported and most of the class points series had higher entries that 1975, topped by the Mirror Summer points withan average of 13 boats. The cadet entry averaged nine and a half and the only de- cline was in the Ladies points and Barnacle points. A short handicap series was intre- duced this year mainly during the summer holiday period when some fleets were expected to be depleted and although 56 boats entered only 11 raced on sufficient occasionsto qualify overall. The trophy events were keenly contested except perhaps the Pilot Cup whegth still fails to be popular. ‘The Helmeman of the Year final was won for the 3rd year running by a helm form the Enterprise Fleet, on this occasion, Rob Swale. The crusiers enjoyed regular monthly social meetings and most members made wood use of the hot weathey, including curises in company to the Thames estugry and holidaying in Holland The Club open events began with our traditional spring bank holiday Regatta which again provided plenty of facilities on and off the water for over 200 boats and sup-— porters. The trend this year was for more single handed fleets. Our thanks to Gerry Bamford who was secretary, Robbie Sims as principal race officer and many others too numerous to name, who gave their assistance. This year we revived our team racing with Osea S.C. for which a splendid trophy "TheBoothby Cup" was already in existence. Sad to say however, we lost after being beaten home end away. The Hallam trophy, open meet- ing for Hornets was again scheduled in September but this year it was combined with a Mirror open event which seemed to work out reasonably well. Finally the Cruiser Cup with 27 entries, and Dinghy Challenge Cup with 34 entries were ran in mid-September the winners being Miss G. Pain (BSC) and Gordon lalmer (SSC) respectively. However one of our members (Dave Harper and Stephanie Gandy) sailing a Mirror won the corresponding Stone Dinghy event run later on the same day.

Away from the Club there were no outstanding except perhaps for the con- sistency of Roger Hance with Peter James, 6th in the Enterprise World Championships and equal first in the Nimbus series. Mona's Cup

I wonder how many of our present members know the origin of Mona's Cup? In the early fifties, when our headquarters were situated at Heybridge Basin, we made frequent visits to the Jolly Sailor whose proprietoress was Miss Mona Clarke, who inherited it from her parents.

As she was a very friendly soul, and took a special interest in our sailing ac- tivities, she kindly presented us with a fine challenge cup to be awarded to the winner of an annual all-in race, and this is still included in our programme.

TM* On one occasion, Mona actually came aboard Mamgu and fired the gun starting this race. In later years, this has rather tended to be supported by dinghies from our present premises at Stansgate but in future, more cruisers should be en€ouraged to participate and it is suggested that Mona should be invited to be present for the occasion.

On one occasion when this race was sailed from Stansgate the first mark of the course was up river, and the Southey Spit Buoy had to be rounded but as the tide was falling some cruisers found there was insufficient water to make it!

Mons has now retired but still lives at Heybridge and The Jolly Saigdor is now run by Eric Priestly, incidentally an ex Murconi man.

Incidentally, our first laying-up supper was held at The Jolly Sailor in October 19575 we hired the large inner room and ate our sausages and mince pies standing up, and went through to the bar for our drinks$ there was no music to drown our exchanges of events during the past sailing season, and it was a thoroughly enjoyable evening.

Amongst our guests was Douglas Thompson, Commodore of the The Blackwater Sailing Club and Sam Poulton from The Maldon Little Ship Club. The price of the tickets was 4/- or 6/6 including the price of the coach which brought us.

-i4-

Our first formal laying-—up supper was held at the New Street canteen, which we were pleased to call The Palm Court, on Friday, November 1, 1958; most of the Commodore's of the clubs on the Blackwater were present as was Bill Hillman, Commodore of the B.B.C. Ariel Club, whoses premis’es are on the Thames at Teddington. The price of the tickets was 9/— including the band, but not the drinks!

We used to race against the Ariel Club at Teddington and in return, they came to Heybridge the following year, but eventually it was dropped largely because of the distance and absence of boats available. However, a trophy consisting of our respective burgees mounted on q plinth still exists, but as the Ariel S.C. were the last to win it, they are retaining it.

HOLLAND CRUISE

Saturday 24th July

06.33 Shipping Forecast. Tyne/Humber/Thames/Dover NW veering northerly 3-4.
Galloper N3, visibility 11 miles pressure 1023 steady

Vic bought two gallons of petrol as we had used more than anticipated yesterday. We now carried enough fuel for 19 hours motoring at full throttle. (Ace's consumption being 1 gallon per hour at full throttle.)

09-00 Slipped lines at Levington. Little wind but what there was came from the east, genoa and main set goose-winged down to Harwich but the engine went on to get us down river and off Harwich by 10.00. The sky was cloudy but plenty of sunshine.

G, 45 Clear of Harwich, off engine. Course set 115°C for Rough's Tower. Main and genoa sete

10.35 Engine on again 4s we are not making enough way for passage making. Genoa down as it was just flogging, log streamed.

11.40 Rough's Tower abeam, course altered to 100°C to allow for tidal set.
Plenty of Portuguese Man-of+War jelly fish and large clumps of weed around must be all the hot weather.
The wind began to freshen slightly and we could see rain approaching from the north west.

12.20 Rain arrived, Robert on the helm in oilskins.

12230 Lose sight of land, rain died away.

1235 Sunk Light vessel abeam.

17° 80 Engine off, sailing about 3kts. I went below to prepare a lunch of chicken sandwiches, cake, coffee and squash. It made me feel so bad I missed the Shipping Forecast again.

14.00 Engine on.

16.30 Galloper Light Ship abeam. Course altered to 110°C for North Hinder,
the really long leg of the trip. Wind beginning to freshen.

18.00 Vic asleep below, so was Robert, at the helm. I took the tiller while he got his head down, it was going to be a long night.

19.00 Unfortunately had to wake Vie and ask if the engine could be switched off. We were clipping along the time and a nasty quartering sea caused the gunwales to go under occasionally. Vic returned to his pit, Mary and I on helm.

21.00 Sighted North Hinder Light vessel.

22 200 North Hinder abeam, and in the very lust of the daylight we sorted out the bout for the night. Genoa down, No. 1 up, naviggtion lights on, all went gmoothly apart. frc Robert and Mary beiNé seasick but this they did with the

03.00 = 06.00 Robert on helm. Life jackets and life lines were always worn at night.

04.00 — 06.00 Vic asleep.

Our course for closing the Dutch coast north of Zeebrugge kept us out of the shipping lanes but we crossed over the Thornton and Raan Banks. This resulted in a very short, confussed, lumpy sea.
The next eight hours I recall very hazily as I felt decidedly "bad" and retired to my bunk. The wind had freshened and was blowing a fitful 4-5. I awoke about midnight and grabbed the washing up bowl quick. Once that was over I felt almost human again, but I had to perform one-handed gymnastics to get myself plus the bowl out into the cockpit avoiding Robert who was fast asleep on the floor cuddling the genoa. Outside in the fresh air things started to improve even more despite my husband's remarks about,"Do you wonder why you joined."
I sat down on the thwart and looked around. Over our stern were the con- stantly changing navigational lights of Vanellus and Natasha as they rode over the waves about two miles away. There was no moon to be seen but thousands of glittering stars above an inky black sea. Ace was tpamping on like a good'un through wave crests laced with tiny gleams of phosphorsce. There were ship's lights everywhere. Vic counted 14 on the edge of the bank. I returned to my bunk and dozed until around 03.00 when Vic awoke Robert to take his turn on the tiller.
Vic was relieved as although he had seem the loom er: Ostende and Zeebrugge and the lights of the ferries going into the harbour he was glad to get below, make a hot drink and check his chart calculations, which had been worked out about a week before we had set out to sea. Our E.T.A. for Breskens was 08.00, and we were about an hour ahead of schedule, which gave us the problem of having to punch a foul tide.
Between 03.00 and 04.00 everyone seemed to be scratching around even Mary
woke up and sat transfixed on the companion way steps gazing with eyes as hig as saucers.

04.00 All quiet again, Robert on the helm, Vic on the floor (his 3 star hotel he called it) and Mary and I on the leeward bunks. Wind blowing harder now.

06.30 Woke up, so I must have slept although it didn't feel like it. Breskens harbour entrance ahead. Log in, engine on, sails down, crept quietly alongside a large ketch moored on the visitors berth.

06.45 We were there.

Sunday 25th July

09 .00 The wind was blowing well now, Force 6, even behind the shelter of the marina wall. We breakfasted on fresh mackerel and decided that a passage across the Westerschelde would be very choppy and that it was worth staying the night and see how things were in the morning; because of this, the Harbour Master allocated us another berth to keep the visitors pontoons clear. Engine on, Robert on the helm, we moved away from the ketch out and across to the opposite line of pontoon. We found our place and Robert began to manoeuvre Ace in between two boats so that she would be lying bow onto the pontoon. I was standing by the pulpit on deck with a bow line ready. Vie shouted to Robert to throw the gear lever into reverse, but horror of horrors the cones did not disengage and Ace stayed ahead. She hit the pontoon with an almighty wallop, her bow rearing up out of the water and then sliding down again. As luck would have it the pontoon was a curved

wooden one, floating about a foot out of the water. We inspected the damage and found it was not as bad as we feared, The paint had been chipped away and the wood bruised in two places on the stem, well above the water line, but this would be repairable without too much difficulty. All we had was explain to Tony!! and handle the clutch with more care. Bresken's Marina is large accommodating approx. 700 boats. The pontoons are excellent with water stand pipes every 30 yards. Petrol and diesel are available. The only disappointing feature were the sh were and loos housed in portable units at the top of the marina wall. The showers were a guilder a time. The Yatch Club is situated along the main road into Breskens about 1/4 of a mile away. The town itself, with shops and supermarkets is about 1/2 mile from the marina.
In the early evening Vic and I strolled around the town and on the way back stopped to look at the Fishing fleet which was in the harbour. Vast nets were spread out to dry and hanging from derricks on the deck were huge "tickler" chains used for dragging the sea bed.
While cleaning my teeth in the lady's loos, I looked up and a vaguely familiar face said, "Hello". I suddenly realised that it was the lady who sometimes sails on Eric Young's boat Snedronning. It was lovely to pave a chat, they were now on thejr way home having been up as far as
Middelburg.

Monday 26th July

09.00 Up and away, destination Middleburg. As we had hoped the weather improved visibility was good, plenty of cloud but the sun was shinning. Fresh northerly wind. Genoa and mainsail set, once we were clear of the marina. Ace beat across the Westerschelde, we kept well down to avoid the large sand bank that lies to tie eust. We turned to starboard once near the northern shore and sailed up towards the lock entrance. Engine on and sails down, we didn't have to wait long dodging the ferries before we were in the lock. There were no difficulties with lines, we went along the wall. Brian brought Natasha alongside us. It wasn't very crowded. The lock at Flushing was the largest th.t we encountered during our cruise, as it is the enctrance to the canal system of Zeeland, it is used extensively by commercial tratfic. The general procedure when entering any lock in Holland is to wait and listen “or the Lock Master's instructions. He will have running bow and stern lines to the rings or bollards which are situated along it. These can then be adjusted as the
I
water level alters, and can be quickly and easily slipped if required. Never, wver have fixed lines. I have seen the owner of a large, expensive motor launch hacking at his ropes with a carving knife as the water receded at least a foot away from his hull.
Once through the lock and into the canal system we made our way up to Middelburg. Brian made a quick dash into the Flushing Yatchhaven to see if twoother Marconi boats, Teal and Jestabel were in residence, without sucess No trouble with the three bridges that crossed the canal butan interesting incident while waiting to go through the last, the mainroad bridge by the railway station in Middelburg.
We were gilling around in company with half-a-dozen yachts and a couple of barges, Vic on the helm bent to adjust the throttle and the handle came off in his hand!! Vanellus took alongside while some fast repairs were carried
out.
Under the bridge we passed with nostalgia the bus stop where the Marconi fleet had moored last year. By Linda Savill

Daddy and I planned to go to Maldon the following morning, Friday 23rd July and leave the club at 8.00 a.m. to go and vet some crusty bread and newspapers. The next morning I was late in waking up. We left at approximately 8.30 asm. Just beyond the hard was a cruiser, the man in it asked daddy something. We tacked and headed up to Maldon. The tide was due to change ut 10.39 a.m. As we passed Osea Island we saw a bixvd diving. It was under water each time for about 30 seconds. As we came towards the entrance to Southey Creek the wind dropped and the tide turned. We did not hardly move. After a while some Curlews came over. We nearly turned back but we just about kept going. As we went over Northey Island road the tide had gone down a bit. I had to pull the centre board right up, and daddy jumped right out, and the road scrapped the hull. Daddy got back in and we were off again. As we were going between the cruisers I was looking for a place to land. The water was past the mud as we got close the shore. I got ready to jump out. I half did and my foot got stuck in the mud and I nearly lost my shoe. I got my leg back in and then we landed in a bit better place. I got out and daddy gave me the anchor. Then he got out and we walked up the steps on to the prom. We went over to a girl ahd asked her the time. She said "Two minutes past twenty five past twelve". Of course we did not really beleive her so we went and asked a man. He said "Half past twelve". We ran through the park, daddy ran ahead I stopped,daddy was gone. I looked around daddy was gone. After about two min- utes daddy came out of 4 bakers shop. We ran back to the bout, wrapped the bread and newspa;ers in my red oilskin top and started back. We did not go buck the way we came because the tide was so that the road was showing quite clearly. We followed the wain channel and got back to the shore at half past two. What en exciting 6 hours.

WHY CHOOSE THE 420 DINGHY?

Further to the discussions held at a recent social meeting I would like to outline the reasons for promoting the 420 as a possible future fleet at Marconi.

When one considers the existing dinghy classes - Hornet, Enterprise, Mirror and
recently the GP14, these were all designed as hard chine, plywood skinned and thus suit— able for amateur construction. As many people are how likely to be attracted by the lower maintenance requirements of G.R.R., a boat designed solely for G.P.R. construction would be preferred (it is acknowledged however that the above classes, except the mirror are available in G.R.P. but these are not accepted as competitive ih all circles). The other requirements as far as I was concerned were to have a spinnaker, to be reasonably light and competively sailed locally without being too demanding physically. The 420 I believe fills these requirements. However the main snag encountered was the limited supply of suitable secondhand boats and as a consequence their cost.

Having acquired a 420 after overcoming the above problem I am pleased to report that the boat can be very satisfying to sail especially in a good breeze, being very stable but quick to accelerate in the gusts and comfortable to sail. Beating in light weather is probably one of its weak points but this can still be a challenge.

The foregoing is not intended to split the existing fleets but to encourage one or two mirror crews to graduate for which the 420 would be ideal or some of the handicap menagerie to change or even for those who are not yet boat owners to come to a satisfactory
decision.

THAT 'ITCK' AGAIN

Roy Battye, writing in the January Navigans, suggested that part of the first winter lecture would be concerned with the choice of dinghys, and that the discussion might help to resolve the issue of a new class within the club. Perhaps not surpris- ingly the meeting did not resolve this matter, and the discussion became the usual hard sell by individuals or groups wishing to promote their favourite class. In the end the clock terminated the discussion leaving the merits of some classes unsung.

I would like to take this opportunity to continue the discussion on a slightly different tack, but I must stress that this is a personal view and not a club view.

I want to consider the question — "Which dinghy classes should be adopted by the club?" But first let us look at the advantages afforded a class after it's adoption by the club. Class racing results are published, and in some cases class trophies provided for the various series sailed. The class is also represented directly on the sailing sub-committee, which obviously increases its influence on sailing matters. Also, the club looks favourably at requests for class open meetings and this in turn gives rise to increased interest in the class.

So, which classes should be adopted by the club? Surely the simple answer is that the club should adopt any class that can justify fleet status. By this I mean, any class large enough to support the race programme provided for it, and large enough to provie it's share of the effort required to run the race programme, namely Race officers and Rescue Crew. Classes no longer able to satisfy the required conditions must be relegated to the Handicap fleet, and the embryo classes must grow within this same fleet. After all it is still possible for the members of small classes to extract their own class results from the handicap results. Once established within the handi- cap fleet a fully grown class can apply for adoption by the club.

So much for the club's choice of dinghy class; what about your choice? You must first decide whether to choose a two-man boat or a single-hander. If you have a reg- ular working relationship with another person, a two-man boat will, ih my opinion, provide the greatest satisfaction. Of course, there are some of us who fail to cult- ivate that good working relationship. We have to be satisfied with a single sail, but don't misunderstand me it has the great advantage of independence, and with only _myself to blame it is sometimes easier to analyse my mistakes.

The list of possible boats has now been reduced, and if your personal require— ment can be met by an existing club class, your ,roblem is solved. If you choose to sail single-handed there is no suitable club cl.ss a present. Even if you choose to sail with a crew there may be many good reasons why the existing club classes are not suitable to you. You are therefore about to join the handicap fleet.

What are the disadvantages of sailing with the handicap fleet? In any single race, even classes having the same handicap number will perform differently and winning is often amatter of luck. It can happen that even a long series of races over one course area will give an advantage to one type of boat due to the prevailing conditions. The handicap numbers will only be correct for along series of races over all types of course on ponds river, estuary and sea conditions with fixed line and co.mittee boat starts. Normél class racing tactics are irrelevant, and in general it is difficult, if not im- possible, to improve your racing performance. Real improvement can only be achieved by racing against boats of the same class. One more of the sane type will do, but the more there are the better the racing.

If you choose a boat class that will not give you the required competion at the club you will have to go elsewhere for your competition sailing. Indeed, if sailing

Gt

is more important to you trun the club, it may be reasonable to move to a club with an adopted class to suit you. There are some advantages for both clubs and the class if this is done. An alternative solution is to choose a class sailed regularly by nearbye clubs, since this will at least enable you to attend their open meetings, It may help to look at the list of classes sailed at our own regatta.

Once you have decided to depart from the existing club classes the choice for you is quite wide because the actual type you bring to the club is not important. However, your choice will be affected by such factors as, do you wish to race, do you wish to improve your performance, are there plenty of local open meetings, price, second-hand market, the choice already made by others and whether your choice is likely to affect the choice of others. The last two factors are quite important since they affect the possible growth of a new class within the club.

Finally let me say that I will not be fully satisfied until I am able to sail in a club adopted class, and if , as might well happen, a Moth class is established due to the keeness of our cadet fleet, I might one day be persuaded to join. In the mean- time I have made my choice and I am very satisfied with the sailing it gives me. Now it is up to you to make your choice and then go out and buy that SOLO or Moth or SOLO or 420 or SOLO or Express or SOLO OFfeceereeee

What's all this about 4 new dinghy class?

I attended a social meeting recently, at the M.A.S.C., held to obtain some tips from Roger Hance on the racing rules and I thought, to discuss the possibility of a new dinghy class for Marconi. Some of the comments made were sufficient to make any discerning class captain turn to sailing model boats and to make me write to Navigans$ This is about the third season discussion has got around to a new dinghy class, how- ever no-one has yet said exactly what is wrong with the present adopted classes. Well, I hope I can start your ink flowing by making these observations :-

It seems to me that as the Marconi Club is made up of people with different needs is sailing, such as:— those who are novices or have a young crew, those who re- quire a cruisihg/racing dinghy, those who want a thoroughbred two sail racing dinghy, those who want an exiegiting threesail racing machine, and finally those who want (or need) to sail single handed. In view of this, several complementary classes of dinghy are required to fulfil these varying needs, and I think the Mirror, G.P.14, Enterprise, Hornet and Solo or Lazer do just that. If there were two similar classes the effect woul be to waste potential of both classes. Therefore any new class would have to be com- pletely different, or supersede one of these classes.

As an enthusiast who wants the challenge of a three sail racing machine, I believe the Hornet to be the best class on our river to fit the bill. I have written about its virtues before. It has after all been selected over the past 25yours by many well known helmsmen, and has been used in Poland as an Olympic trainer. I don't intend to go into details about it's attractions, except to say that over the past ten years of sailing Hornets, I have had a lot of enjoyment from them, and made a lot of friends both at our club and around the country, and I would not wish (short of winning the pools) to sail any other dinghy. If you fancy the challenge of a three sail racing machine, why not try a Hornet? Anyone who wants to sail or maybe just crew,can contact Pete Clayton, out fleet captain who will make you very welcome, and may even buy you a beer at one of our Friday social meetings:

Mike Turner,

HOLLAND CRUIS

TUESDAY 27th July

09.30 We discovered that the wrought iron bridge was opened on the half hour, so after breakfast we left heading northwards for Veere. The wind was fresh northerly, cloudy sky. Approaching Veere we spotted a familiar boat flying the M.S.C. burgee, Davolas II. A quick tate-a—-tate, or should it be tate- a-Tate, with John, who after a pleasant holiday was homeward bound. He told us that Tealand Jestabel were staying in Goes for a few days.
The Veere lock was very crowded, everyone jammed together like sardines in a tin. The Dutch coped in their usual efficent way, despite the help of an Irish gentleman, single-handed in 4 tiny but obviously well travelled boat. Locked out, into Veerse Meer turning to port and through the harbour entrance. 11.00 Tied up by the old town quay, occupying the same position as lust your. Veere is beautiful, the town skyline dominated by the vast Groote Kirk and spire of the town hall, although like Middleburg, it was full of holiday makers.
The facilities at the Yacht Club, which is situated by the harbour entrance are excellent, meals are available, and their showers were the cheapest that I encountered (25c.). Petrol and diesel can be obtained from the Yacht haven near the entrance to the lock. The Post Office, shops and bank are literally across the road from the quay.
After lunch we set off for Goes. Vic had bought an excellent map of the atfea from the local chandler's, costing 95c. Studying this we decided to leave the boats behind and take to the Dutch publié transport system. The Tovey's joined us, Brian and Jackie were waiting to meet some Dutch friends.

16.00 The bus journey from Veere to Goes via Middleburg was uneventful. We sat back, relaxed and enjoyed the countryside.
17.15 We arrived at Goes Yacht haven to discover it was my niece’ Fiona's birthday so we joinedthe party and enjoyed 4 magnificent feust on Jestabel. The weather and setting were really superb, the wine flowed freely, and we very reluctantly took our leave just after 21.00
We caught the local train back to Middleburg only to discover that due to someone mis—reading the bus time-table (MZ), we had missed the las6 bus home. It was a very weary party that bundled into taxi's to take us the last 7 kilometers into Veere, but it was all rather fun, I've never ridden ina Mercedes before.

WEDNESDAY 28th July

The wind had freshened and a good NNW Force 3-4 with the occasional stronger gust was blowing resulting in very choppy conditions in the Meer. Vanellus and Ace left mid- morning leaving Natasha who planned to travel further afield than us. Motored out of the harbour entrance, turned to the north set main and genoa, cut engine. Invigorating sail up to the North Sea dam, keeping a sharp look out for the marker buoys, there's no tide here and going aground here means a lot of trouble. Dropped the hook for lunch and then hitched a lift on Vanellus, who with her bilge keels could go alongside the jetty at the edge of the Meer.

We hal a bracing walk along the top of the dam, the sea looked very unpleasant for sailing, but plenty of people were swimming. Ice creams by the rather murky water- side, interesting to note, plenty of portaloos and rubbish bins. Up anchor and sailed back down keeping to the north shore, still main and genoa.

COMMODORES NOTES

It is now two months since I contributed to Navigans and during this period I have felt very much akin to a boat in winter with polythene wraps over parts of the house and damp creeping in everywhere while alteration and rebuilding has been goimjon. I am now pleased to say that with the advent of the brighter weather the work is complete and like most of you I 4m beginning to think about sailing again.

It is pleasing to note that even in these hard times our level of membership in renewal this year has dropped by no more than is normal in any year and may actually have dropped less than usual. It could be that people are inclined to see 1977 as a stay at home year and will be enjoying more of the excellent facilities they have on their own door steps.

As was reported last year the Stansgate farms were being offered for sale and we now know that the whole estate has been sold by Gonville and Caius College to a Dutchman who we understand has bought as an agricultural investment and is not aiming to build the projected marina in Ramsey Marshes. We have not as yet had any direct contact with the new owner or his agent but we hope to establish the same fraendly relationship we had with Gonville and Cauis. We also understand that the farms will continue to be farmed by the existing tenant farmer.

Some of you may also have seen in the national and local Press suggestions that there might be a district refuse tip sited at Stansgute but I am pleased to advise you that common has prevailed and Maldon is going to keep its own rubbish and enlarge the existing tip.

With the Sailing season approaching the question ef who is going to sail which class is again being asked. I have been following the discussion and cor- respondence with interest as it is a route we have been before. The main difference is that this time we already have four established classes (Enterprise, Mirror, Hornet and Handicap) and if we made the count a year or so ago five if we include the GP 14. Last time there were two classes (Enterprise aid Handicap) and three if we included the then ailing Fleetwind Class. At this time we were, as now, con- sidering what additional classes the Club should adopt. Many suggestions were made and many hobby horses mounted but in the end the new classes adopted, Hornet and GP 14 were determined by the endeavours of the protagonists of their classes overcoming the attempts of others to establish such classes as Snipe, Fireball and Flying Dutch- mane This was achieved without destroying any of the existing classés. In a Club like ours, which is basically a family one open to any employee of the G.F.C. - Marconi Group of Companies, it is not our custom to make membership conditional on ownership of a particular class of dinghy or to stipulate that one must race a certain number of times a year. For these reasons the Committes cannot dictate the classes that will be sailed but can only recognise a trend and endeavour to steer people towards a particular class which when there is sufficient interest may be adopted. As I see it, and this is a personal view, there is a need to re-establish the GP 14 or to find a suitable alternative such as say the 420 so as to re-introduce the variety of choice of class for those wishing to graduate from Mirrors. There is also a very obvious need to look closely at the Singlehanded situation er, like most other clubs have at sometime or ot’ery we are going through the phase where there is a demand for single handed class sailing. It is now probably too late to adopt a singlehanded Handicap Clauss within the Handicap Class and bears on the sucess of this make some recommendations for next year. In the final analysis however, the choice of classes must be arrived at by examining the track record of those offered. This means that a common end proved desire for a particular class must be demonstrated so if we really do need a new class or two some effective lobbying will be necessary to establish a class that meets the specification re- quired by the majority seeking a charge. This I believe is now beginning to happen

but followers of our existing classes must not be complacent and will need to continue to canvas in order to maintain their existing strength as it is inevitable that in building up another class some converts will come from our already establish- ed classes and we could end up by weakening our competitve sailing and setting back the clock.

John Witter,

HOLLAND CRUISE:

Saturday 3ist July

Up late, still raining. Vic and I spent the morning shopping and looking over 4 Sabre that we had noticed was for sale. Could this be our next boat? We certainly liked the look of her.

12.30 Left the marina heading up the Veerse Meer, main and genoa set, close hauled wind NNW Force 4. A fierce rain squall blew up after we had been out for 15 min- utes and after 2 little arguing it was decided that the jenny was unsuitable in the adverse weather conditions and some what crowded waterways. We ran under main for a time and then set the No. l.

All went well untill we reached the most southerly point near Aarberien Hiland, we now had to beat up towards Veer and this made conditions below somewhat unpleasant. We took down all sail and started the engine and motored on past Veere. We saw "Lady Ann", a boat owned at various times by several members of the Tate family and now kept in the canat at Heybridge, with Mirror tender anchored just north of the harbour entrance.

We carried on for another mile and went into Oostwatering. This is an enormous marina still uncompleted and we were the only English boats there.

We had a walk roun between rain squalls and then settled down for the night and listened to the wind howling in the shrouds.

Sunday lst August

Clearer skies today, with the sun doing it's best to shine. I took advantage of the excellent facilities, shower's were a guilder and I washed, spun and tumble-—dried a mach- _ ine load of clothes for a &1. A bit expensive but well worth it. Robert visitéd the wery luxurious chandlers (fitted carpets) and finished up repainting’ the bow damaged in
Breskens. Vic cooked the lunch, we had salad$
—

In the afternoon we walked along the sea wall or rather Meer wull into Veere, which was more crowded than ever. Nick and Daphne treated us to some splendid ice creams at the quay side cafe, so we sat down in the sunshine watching the people and the boats come and go. We saw several yachts flying the Lawling Cruising Club burgee.

19.00 Left Oostwatering and in the evening sunshine motored back towards Were and the lock. Vic demanded his camera every few minutes as the light was so fantastic. The lock was almost empty, 1 barge and 3 yachts including us.

21.200 Tied up in Berth 34 at Middleburg. Everyone went to the Yacht Club except me, they sneaked away while I was putting Mary to bed.

Monday 2nd August

The day was spent shopping in Middleburg and amongst other things large numbers of clogs were purchased. I had hoped to have a good look around the Town Hall, which is Situated in the main Market Square, but a modern art exhibition was being held there with an exorbitant ehtrance fee, so I didn't bother.

The Bowsher's came in during the day and we all congregated on "Ace" for the evening I can't remember if that was the night I cooked a beans and sausage supper for everyone or not.

We were now heading for home so it was agreed that detailed reports of the
06.33 and 17.55 shipping forecasts would be kept. Our route home was to be via
Ostende, this made the North Sea Passage a little shorter, and was the best port for picking up duty free.

17-55 Shipping Forecast. Gales in Finistere.
Fisher/German Bight W 4-5 veering NW 5-6
Humber/Thames W5, 6 later veering NW.decreasing 4-5
Showers, visibility good.

Tuesday 3rd August

06.33 Shipping forecast. Gales in Finisterge, ridge of high pressure filling in Shannon moving across Denmark Straits. Fisher/German Bight NNW 4-5 showers visibibity good. Humber/Thames/Dover NW 4-5 decreasing 3, isolated showers, visibility good.

10.00 Vic and I took the kids to the local swimming pool and then had coffee,

on the terrace, pleasant but chilly. We paid up our harbour dues which were
6 guilders per night (about £1.30).

15.30 Out of Middleburg and turned right down the main canal towards Flushing. On this occasion our timeing was bad as we came down to the Flushing road bridge and caught the full flood of the rush hour traffic, 80 we had to stooge around for about an hour, This was rather annoying, as the Yachthaven was almost a stone's throw away through. the bridge tucked away on left going towards tie lock.

1739 Tied up in a cut's cradle of lines, with a lethal access to the pontoons,

We enjoyed a drink in the clubhouse with some rather boisterous German gentlemen and then the Bowsher's joined us on Ace for coffee, crackers and cheese.

Wednesday 4th August

Mary and 1 began to have attacks of the queasy tums again so Vic gave us someéhang to do I went on the helm and liary became flag officer taking down the Dutch and hoisting the Belgian colours and the yellow duster.

The following article has appeared in Navigans in previous years but a reminder at this time of year can be useful.

FALLING IN THE WATER

Compared with the high accident rate of road users, sdiling is 4 relatively safe pastime. However accidents do occur, and when they do are usually more serious as often rescue is either a long way away or more difficult to obtain.

It is therefore more important to take precautions and also to know what to do when an accident does occur.

Why do people die when they fall in the water? Other than a n attack by sharks or mechanical injury them are three main causes of death.

1. Hypothermia, i.e. lowering of body temperature due to the cold environment.
2. Drowning i.e. thexukwekxnfxwatar filling of the lungs with water,
and 3. Vaso - vagal shock, i.e. the shock of water entering the lower pharynx or
upper respiratory passages causing a nervous reflex which stops the heart.

To deal with these in turn, the first is by far the commonest cause of death due to immersion.

5 It has been shown that few people survive for more than seven hours in water at 59 F., muchhigher than British sea temperatures, and the survival time in water at 32°F. is only a few minutes.

As on land, the best way of keeping warm in the water is to wear warm clothing. Intom this category come ‘wet-suits' of whichthey should be best of all. If you can get out of the water and sit on your dinghy, so much the better as unless the wind is particularly cold your heat loss is slower. Contrary to what might be expected, movement in the water accelerates heat loss as the extra heat generated by muscular effort is more than offset by the removal of the warmer layer of water around, and heated by the
body.

Therefore unless it is to swim a short distance to a rescue boat or the shore it is much better to lie still as possible in the water supported by a life-jacket. As the time of immersion is obviously an important factor, one should stay as near as pos— sible to the point where rescue might by expected. This is usually near the boat.

There is no evidence to show that alcohol in normal quantities accelerates heat loss, which may be of comfort to those of us who indulge.

The quickest method of warming someone is a warm bath - tempera tue 97°F - 100°F,
but this is only of use if they can be bathed within 20 minutes and is seldom feasable. A warm atmosphere, hot water bottles, the close proximity of another human body and warm blankets after removal of the cold wet clothing are the usual methods.

So, if you cannot rescue yourself, wear warm clothing, keep still and make it as easy as possible for your rescuers by staying near the boat or where they expect you to
be.

To pass onto the last two headings, prevention is — wear a good life jacket and hold your breath as you go in.

Once a person has ceased to breath irreversible brain damage occurs with 3 -5 minutes so that any attempt to revive them must be made immediately. If drowning is complicated by hypothermia the chance of successful revival is very small.

- )-

Before considering how to revive a person let us consider briefly what happens when lungs fill with water. The water may be fresh or sea water. In the former case the osmatic pressure of the blood causes a rapid absoption of water from the lungs into the blood stream which so lowers the osmatic pressure of the blood that the red cells burst, releasing a large amount of potassium whcih the heart can not tolerate and it stops. This takes place vepy rapidly, as roughly speaking the minute sacs in the lungs if all were spread out would cover ia tennis court and they are designed specially to
absorb.

In the latter case the r-verse occurs as the osmatic pressure of sea water is higher than that of the blood and this causes an outflow of fluid from theblood stream, flood- ing the lungs and preventing oxygen getting into the blood.. The heart can keep beat-— ing for a few minutes after this occurs, so the chances of successful revival are much
higher.

The treatment of drowning and also of vaso — vagal shock is the same, namely - artificial respiration. I am sure that the simplest and most effective method is mouth to mouth respiration perhaps better known and the kiss of life.

As with all unconcious people, including unconciousness due to hypothermia, the first essential is to maintain a clear airway. This is done by hooking the forefingers of each hand behand the angle of the jaw of the rescued and lifting the jaw, and there- by the tonge, forward. If possible the lower teeth can be hooked over the upper teeth.

It ig a waste of precious time attempting to empty water from the lungs of the rescued. It is much better to attempt to inflate that part of the lung which is not filled with water -— usually a considerable proportion. If you kneel facing the feet it is possible to lift the jaw forward, hold the lips together in an airtight joint and breathe gently down the nose. In this position one can watch the chest to see it inflate. Remarkably little effort is required and adequate time should be allowed for the chest to deflate, about three times as long as the inflation period. If the airway is clear i.e. the tonge is not blocking the back of the throat, the movement of the chest should be gentle and easy.

I don't know how long one should continue this as it is mainly a moral question. If one considers that the brain is dead after five minutes and quadruples this time I think this is reasonable and is the criterion I have taken on the few occassions I have

It is important to realise that if the rescued is breathing it is positively danger- ous to give artificial respiration. This will only hinder theri own respiratory efforts and possibly inflate the stomach, blowing vomit into their air passages and killing them. It is only necessary to keep a clear airway and keep them warm.

One last point which I must mention is the question of vomiting. In a concious person they will get rid of their own vomit but in an unconscious person they may well inhale it with fatal results. Turn them on their side with the head lower than their waist and no fluid can possible enter the lungs.

This article has turned out to be much longer than I anticipated but even so is only an outline of what ha»pens when one "falls in the water". Greater pens than mine have said "prevention is better than cure" and it is never more true than of sailing
accidents.
A. Doctor.
