Half way through May and we seem to have slipped from a wet winter to a wet winter to a wet spring without noticing the start of the Sailing Season and the im- provement in the weather which we expect to accompany it. The club is however coming alive with the moorings filling up and the dinghy park sprouting masts of varying lengths as Members' winter deliberation turn into reality and the fresh boats arrive at the Club.

The Committee and particularly the Regatta Organisers have become very conscious of the approacl:ing Spring bank Holiday and are considering the detailed preparation for what promises to be a bumper Regutta again. Some volunteers have already come forward to help with the work during the holiday weekend but as always we shall be pleased to hear from other members who are willing to lend a hand on the day. In particular Jill Savill will be pleased to hear from anyone willing to help in the Galley, Ron Greygoose from anyone who likes being behind the bar and John Weedon from people who like watch- ing the sailing from the race box where there is a constant demand for spotters. Vol- unteers are asked to contact the above as soon as possible.

So as to prepare the site to welcome our visitors we are holding our usual] pre- regatta working parties when we shall be cutting grass, trimming hedyes, disposing of rubbish, clearing the hard and generally tidying up all the facilities. The Working
Parties are being held on Saturday May 28th from 10.30 and Wednesday June 1st from 6.00
when we would ask as many members as possible to put in an appearance and help to prove the old proverb "Many hands make light work". Please bring with you a good selection of tools including shovels, forks, brooms, rakes, hammers, saws, shears etc., and any members with rotary grass cutters or flymos would be particularly welcome.

Many of you will have heard by now that the Club was broken into on the night of May 1st/2ndwhen a certain amount of damage was caused and property taken. Although at the time the gate was shut and all doors and windows secured it would seem an ap- propriate tune to remind all of you of the need to ensure that everything is when you leave the Club and to be vigilant for your own and Club Property and not to put temptation in the way of the casual unwanted visitor. It also appears that there is still a mar-et for inflatable dinghies and even lucking them down is not an entirely effective deterrent. notice.

13.00 Zeebrugge harbour entrance abeam, larwe dredyer working about 2 miles off shore We had noticed a large cruising catermaran with a bright tri-coloured sail ap- proaching from the south. With a very spick and span, new Dutch best next door, I cringed at the thought of the sand that would get onto the children's shoes and then be deposited on the deck.

NORTH SUA PASSAGE

This is the story of the delivery of 'Victoria', a new 48ft. Motor Sailor from Maldon to Flushing in Holland, and the problems which were overcome during the North Sea Passaze, on the lst of September 1976.

Some Sailing Club members may have seen the boat, either at Dun Webb & Feeseys Yard or at anchor off the Club (Sat/Sun 28th/29th August) the weekend before we left. She was moulded by Tylers and fitted out by Dan Webb and measured 48 ft LOA, 36ft. LUL, 13ft 5 Beam. 6ft 6 draft. Her power plant was a prototype heavy vehicle Volvo engine
of 120 Horse Power. Her working sail area 1,190 sq. ft.

The crew were as followsi— Capt. & Owner — Jim, because it was easier to say
but real name - Thage Bergrenn, from Sweden.
Navizitor:— Bill Basson, the one armed ex bomber
Pailot, Grand Prix Rac r, come Deep Sea Sailor (Age 65+)
John Swinton of Dan Webb & Feeseys,
Jane John's
16 year old daughter.
Stan Cumpbell the writer
‘ ,
I think that it could be said that the Grew
Campbell his 1 Jimmyold 8
were-easonably experienced sailors, though

not seasoned ones.

Navigational Gear

We had all the charts that were needed, hand bearing compass, radar, and radio direction finding equpment. We were,one could say, amply equipped for such a passage.

Time of Departure and Proposed Passage.

We were to leave Maldon at high water (6.20) p.m. On Wednesday lst September and our passage was to be made in roughly four tides (24 hr. approx.)
The route was to be via the Spitway buoys off Brightlingsea, north up the Hast Swin to the Sunk Sand Towers and across to Longsand Head (off Harwich) thence via the Galloper Light Vessel between the North and South Hinder Light Vessels and then direct to Flushing, which was an overall journey of 120 odd miles.

The coastal Weather Forecast for 6.00 p.m. Thames and Humber was fairly good
- Northerly 4 - 5 backihg North Westerly later. Gales forecast from Heligoland, Dogger
and area North, but a high was approaching from the South West.

Departure

This was made between 6.00 and 6.30 and before long we had settled down to what
should have been a pleasant and straightforward trip. To our surprise we were showing 8 knots on the log although the Skipper had his doubts, chart checks confirmed this.

We agreed to have a hot cooked meal before we cleared the river, so Jane provided a meal of stew and dumplings (or were they golf balls?) followed by fruit and hot coffee. This ultimately proved to have been a very wise decision because our next meal was some sixteen hours later for reasons which will soon become obvious.

The first major problem came at nightfall when it was patently obvious that steering by compass was going to prove very difficult, if not almost impossible, as it was too small and mounted too far away from the wheelto be readab'e. All crew members tried with varying degrees of success, which did prove that it was not the crew members eyesight and that it had to be accepted and lived with.

However, the Benchhead and Knoll were passed, tye Spitway Buoys negotiated and then North up the East Swin. At 00.30 we listened to the Shipping Forecast, which was as follows :- Thames, Humber N.W. 4 — 5 Gales in the area North still and a cold front moving South.

Jim (th Skipper) asked how long a front took to pass and I said that it could be days or hours, but at this time of the year it should not prove a problem, So we de@ided to press on. Galloper gave 4, but we thought it ought to be 5 and made 4 remark at the time. We were still in sight of Harwich and Felixstowe and Sunk Sand Tower Light. Not:-— To sailors coming up the East Swin, remeber the light is on the north side of the Towers for the use of shipping out of Harwich. The Towers looked big and menacing in the dark and were passed quite a while before the light protecting them was left
behind.

As is invariably the case following the Annual Regatta many views are expressed and at the first combittee meeting a review of the event is undertaken and this year we had the added benefit of Tom Gaskell's observation which naturally stimulated lively discussion. At our meeting we analysed at length the various facilities required for an event of the nature of our Regatta and the following are brief summaries of the feel- ings of those directly responsible for the various crews of organisation.

Sailing - Well covered with good distribution of help. Minor problems with
spotting due to inclement weather. Rescue facilities stretched but coped despite the Club being without a permaneant coxon at presetn.

Galley — Good preparation and supply of food etc., Some people spent more time in Galley than ideally we would like but this is ofter at individuals own insistance.

— Good service given by Brewers.
Bar Generous sup.ort behind bar during peak periods but in general too much on one person outside peak periods. Some spells of duty particularly during Saturday evening party became stretched and mere advance com mitment required to spread load.

Clubhouse Facilities - This is the area in which we are most stretched to meet
the demand. There are however problems with providing extra facilities but these are under consideration. Despite this shortcoming mapy people return each year knowing what to expect. This deficiency must therefore have its compensations.

No conclusions on the future of the Regutta were reached as the views expressed so far have been of an organisational nature and generally about people who have not in themselves taken such a pessimistic view.Before reaching any final decision the Committee also needs to hear the views of the Sailors on whether this sort of Open Competition is what they want during the Spring Bank Holiday where there is an op= portunity to stage an event of at least two days duration. The question of Regattas is clearly an emotional one and unless some of these who enjoy it and want it continue say so the view will be one sided and it will surely die.

It should also be borne in mind that the problem of getting voluntary help to do things at the Club is not unique to the Regatta but is present throughout the year and is a older problem to which we have to find a solution if the Club Officiers and Committee are not to become disillusioned.

Continuing North Sea Passa,e

The Skipper went right up into the bows when we found «a point of steering which seemed to be most stable and after .n inspection he called for the knife, John took this for- ward and when the necessary rope was cut, the sail dropped low enough to be got at and wen eventually stowed. This is an over simplification for the job took almost an hour under the impossible conditions. No words can describe the boats movement, the noise of the wind
and rain, the we cold hands which together with tiredness had to do what had to be done |
we could not have entered harbour.

I at the helm gave u hearty cheer, but even that was carried downwind and away, This then was our first bit of luck in a night of stbacks. With our large (pennant) down, which had acted in some ways as a steadying sail, we began to roll violently. Rrightaning noises below subsequently proved themselves to be tool boxes and provisions. A throrough inspection below showed that we had made water, but nothing serious. The c'ue was a very wet curpet up forward outside the toilet compartment. It was condirmed later that tie water had spi’led out several times w}en we were heeled ore were tossed about.

To prevent further noise and damage we decided to put the mizzen up as a steadying Sail. One had to experience the chunge to appreciate the difference a very small sail can make. Notet- Whenever faced with a situation such as we were experiencing, always get some sail on, no matter how insignificant, for it can be the difference between acute discomfort and danger to bi.dy and limb, as opposed to a damped sideways movement which is fur m@re bearable and much kinder to ship and crew, After an hour or so we had come inside the shoals off Ostende and we were comparatively sheltered. All hands came on deck and with great relief 1 am sure , watched as ‘yours truly' (became: he had been on the helm most olf the time) was given the great privilige of taking 'Victoria' through Ostende breakwater to make her first landfall. That was one of the most satisfying mom- ents of my lire. Within an hour we were tied up and asleep.

On waking we inspected the boat and tidied up prior to going ashore for 'big eats’. The inspection showed the following:—
1) The Genou was only slightly torn and damage marginal to one seam and the eyelet
were the sheets were attached.
2) There were two deck leaks, one caused be the strain put on the handrail protecting
the steering console and one round tie forehatch.
3) A starboard side stunchion was bent us was the guardrail running from it. It's base
screws had also gone and the angle plate strengthening damaged. It was where t e end of my lifeline was attached wehen I was flung across the cockpit:!

Other than the above, no damage was found. On finding that we were still seuworthy and having had «a sleep, we were ready for a night passage north to Hoiland. The coastguard however, informed us that the gales would continue for at least 48 hours so we decided to stay put. We walked out on the mole to the Harbour bntrance to see what the seas looked like and deceded that we did not want a repetition of the night before. The follow- ing morning we went to.Zebruwge and took the Ferry home to Felixstowe in absolute comfort —oven if for the firsttwo hours we were in heavy seus. As we neared the English Coast the seas subsided and off Felixstowe we saw the familiar lights of Walton and Harwich.

In retrospect it is very difficult to know how some of to problems could have been avoided as it is easy hindsight to hold a post mortem. I would rather say that it added to our overall experience and showed thxut both young and old can co-operate as a team and face serious situations equally as well when the chips are down. Again in ret- respect I feel that nor wiaiden Voyage should have had such bad luck. However, it proved the boat for the Owner and proved the Crew to themselves.

The following advise could be given as guidance should somebody wish to make a similar
passaygee

1) Do mat a short nivht sail peior to the crossing to see that the compass is
adequate.
2) At the same time familiarise the crew with working on deck in the dark for
sail chap jing and any other necessary activities.
3) Have an alternative destination well planned should the original not prove
feasible.
4) If there is a chance of seasickness take all the precautions for avoidance well
in advance.
5) Remember that cold fronts invariably mean foul weather, 80 don't be afraind of
them, but be prepared for 4 change of plans and some very uncomfortable sailing.
6) If it is ever intended to cook of even boil water on the passage, a fiddle
rail and gimbals on the cooker are most essential even if only for safety.
7) idake sure th.t some of the crew hu@e enough experience to take care of the
boat under any conditions that might be experienced on passage.

I think apart from the compass, which was vat.l and the cooker which wasn't, Victoria's crew fulfilled all such requirements and a successful passage was made even if the origin- al destination had to be changed.

Would I do it again tomorrow? - Of course I would —---

COMMODORES NOTES

September; the evenings drawing in, holidays over and ohe wonders where the summer has gone and with it all the enjoyable sailing in the longer days. With the comig of Autumn your Committee's thoughts turn to the events of the winter and the Club's future.

Now is the time to start actively thinking about the Laying-Up Supper which is only about 6 weeks away. There have been good turnouts for the sailing act- ivities this year and we hope that you will all maye a special effort to come to the Laying-Up Supper to put the seal on the season and to sample the cuisine
at this year's venue - The Lion and Lamb - where we succeeded in getting a booking
after a large body of opinion expressed a preference for a venue away from the
M.A.S.C. We look forward to seeing you and any guests you may like to bring on
November 4th. For those who find it difficult to meet the cost of tickets in
one go, an "easy payment" scheme has been devised. To take advantage of this all you have to dois to purchase vouchers with your drinks over the bar in the Club or see one of the members of the Social Committee.

Following swiftly in the wake of the Laying-Up Supper is the Annual General Meeting at which the Committee for the ensueing year is elected. This year several of the existing Committee come to the end of the period they can serve an office and a number want to retire after giving many years of service to the Club. HORNET FLEET NEWS

Six Hornets from the Club travelled to Cramond Boat Club for the European Championships. The club is situated on a small tributary to the Firth of Forth just outside Edinburgh invery picturesque surroundings.

We travelled up on the Friday, leaving early in the morning to arrive in time to pitch our tents. The practice race on the Saturday set the patten for the week by blowing force 5/6. Only two club boats were ready in time for this race. J. Tillotson and M. Turner who acheived their best position of llth and
E. Richmond aid M. Strong. The wind increased for the first race and had to be
abandoned after the first heat. We all managed to return to the club without serious mishap although Mike's store of spares was seriously eroded on Sunday evening. Monday's race had to also be postponed due to the strength of wind which was fortunate for those of us who needed to repair our boats. The rest of the week went well with one race on Tuesday, two on Wednesday and one on Thursday when the wind increased again to gale force.

Socially the week was very good which perhaps reflects our poor showing in the results. Mike and John did best with a 22nd overall.

We travelled back in time for the Hallam Trophy. For Saturday's racing it blew force 5 for a change, but at least it wasn't raining. Unfortunately the first race of the series had to be abandoned due to lack of water round F mark and other administrative problems but Saturday evening was enjoyed by all and
Sunday dawned bright and sunny. Mike and John won the 2nd race easily in ideal
conditions. The 3rd race was much harder work for them and they finished 2nd but this was enough for a win overall.

Don't forget the Fleet meeting this month.

Peter Clayton, Hornet Fleet Captain.

COMMODORES REPORT

During 1977 members have continued to enjoy the facilities of Stansgate with a wide variety of sailing activities and good social fellowship. Membership has stayed much the same as for the last few years and we seem to have settled down to a level which is about the maximum size that can be coped with on a mainly voluntary basis. This year we have not needed to call many working parties to assist with the general maintenance of the Club but the one held towards the end of October was very well supported and demonstrated a good spirit of co-operation and enthusiasm. If we can count on this sort of turn out when required we should be able to continue to operate with a minimum of paid help and thereby maintain our fees at a reasonable level.

As you will have seen from the agenda, there is no proposal to increase any of the fees this year which I am sure you will all welcome. Although financially all looks very healthy at present we did discuss the possibility of needing to raise fees by 4 small amount to keep pace with inflation. Your Committee decided, however,that if it was possible to delay this for a year we should try, as financially the year has been hard enough for everyone without adding to the burden.

Since last year's AGM no progress has been made with finding suitable alternative locks for the Clubhouse and gate but apart from the gate lock being rendered unservicable at the time of the break-in in May they have proved to be reliable. We shall continue to look for an alternative for when it is needed.

While on the subject of locks, one of the causes of serious concern to your Officers and Committee is the apparent lack of concern by Members for the security of the Clubhouse and site. During the year there have been many instances logged where the Clubhouse has beenfound to be insecure and the gate left open. We are also aware of many occasions that have not been logged. It would appear that we are not succeeding in getting the message over to Members that the Clubhouse must be locked when there is no OOD present even though you may be remaining on the site. In making it possible for all members to have access to the Clubhouse we rely on you, the Members, to protect your property by ensuring that you always secure the premises immediately after use. These instance have increased this year and we must remind you all that with Stansgate being so remotely situated it is not possible for a daily checking procedure to be established and I therefore appeal to you all to be extra careful to secure the Club after use.

The Committee, Sub-Comittees and volunteers have again worked hard in the service of the Club to provide Members with the facilities they have come to expect, including a galley, a bar, a well maintained Clubhouse, Dinghy Park & Moorings and busy Sailing & Social programmes. To all those who have helped to organise and provide these facilities may I say thank you on behalf of the Club and myself. It is perhaps an appropriate point to stress that these services are provided by voluntary help and that the same people cannot go on for ever and new helpers are always required and welcomed so as to spread the load during the year and across the years.

Claud Emerson has again served the the club exceedingly well during the past year and we must all be grateful to him fa the excellent state in which he maintains the Club and the Precincts.

This year there will be many changes on the Main Committee as a number of members have decided it is time to take a rest and let some new faces take a turn. At this point I would like to mention a few of the retiring members who I have been pleased to serve alongside and who will be taking a rest. These are Jill Savill, who after 2 years representing the ladies and running the Galley deserves a rest, Vic Tate who is stepping down to take a well earned rest from active office after championing the Cruiser's interests for many years. Ted Barnes, who has been keeper of the Coffers for the last 3 years, is recharging his calculator. Roy Battye, who after 3 years as Social Secretary, during which time not everything has gone his way, would now like to rest on his laurels after a highly successful Laying-Up-—Supper. The other retiring members Les Mendoza and Rob Swale have had less specific jobs but have nevertheless been valuable members of the Committee. The remainder of last year's Committee are offering themselves for re-election, To all of last year's Committee I express my grateful thanks for your support and service to the Club and to those carrying on "Good Luck".

Sailing highlights will be covered by our Sailing Secretary in his report but it would be remiss of me, as your Commodore, not to draw your attention to the contribution made by those members and friends in the race’ box and resuce boats who make the racing possible each week and express our gratitude. Also the cadets, who have sailed so enthusiastically again this year, and under the shippership of Rick Anstey and Colin Leveridge have worked on their Elementany and Intermediate Day Boat Certificatesto achieve a high level of sucess, are to be congratulated.

In making my report this year I must refer to the Annual Regatta of the Marconi Sailing Club. Many of you may not realise that I was Sailing and Regatta Secretary at the time the first one was put on some 12 years ago at the request of a number of the local Clubs who, because the date of the Bank Holiday was at that time fixed by the moon, and not the Government rarely had any water for sailing during the weekend. During my years in Office I have seen this event grow to what it is today; the most popular event on the Blackwater and probably in the East Coast Area.

It has always had its problems, even from the first year it was run, but a true test of its popularity is the fact that sailors return each year for this one event. I sincerely believe it is an event which the Club should be proud to present and should make every effort to improve for the benefit of all keen racing sailors as open competition on our own waters offers unique opportunities to our members. An analysis of the classes sailed during the weekend shows that we have our own members sailing in about 80% of the classes.

Since all the discussion in the summer, the Committee have considered the various shades of opinion and have concluded that there is a very strong body of opinion among the active racing members, whose families, incidently provide the majority .of the help, that the event should continue. We hear from neighbouring Clubs that there would be great disappointment if we did not offer our hospitality during this one weekend in the year and all those enquiring have been advised that the Committee believes there will be a Regatta in 1978.

During the year there has been a growing demand for Cruiser moorings and particularly for winter storage. Your committee recommended revised arrangements for this year, which will just about cope with the demand for 1977/78 winter, and have passed forward a recommendation to the new committee to review the situation for futue years during the early part of 1978.

-7-

Finally, as I retire from office I would like to say that I have been proud to be the Commodore of what must be classed as a very successful Club and to thank all with whom I have worked during my term of Office. I know you have spent many hours on the business of the Club during this time and we must all be grateful for this time voluntarily given to an activity which we all enjoy and in which we have a common interest. To you all I express my own and the Clubs appreciation.

After tonight you will have a new Commodore and I would ask you to give him your support and help so that he can undertake effectively the job for which he has volunteered to accept nomination, Ron you will certainly have my support and I wish you good luck and I hope you will enjoy your term of office as much as I have mine.

Thank you John Witter.

An experimental scheme of committee meetings was followed this year; with the Main Committee meeting every Second month and the Executive Committee meeting during the alternative months.

Those with drying moor- ings may of course also get a bonus from wave action which those permanently uflo.t don't receive. A CAUTIONARY TALE

A few weeks ago there was a lot of news concerning small fishing boats which were lost in mist and fog off the East Coasts and stretched the services of rescue facilities. The following story relates to a works colleague of mine.

Having gone out for the day with a friend who keeps his boat in Walton Backwaters a day's fishing was completed somewhere near the Medusa Buoy off Walton. The boat carried a compass and torch but not a lot more. The return passage, under outboard power was commenced in conditions of slight mist. The ownerimew the vacinity pretty well. Pye End Buoy came up through the mist, then No. 2 Buoy appeared. Stearing mainly by Compass due to the mist. At this point buoys
are closely spaced - everything should be fine. Compass bearing O.K. -— where
is the next buoy? Time passes - open sea — more time passes - and more — fuel
running low. Friend says we can't keep on like this - drop anchor. Kept warm
in small cabin - 2 adults - 2 young boys. A shore rescue service noticed
parked trailer and started searching.

Through mist my friend identifies Medusa buoy flashing. Darkness fall - good
torch curried, several pussing ships signalled — not seen. Eventually boat
passed close — flush S.0.5. —- its the lifeb.at - rescue. Marvellous attention
from the lifeboat crew, eventually everyone home safe and well.

Several days later small boy seen playing with magnets. Yes they were in his pocket that day. Do some tests, boy moves across cabin — compass swings about
120°.

Have your chidren got any magnets?

R. Fuller.

LIFEBOAT RESCUE AT STANSGATE - MAY 1977

The article below is reprinted from’ THE LIPTMBOAT journal. We happened to be at Stansgate that afternoon, finishing our fitting-out, and watched the whole affair, It was eerie, and perhaps a little sobering, to see red flares coming from Goldhanger Spit which is the sight of such innocent pursuits as our Mud Race. The rescued yachtsmen took advantage of our clubhouse for a ‘warm-up! and a cup of tea before going their own way, Perhaps this is a good reminder that any of us may need the R.N.L.I. no matter how modest our voyaging.

"Rradwell Coastguard Mobile was in the vicinity of Stansgate on the afternoon of Friday, May 20, keeping watch over a number of yachts off Osea Island, when, at 1723, a yacht was seen to be heading for the sand spit at the eastern end of the island and a red flare was sighted. Life- boat attendance was requested and the honorary secretary of West Mersea ILB station immediately gave authority for maroons to be fired. Meanwhile, it appeared that a second yacht was altering course to go to the aid of the first, she also ran aground on the spit, at the north-eastern edge.

The wind was north east, strong force 6 gusting to gale force 8, and, with a strong ebb tide, the seas were heavy and short. Predicted high water at Rradwell was 1548. The weather was fine with fair visibility.

At 1732 West Mersea Atlantic 21 ILB launched on service, Once clear of the West Mersea approaches she had to reduce speed in the heavy seas, but she reached the 23' sloop"Contessa", the second grounding, at 1752. Approach to the casualty was difficult in the shallow water as the two streams of ebb tide around Osea Island, reaching a rate of 3 knots, were meeting and causing very heavy confused seas of up to 6 feet against the gale force north-easterily wind, One crew member boarded "Contessa" and an anchor was run into deep water by the IIB.

Roth this yacht and the first casualty, the 25' sloop "Lionheart", were chartered from Maldon, The two men in "Contessa's" crew of four were loath to leave until told of the continuing bad forecast and an estimated re- floating time at 0100, All four of the crew were then taken aboard the ILB and landed at Marconi Yacht (sic) Club, Stansgate, where the Coastguard mobile awaited them,

The Atlantic 21 then went on to "Lionheart", reaching her at 1807, After the ILB had run an anchor away for them, the yacht's four crew members were taken off, the transfer, once again, requiring careful manoeuvring: the four people were landed at Stansgate at 1830.

Before returning to station the ILB continued westward to warn other yachts to remain west of Osea Island. The 6-mile passage back eastwards was again made at reduced speed with the ILB leaving the water frequently in the heavy seas. She was refuelled and ready for service at 1922,

For this service a letter of appreciation signed by Captain Nigel Dixon, RN, Director of the Institution, was sent to helmsman James Clarke, Letters of thanks signed by Commander Bruce Cairns, Chief of Operations, were sent to Crew Members Graham Knott and David Mills.”

Ray and Maureen Ball

SAFETY AFLOAT

It i. the time of your when a reminder concerning the subject of safety is appropriate. When sailing on one's own be especially cautious and at other times at the club the following notes are reproduced for guidance:-

1) Officer of the Day

a) Responsible in the vicinity of the Club.
b) Snsure that the Rescue team have to their equipment and
are ferried to the bout(s).
c) Maintain radio contact with the bout. (This responsibility
may ve delegated tu the Race Officer.

Safety Afloat cont.

2) Race Officer

a) Check off the competitors at the start and as many times as is
practical during the race, Reprt any boats missing to the resuce crew.
b) Snsure that any boat not completing the course has returned to safety.

3) Rescue Crew

a) Check the boats sailing as often as is practical and if any are missing
confirm threar whereabouts.
b) When the racing has got under way take up station near the gybe mark
in heavy weather or downtide in very light weather. In medium conditions a central position may be chosen,

4) Members

a) Ensure personal equipment and bout is adequate for the conditions. If
the weather is such that you will not be able to cope do not venture out, ask if in doubt.
b) If, however you do require assistance on the water, stay with the boat
and wave both urms up and down. Do nut use more energy the n can be helped and drop anchor if in danger of drifting away.
c) If racing sign off immediately afterwards, this is most important when
retiring.

John Weedon

Continuing the log of ‘Ace of Diamonds’, Summer Cruise 1977

Tuesday 26th Julye

Wind still N.W. Force 5 which is making the anchorage uncomfortable. Wendy took Rachel and Philip ashore whilst Andrew had his morning sleep. At the turn of the tide we motored up to Waldringfield where we found a mooring to pick up, with the advise of the "Fairways attendant", opposite the Waldringfield S.C. Jetty which has a freshwater tap at the top end.

The Mirror was rigged after lunch and we spent the afternoon sailing it
around.

In the evening Rachel, Philip and I took the Avon behind the island at Waldringfield and put out our drift net. I had just been asked how we would know if we had caught anything when the floats begin Bobing up and down frantically, hauling in the net we found we had caught five Mullet and one Jobe, all in about five minutes. This beats rod and line for productivity Fishing was stopped then as we had more than enough to eat.

Wednesday 27th July.

Went on shore to collect stores from the shop at Waldringfield, which is very well stocked, had some liquid sustenance from the Maytree and returned to the boat for a fish lunch, sailed in the Mirror with the children during the afternoon.

We debated whether to go up to Woodbridge on the evening tide but de- cided to do this tomorrow morning, at which point the owner of the mooring rowed by and said that he would like it back in a couple of hourse Decission reversed and we motored up to the marina at Woodbridge arriving about 21.00.

Thursday 2Sth July.

The day started with an unpleasant drizzle which persisted whilst we went into the town which we find fascinating.

The facilities at the Marina have been improved, since our last visit in 1975, with the addition of a toilet block with showers which we found were kept clean and had a good supply of hot water.

We met Peter Hammer, his wife and brother-in-law in the afternoon, they were over on holiday from Holland in the boat knepie II which was a Deb 535- They were very enthusiastic ..bout the quality of British:boats and gear but were dismayed at the lack of stock held by chandlers as they were undble to buy several items they wanted.

Priday <oth July.

We all went to the swimmin:; pool this mornings it t& an excellent pool and for those who don't know, issited just beyond the railway station. The weather is brighter now but the wind is still strong so we will stay a few days more. The chidren are making friends and I ave been varnishing, fitting out has to be done when possible, The evening was spent on Knepie II.

tachel and I took the Mirror out of the marina and sailed up to Wilford Bridge, this is something I have wanted to do for several years but haven't found time before.

We met Alan and Were Jupp, from liersea today. They had brought Pelican, Jack sates last boat, up from Nersea for the first time and were enjoying their journey despite seasickness amongst the crew.

Knepie II left gm the tide bound for Holland having obtained a reasonable forcast for the tripe

We spent the evening on board with Alan and Were.

Sunday jist July.

I finished some varmmishing and the children were playing with Pelican's crew and Isobelle Deveedt from Palanis II, a Belgian boat belonging to her parents Ian and Hilda.

We took a walk in the afternoon along to the playing field behind Eversons boat yard and then onto a ‘green lane' which led down to the river near Kyson quay and we returned along the sea walle

In the evening we went aboard Palanis II, Ian is an architect and he also likes to paint and were show some beautiful water colours of the Woodbridge river area.

Monday ist August.

The weather had now improved and we left the marina at 12.45 with a gentle S.W. breeze to go back to the rocks where the children went swin- ing and looking for sharks teeth and were lucky enough to find half a
dozene

Pelican and Palanis II came down to join us and in the evening we had an enjoyable barb-que on the beach. We decided that tomorrow we would all go round to Woolvastone on the River Orwell.

CRUISER FLEET NEWS

Now that laying up has more or less finished and many of us have taken @ look at or even taken up our moorings, there is @ good opportunity to check over these vital items of equipment. A word of guidance might be useful regarding what is good practice for moorings.

A point often misunderstood with ground tackle is that electrolytic corrosion
can be our worst enemy - far worse than abrasion and rust. The worst thing
you can possibly do to a mooring chain is to put stainless steel wire onto your shackles. The combination of stainless steel and ordinary steel or iron produces an electrolytic cell which will rapidly destroy the shackle. Many an old hand has taken up his maring, found the shackle pins to be floating, held only by the wire and then said to others — "What a good thing I wired it or the pin would have fallen out". Poppycock!: If he hadn't made an electrolytic cell the pin and shackle would have been as sound as any other part of the chain. If you feel you must wire your shackles then the wire must be compatible with the chain and shackle. Galvanised iron wire does no harm but may not last very long. wonel will last forever but will cause just a little corrosion. I suppose belt and braces technique would
be to put two shackles at every joint if the chain would accept them - I
know which one would be in perfect condition at next inspection - the un-
wired one!

Finally on moorings - for anyone putting down new chain - the major cause of wear
is movement between the links and the best investment is to put down the heaviest chain you can get. It will always move less and so wear less than a lighter chain, and when it has eventually worn a little will shill be stronger and much heavier. However, movement causing abrasion is always more critical than simple rusting so it would be a waste of money to pay
the extra for galvanised chain - the zine coating will be removed in the
first few weeks. The only exception is if you put a foot or so of chain on deck where you don't want rust marks.

When it comes to wire rigging the situation is completely different. One hopes the rigging is not immersed continuously in water and so the electrolytic business is not quite so important though must not be forgotten. On the other hand rigging shakes in the wind and I fvel wiring is most important. Stainless rigginy needs monel shackle wire. For galvanised rigging gal- vanised rigging in a mixture of boiled linseed oil and white spirit, then hang it ap in the garage to dry. It should then last at least as long as stainless, which some people say can be brittle.

Finally, if you are still with me, an interesting observation on the above subject. If you have any assemblies of stainless steel, such as certain putley blocks for example, take a close look and see the rust forming at the junctions between two different samples of stainless steel’.

See you at the Generals Arms on the 1st Wednesday.

Russ Fuller, Cruiser Fleet Captain.

Continuing the log of ‘Ace of Diamonds', Symmer Cruise 1977 (sorry Tony, I left you in Woodbridge in August Navigans:)

TUESDAY 2nd August

Up early, our baby alarm working to schedule, weather forcast was good and we were ready to leave as planned at 09.00. We beat down river with the last of the ebb and against the start of the flood to arrive out at the entrance about 2 hours after low water. We motored out of the Deben, Wendy throwing a well aimed line to Pelican, as she was having difficulty making over the tide, and we towed her out casting off after we had crossed the bar.
Sail was raised again and we had a most enjoyable sail into Harwich Harbour on into the River Orwell to Woolverstone where we found a berth in the marina along with Polaris 11 and Pelican.
We spent the evening in the Royal Harwich Y.C. who extended their usual pleasant welcome.

WEDNESDAY 3rd August

A large group set off this morning to walk along to Pin Mill and Chelmond- iston for stores, then we went into the Butt and Oyster for lunch which we thought was good value for money. In the evening we followed a path along the river as far as Freston Tower then turned inland on footpaths which finally led back to Wolverston. The crew became quieter and quieter the further we went. I would do this more often if I was fit enough.

THURSDAY 4th August

We had decided to go to Walton backwaters today with Pelican, Polaris 11's crew wanted to stay another dayand then all meet again in Brightlingsea on
Friday. Our intended 08.00 start was delayed due to fog until 10.00 which
meant we missed the ebb. We motored out of the marina and across the river While Wendy was hoisting the sails and telling me how near the shore was. I thought I knew better and we went aground. Soon off as the tide was now flooding. It took us five hours to reach Stone Point which brought home the lesson about working the tides.
The S.W. wind was now increasihg raising doubts about our Coastal passage tomorrow. Over a beer in the evening on ‘Ace’ with Alan and Vera we decided to listen to the 06.30 forecast tomoprow and decide then whether to go or not.
FRIDAY 5th August

06.30 forecast S.W. force 4-5 so we decided to go out and have a look. Weighed

anchor at 08.30. Sailed to Pye End buoy by 09.00 and were abeam of
Stone Banks buoy by 09.35. The seas were rough and with the prospect of a beat down the coast in wind over tide conditions we decided to turn and go back to Pin Mill. Pelican could be seen ahead beating on. (We learnt later that they turned and went back to Walton) Just into Harwich Harbour we met Polaris 11 beating out and they turned around to join us We picked up adjacent moorings at Pin Mill where we spent the rest of the day laying about. We decided to try again tomorrow.

SATURDAY 5th August.

06.30 forecast E to NE 4-5 occasional 6. As the wind was only about force 3 at present we decided to go as with luck we would be getting shelter from the shore further down the coast when we thought the wind would be strongest. Let go the mooring at 09.20 in company with Polaris 11. No.1 jib and main set. Left the Orwell at 16.10, worked the tides right this time!. Once out of Harwich Harbour we realised tthe wind was stronger than anticipated, ‘Ace's’ handling made it apparen that we must reef. Wendy volunteered, she would rather be on deck than " take the helm, I was unhappy about this as the waves were very steep about 6'-7' high, however in a joint effort we took down five rolls in the main and ‘Ace’ handled well again. The Naze Tower was abeam by 11-15 and as we were now runnin g the jib was taken down to atop it flogging. Clacton pier was abeam at 12.35 and the seas and wind were moderating. Past the Bench Head buoy at 14.15 and picked up our mooring buoy at 15.30. Todays trip had been an experience for us as the seas were the worst we had been in and I was please d with the perform ance of ‘Ace’ and her crew.

In conclusion we all felt our holiday cruise had been q pleasure, we hadn't covered a great distance but we had met some nice people, which is probably what a cruise is all about.

COMMODORE'S REPORT — 1976

It seems mo time at all since we met here last year, but during that time many things have happened. Not the least some 300 races have been sailed, excluding our Regatta, and many successful cruisers have been made on waters near and far.

When you get wrapped up in the organisation and management of the Club it is easy to forget that we all joined to enjoy ourselves and if your Commodore and Officers always seem to be pleading for help it is because the Committee is trying wry hard to provide you with the club it believes you want. They can only go so far, however, and if help is not sufficiently forthcoming some standards must decline.

J know from your very presence here tonight that those remarks do not apply to you. I certainly do not wish to imply that this year has not been anything other than successful or that the committee have in anyway been remiss. On the contrary they have all done sterling work and deserve the appreciation of us all.

I have however, detected a feeling that some of the enjoyment may have gone for that diminishing band of stalwarts who will always offer their services rather than see standards fall.

Nol the ladies of the galley are not paid staff‘ Nor do any other helpers have any special privileges. I believe we must all take heed of this warning and share
the work and responsibility willingly - it must be enjoyable Yor allt if you
have any views on how we could improve our organisation please tell your committee as they do need your support.

After that cry from the heart 1 shall confine myself to the huppenings of the year.

The lounge and exterior of the Clubhouse have been repainted. The lounge was decorated by our caretaker Claude Emerson who has again maintained the Club and its surroundings in a clean and tidy condition throughout the year. The lounge has been likened to an Art Gallery rather than a Sailing Club. They are nautical pictures after all but if anybody has any alternatives to offer lets ‘have them'.

It is our intention that Claude will complete the decoration of the changing rooms and corridors, this winter.

Warly in the year a severe storm damaged the sea wall and the site and the Clubhouse lower ground floor areas were flooded. Fortunately very little damage was caused, although the aver Boards equ. pment made rather a mess of the dinghy park. It was however a reminder of the power or the sea and the fact that the sea wall is only just high enought That is the reason why our newly aquired freezer cabinet is now standing in the lounge.

We have had several brushes with officialdomthis year. Following the publishing of the River Blackwater Survey we were approached by the Maldon District Council with a request for a licence fee for siting our concrete hard and scrubbing parts on ithe foreshore. The sum of money involved was quite modest, but as a number of clubs had received similar requests and most were not satisfied with the terms and conditions of the licence the matter was referred to B.a.C.S.).A. to investigate on everyones behalf. As a result of these investigations a new and more acceptable licence agreement is being drawn up.

Whilst on the subject of B.A.C.S.P.A. I must mention the able work done by Stan Allerton and Frank Savill who have only just relinquishec their positions of Ghairman and Secretary after 35 years -f hardwork. Stan has agreed to continue on the B.A.C.S.P.A. Committee as our representative and Frank has agreed to rejoin our

—- 4 —

Committee — a potential Flag Officer if ever I sa one’
In July we received another letter from the Council saying that Stansgate was situated in a zone on the Southof the Blackwater where Camping and Caravaning amongst other things was forbidden without specific Planni ng Permission to do report that we
so. Application was immediately made and I am pleased to be ableed,tobut have been granted permission for the 28 days per year we request only for a limited period until December 1941 when it will be necessary for us to re-apply. control our
It therefore behoves us to be very circumspect in how we regulate and Camping if we wish to retain this permission in 1982. There were several legal objections to our applications. Our Campin g mersea l Jim Coy, ably assisted by Corrinnehas laid the foundation for good campin g behavi our but next year we will need to be very careful.

Our immediate neighbour has complained that members, particu larly on busy camping weekends, trespass on her property. The Club has always enjoye d very good relations with its neighbours and I would ask you all to ensure that none of our members or visitors are allowed onto neighbouring land.
The River Blackwater has also become very popular as a potenti al Fishery for Oysters. The Committee have been watching developments very closely but so far nothing is planned which will prejudice our interests.
The Regatta is obviously the major event of the season. More races are sailed, more beer is drunk, more people visit the site than practically for all the rest gave rise to a record of the year put together, and the exceptionally fine weatheronslau attendance. The additional toilet facili ties surviv ed the get.

The Barbecue however saw the other extreme and for the first time in many years the rain came and many people stayed away. ‘This event require s almost as much physical effort from Club members as does the Regatts . The erectio n and removal next day of the Marquee, Bar, disco and barbecue scaffolding, equipment and coversnk isthea mamouth task for a social evening. I am convinced we could well re-the layout of this event and reduce the work load without detracting from the uniqueness of the occasion.

It was heartening to see the Cruiser Fleet and other social events taking place at Stansgate; it has always seemed a pity to me that we do not make greater use of our fine new Clubhouse on other than Sailing days.

The Sailing Programme will be reported on by our Sailing Secretary, but 1 shoulding like to take this opportunity to thank hi and all the Sailing team for organis such good sailing throughout the year.

The number of dinghy helms attending open meetings and winning glory for the
series,
Club has diminished considerably of late but support for the houevigorou particularly from our up and coming cadets has resulte d in very s and enthusiastic racing at the club. I chose those words carefull y as 1 believe our knowledge of the racing rules and procedures is a little sketchy at the moment but this I am sure will improve with training and experien It was certainl y most gratifying to see the Cruiser Racing Series really heginning to take off.
Our collegues from Marconi Avionics at Rochester visited in force again and came very close to beating us.

A significant milestone in the history of the club was reached at the Laying Up Supper when Sir Eric Eastwood resigned from the Presidency of the Club. A small parting gift was made on your behalf as a memento to 25 years in office, and the last act of the retiring Committee was to bestow Honary Life Membership onto Sir Eric and Lady Eastwood and we hope to see both of them at Stansg ate next
summer.

ai She

Our new president eleci Jack Pateman has made the journey from Kent to be with us tonight and I hope you will make him welcome.

Security has continued to be of increasing concern. The Clubhouse doors and windows, and the gateway are frequently left open. Several items of members property have been stolen. We must all take more pride in our Club and make sure that everything is secure before the site is left unattended — security must become a ritual. The gatelock was broken open mid-season and the code key stolen. In view of this and the increasing number of cards lost or not returned, the committee have decided to change the security codes and issue new card keys to all members as they renew next season. ‘The locks will be changed on March lst 1979.

As outlined in Nuvigans the Committee consider that it is now necessary to increase our subscriptions. The subs have remained unchan,:ed for the last 3 seasons and it is intended that the increases proposed will see us through a further 3 years.

The major item of expenditure will be the repair and resurfacing of the road. for the past few years we have done the absolute minimum amount of work on the road in case the Marina Project came into being. Whilst this may yet still happen the prospect becomes more and more unlikely as time goes by. The road can be left no longer without running the risk of rapid and serious, ieterioration and astronomical expense.

To patch and shingle only the bad areas will cost around £1,500 and to tar and shingle most of the road in about 2 years time will cost a further £2,000 and we have been advised that it would be prudent to consider resurfacing every 5 years or so to retain a waterproof layer on the surface. We must therefore be putting aside some £60 per year just for road maintenance. Whilst we have a reserve capable of funding the initial stages of this work, we believe that we must maintain a reserve of around £2,000 in order to preserve our independence and cope with those unexpected expenses which pop up from time to time. ‘The immediate provision of new radio equipment plus the prospect of an increased rental contribution to the M.A.S.C. make it necessary for us to raise an additional £1,200 per annum over the next 3 years. This is roughly equivalent to £3 per membership — still very good value I believe.

I cannot finish without making a special reference to our lady members. Can you imagine the Club without Jill, Margaret and the galley team, without Shirley or Navigans, without Joyce and Pat in the bar, without lady Race Officers, without our Wives and girlfriends to feed us when we return from sailing or load the stores if we are going cruising? I hopenot all of us take you too much for granted.

Finally I would like to offer my personal thanks to the retiring committee and to the many members who have helped make my year of office so enjoyable and inparticular to David Lawson and the social committee for the Laying Up Supper
arrangements.

THE NAUTICAL MILE

The length of a nautical mile in relation to navigation

When I was young, I looked out of the club windows across the marshes into the far distance and it seemed to me that the earth was flat. When I went to my first school, I told my teacher that the earth was flat. "No" she said, "That is not so} it is a sphere." "What does that mean?"”. "It means that it is round like a ball" I wrote that the earth was a sphere and they thought me so clever th t they sent me to Grammar school. I told the geography master that I knew that the earth was a sphere. "No" he said, "It is a spheroid". Wet does that mean?" "It means that it is slightly flattened at the Poles". I wrote down that the earth was a spheroid, and they thought me so clever that they put me in the sixth form. I told the Senior Geography master that I knew that the earth was a spheroid. "No" he said, "That is not se; it is an oblate spheroid! "What does that mean?" "It means that one Pole is flattened a bit more then the other". I wrote that the earth was an oblate spheroid and they thought me so clever that they sent me to University. I told my Tutor that I knew that the earth was an oblate spheroid. "No," s aid he, "That is not so; it is a geoid". "What does that mean?". "It means, earth shaped," He replied:

(Note:- Greek, Geios means "To do with the earth")

How does all this affect our navigation?

Although there are 360 degrees in a circle, because of the flattening of the earth at the poles, they are not all of the same length. At the equator their
length is 1842 metres, while at the poles, they are 1861 metres. However, the
Admiratly issued a notice to MarinersNo: 1518 in 1970 announcing that the
International nautical mile was precisely 1852 meters, which is, in fact, the length of a sea mile in latitude 45 degrees. When we wish to measure distance on our charts, we place our dividers along the (vertical) latitude and@le which caters for the variation in length at different latitudes and are therefore quite safe in taking one minute as being the length of a sea-mile for that
particular chart. In other words, we have no need to worry - all this has
been thoughtfully provided for on t e charts which we use.

Eric Payne.

The 1978 season saw two new fleets in the club, the 420 and Solo. These fheets
to date are totalling 14 & 17 respectively, with additions to both certain before the commencement of the 79 season.

The dinghy series last season saw averag@ entries for the Spring Series ranging from 3 for the Enterprise to 7.5 for the 420 & the Summer Series averaging between 3.5 for the Enterprise to 7.6 for the 420. The most popular races which were sched- uled during the season was the Wednesday Evening Races, these attracted a total number of 156 boats, averaging at 13 per race.

The Cruiser Barnacle Series has received anincreased interest last year, with four races scheduled. The rescue boat organisation during the past season has seen a great improvement under the auspicies of Norman Kerridge. SPRING SAILING

The calender on my kitéhen wall is trying to tell me that Spring isn't far away, while the appearance of paint and anti-foubing colourcharts and the smell of varnish emanating from the lounge shout out the fact that the fitting out has begun. In a few weeks time, amongst a melée of daffodils, Easter eggs, why haven't I washed the sails yet, and where oh where are all the East Coast charts, the sailing season will have begun again.
With this in mind, I thought members might welcome a couple of suggestions for trips at the beginning of the cruising season. During April and May, the weather can be a bit nippy and unreliable and a short sail with somewhere to go at the end and back,
of it is more appreciated by the family than roaring off to the Bench Head long. when everyone except Dad gets cold, wet and miserable and it all takes too

So, where to go, first there's Bradwell. A quick sail down river to the power
channel
station, turn right and you're there. A couple of points to mention, the and is very tortuous and should be negotiated with care. Follow the witheys makingbuoys, it is very easy to run aground on the mud banks. Excellent practise for a passage using the echo-sounder, 4 useful job for a junior crew member calling out the depth. Moorings are available in the creek and there is usually someone around to ask it it's O.K. to pick one up.

There is also the marina, convenient for taking on water and fuel, but it is expensive. For a warm welcome ashore you don't have to go far, just walk up the slipway and stop at the first building on’ the right, The Bradwell Quay Sailinga Club. Here, the majority of members are cruis@zsowners and although they have comprehensive, keen racing fleet, there are plenty of potters to exchange gossip with over a pint or two.

We called here during the autumn las$ year, and met Bill Basson, one of the founder members, who due to an injury received in the war, looks like a benevolent Captain Hook when he gives you a wave. We were invited to a "Pirate's Evening" and for a £1 a head, no charge for children, we had an excellent cold supper, and there was draft Abbott and a band as well. All very informal and pleasant. If you ike walking, it's . very pleasant to stroll round the village and if you really like walking you can go to St. Peter's on the Wall, the first church in England.

Another easily reached port of call is Heybridge Basin. Just leave the moorings and head up River towards Maldon and stop at the "Jolly Sailor". Here, one can lock into Heybridge Canal, although a few moorings are available on the river. The lock is small, but good practise with fenders and warps, if you are thinking of being adventerous and going foreign later in the season. It is good manners to let the lock-keeper, George Clarke, know you are coming if a few boats intend to go together.
Once safely moored up in the canal, and if you can get Dad out of the pub, put the outboard onto the stern of the tender and potter up the canal to Beeleigh. It's well worth the effort. The factories and cottages built by Bentalls at the turn of the century are reminders that Heybridge was then a thriving industrial community and not the rather sleepy backwater we know today. You pass around the back of Maldon alongside the golf course and then up to the first lock at Beeleigh. Here you can wander around the outskirts of the Abbey grounds or along the tiny country lanes edged with oak and horse chestnut trees’tn the meadows, beds of wild watercress grow, dark and green.

This trip is more fun in company, and ideal for children, big or amall, when you play dogems with one another or Trace someone along the tow path. You can even atop off at the shops and buy the odd Mars bar,

As I said previously, the idea of these two “excursions” is an hour or two's

tw

sailing for Dad, combined with an outing for the family. For all the inform- ation proper required, you should beg, borrow or buy a copy of Jack Coote's "Bast Coast Rivers". Bradwell Sailing Club produce a very useful chart showing the creek and it's entrance with all the relevant marks in full, which is well worth acquiring.

This article was written with new cruiser owners also in mind, who are about to discover the delights of sailing the Blackwater. May I wish everyone good sailing
in 1979.

I can't believe iti! It's snowing as I pen these notes, and the Regatta is only a few weeks away.

The bad weather has one compensation in that it delays a little longer, the resurfacing of the road, and so gives us time to finish clearing the road edges. The support for the working party called on Easter Saturday was dismal =— less than 20 people came, and half of those were youngsters. The farmer kept his promise to help by bull-dozing the worst of the overgrowth but the task can only be finished by hand. If everyone who attends the club over the next few weeks brings with them a fork, spade or shovel and spends just 20 to 30 minutes working the job will soon be donee. A job well done now will last for years. For those who are not sure just what is required I will explain.

The road, over its' entire length is edged with concrete. Grass and soil have gradually grown over the edge, both narrowing the road and preventing water from draining off the road into the verges and gullies. We need to remove all of this material, to fully expose the concrete road surface and edge. It is hard, but worthwhile work. So please help if you can. The O O D will advise if you are not certain what is needed. The section most in need of attention stretches from the second corner after the Eagle Gates entrance for some 300 yards towards the Rainbow Cottages.

1979 GILTONIAN WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP FOR 18FT SKIFFS

SYDNEY HARBOUR

Just before Christmas I received an invitation from the New South Wales 18 footers Sailing Club in Sydney, to participate in the forthcoming Giltonian World 18 foot Skiff Championship, to be sailed in the Harbour.

With snow lying thick on the ground I decided that, in spite of a very pregnant wife, and an imminent house move, this was an offer I couldn't refuse. Travelling expenses were to be met by British Airways, who had also chartered the Australian "Overseas Containers Limited" boat for the event — all I had to do was get in it and sail it. Unfortunately my crew once again were to be left behind. Sailing an Eighteen is very much coordinated teamwork by 3 specialists, all jobs are equi- important and a scratch Australian crew, however good, would not substitute for the 4 years that Bob Fawkes, David Elphinstone and myself have sailed together.

After the snow and 24 hours sitting in a 747, stepping into the Sydney sunshine was like stepping into Paradise. All the British team had arrived at least one week previously and had quite established suntans, made me feel like a maggot by compar-
ison’ After the initial Board of Control meeting - the Board governs the affairs of
the "Titles" and is comprised of the member clubs throughout the World, I went to see "British Airways". The boat was beautifully turned out sporting the British Airways logo lettering up the side in red and blue, and 8ft diameter smiling cartoon Jumbo's, B A's latest advertising gimmick, on the mainsails. The boat was of very
light wooden construction - about 160 lbs with rope and fittings, excellently built
using Cedar and Gaboon ply. A glance around the dinghy park however, showed that in the past year tremendous advancements have been made, particularly with plastics and foam on paper honeycomb cores. At Plymouth, all the Australian contingent with the exception of "Color 7" were wooden, now all the top twelve boats are plastic reinforced with aluminium "space" frames to take the stress points. Mechanical rig tensioning gear, has in many cases been dropped, in favour of hydraulic mast jacks. "Color 7" still retains a mechanical system at 64:1 on each shroud, but has boxed the whole tension system in along the hog in case one of the muscle boxes ‘explodes’ damaging someone's foot.

Masts are now moving aft, and so correspondingly are rudders, which are being slung from sponsors about 9" to 1' behind the transom, and of course, they're still getting
lighter - or so any true Australian Eighteen sailor would have you believe.

Ingenuity is the watchword. Simple ideas such as sprinkling sugar on to wet varnish or resin to create a nonslip finish, the sugar simply disolves away, leaving a rough finish, but no messy sand for fitting out next time round. "Clam Cleats" are extensively used (metal version), however the Australians streamline them by filing away unwanted metal and drilling lightening holes in them. Just a few grams saved, but the top racing is very, very close and no gear lightening is too much trouble.

Incentives to win are high, an Australian 18ft Champion is ranked among the leading sportsmen, and will undoubtedly be featured sometime on Television and in the papers. He also has to consider the new boat for the coming season, which may cost over
$35,000 (approx £18,700) for one year, poor results will mean the sponsor will either
pull out, or look for more promising materials - only the winners get publicity.

5

Innovation in the Eighteens, for many years was slow in coming. Like so many classes the crews were not prepared to look around for inspiration from other dinghy sailors and failed to take stock of the changing techniques.

Bruce Farr arrived on the scene in 1970 and developed a line of light weight, wooden, functional thoroughbreds for 3 handed sailing, 70 lbs lighter than anything designed before. Furthermore, the bouyancy incorporated into the hull shape of each design was geared to fit the crew weight expected to sail in the boat, along with the exact requirements and details for the sailplan and the rig change and wind speed.

Farr's designs reigned supreme for 5 World Championships until 18 year old Main Murray appeared with a radical, 10ft beamed boat, sponsored by Color 7 TV. The Murray/Color 7 combination have now won 3 World Titles in succession, and Murray has led the Eighteens from "night" into "day", by revolutionising construction methods and making the glass fibre/paper honeycomb core construction work. His designs are
faster than Farr's and carry incredible amounts of sail - almost as much as the old
4 handers. He is a crack 12 footer sailor (much harder to sail than an 18 footer), and bared his ideas on the radical Twelves. He incorporated high freeboard, hitherto frowned on because of the extra weight of higher sides, wide aft chines and a very 'U' shaped forward entry for improving "nose-dive" characteristics. Perhaps this progress is the good side of sport sponsorship, development has now reached fever pitch and the money is there to see new ideas succeed or fail, anyway, new ideas have
now come along to benefit all dinghy sailors - if they care to look that is, and
progress makes development in the 470 and Flying Dutchman look Medizwval.

I won't bore you with details of my efforts in Sydney, fact is we weren't so hot, but certainly one of the biggest problems for all competitors were the washes set up by the spectator craft. Hundreds of people turn out in craft of all shapes and sizes to watch the Eighteens. The water's natural wave pattern soon gets broken up into large confused On the fourth race British Airways was doing about 18 knots with the biggest Spinnaker set, and the crew all trapezeing ("three stringing under the biggy"
- Australian slang), when we happened upon two large converging washes. I had no
option but to steer for the centre of the subsequent eruption, only to find as we careered over the crest there was no water beyond, just a large trough. With nothing under the keel of course we just nosedived and that was that.

The following race we found ourselves on the wind with "ITEL Computers" just above us. Gear failure aboard "ITEL" caused her to capsize slowly, but as she did so her mast head picked up my trapeze wire. The next second I was hoisted 15ft in the air as the wire was pulled by British Airways across ITEL's mast head. I must have hit a shroud on the way up, as my face felt as if it would fall in two. With no one at the helm, and my Aussie crew, Phil and Les looking extremely worried, British Airways never faltered, and sailed straight and true. The next second I was back in the drink and swinging back to my position on the side. Undamaged, I might add!
However, while British Airways fuddled about, the real battle was between "Color 7", "Steelstocks" and "KB". The racing was filmed by the "Color 7" Helicopter and Launches, and we were able to view the smooth operations of the leaders on TV in the evening sport's bulletins.

I'm afraid to say that we in British Airways did not do so well, finishing 3rd out of the 4 British Skippers and 29th out of 34 overall, a result which will take a lot of living down. Entries were received from America, Italy, France, New Zealand, Australia and of course Great Britain, and the Eighteen now appears international if only in small quantities.

Bruce Long

Well the Regatta is behind us, and it would appear that an interesting time was had by all. Unfortunately due to many circumstances ranging from "No Petrol" to "Hay Fever Eyes" I opted out this year. Instead I packed boxes and cases and prepared to move — new address above.

COMMODORE
'S NOTES

The view was expressed to me quite recently that the discipline and involvement of Club Members is declining. My reaction to this was one of disbelief, fortunately, in view of the achievements of the past month. On reflection however, I feel certain that you must have some suggestions for improving the quality of our Club
- if so, please tell me, or any committee member, of your views.

One area where I believe that we can all help to make our surroundings more pleasant and hygenic is to take our personal litter and rubbish home with us. Also, as we are strictly a "Do it Yourself" organisation, if you see anything in need of cleaning or repair, please D I Y, help to get it done.

As I mentioned we have several achievements to our credit since I last wrote in
Navigans.

All those members and friends who helped in anyway towards the running of the Regatta have my grateful thanks, and they can take pride in the fact that it was a great success, despite the rain, mud and wind. Anybody who read their local newspaper will realise that we had several anxious moments, but good sense, fortune and humour prevailed throughout.

The Camping Week and Social Activities were well supported and the highlight of the final weekend was the visit by our President and his team from Rochester. We beat them again, of course, and it is rumoured that our President enjoyed himself so much that he decided to stay and guide our dinghy fleet through the fog at the Bench Head buoy = or was he lost too? Sorry Jack, Louise and I might never have made it back without you.

The road is being resurfaced as I write these notes, and I hope it will make driving to the Club more comfortable for several years to come.

Don't forget to let me have your views, but above all ENJOY YOUR SAILING.

Ron Greygoose
Commodore

REGATTA REPORT

As usual the Regatta, held over the Spring Bank Holiday weekend had it's fair? share of Wind, Rain, Beer and Social Activities. The Club received more than
250 visitors over the weekend, and there were 224 dinghies entered in races.

The Pennant race held on the Saturday, in aid of the R NL I, raised nearly £30.00, even though high winds — up to Force 6 = and choppy seas prevailed.

Sunday began with light winds, Force 2, and the day passed with frequent rain,
despite which sailing proceeded and 2 races were held.

Monday proved a little different, however. The morning race, with winds up to
Force 5, against a flood tide proved exhilarating, although a little wet for some. With an imminent Gale Face 7 forecast, the afternoons racing was unfortunately cancelled.

CRUISER FLEET NEWS

A question was raised recently concerning occasional use of the Club 14' Fisherman by Fleet Members for getting ashore.

Club Policy for the Fisherman is that it is a back up rescue vessel, and as such must always be under the direction of the OOD. However, the safety of the Cruiser Fleet is important and if, for example conditions are too bad to row the family ashore in the dinghy, then ask the OOD if you can borrow the Fisherman. Be prepared for delays however, as crews of upturned dinghys are at more immediate risk than the cruisers on the moorings.

Concerning safety, may I again remind members of the inadequacy of plastic row- locks. In my opinion they are unsafe for use at Stansgate.

Contrary to the above implications, we do of course get gentle conditions sometimes, so happy sailing everyone, see you on the water.

CRUISER RACING

Although we managed a trio of cruisers to run the ist Barnacle on 16 June, a postponement of only 15 minutes on the start, plus a wind change of 180 with the tide within a stones throw of Bench Head prevented everyone from making the mark, and so the race had to be abandoned. However, we had a jolly good sail, and this race will now take place at 1030 on Saturday 22 September.

The 2nd Barnacle on 2 July was also eventful. One cruiser helm arrived for the race and the sight of his cruiser reminded him that his main sail was still at Taylors at Maldon. This led to a 30 minute postponement which made the course of Herring Point via the Stumbles quite tense, and the beat down to Colliers Reach against the tide fairly challenging. In spite of a variety of start times due to the failure to recognise the start flag, the sailing committee assure me the race is valid, although I am slightly embarrassed to claim a win.

The moral so far is that we must try to start on time.
